News.title: Ann Widdecombe's family plan her funeral at famous Buckfast Abbey
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe's family plan her funeral at famous Buckfast Abbey

Ms Widdecombe was found dead in her home in Haytor, Devon, eight miles from the church site, which includes a working Benedictine monastery, on July 9. Police believe she died 24 hours earlier

View 3 Images Ms Widdecombe was a regular worshipper at Buckfast Abbey, eight miles from her home (Image: Western Morning News)

Ann Widdecombe's family are making arrangements to hold her funeral service at her beloved Buckfast Abbey, church bosses have revealed. The former Cabinet Minister and Reform UK spokesperson had attended the place of worship just three days before she died on July 8 and was a regular parishioner there.

A spokesperson for Buckfast Abbey said: "We are working closely with the family regarding funeral arrangements and will provide further information in due course, when appropriate. We respectfully ask that the family’s privacy is honoured as they make these arrangements."

The statement added: "Fr Abbot and the Monastic Community of Buckfast continue to hold Ann Widdecombe, her family and loved ones in our prayers during this difficult time. Fr Abbot and the Monastic Community are grateful for the many messages of sympathy and support that have been received."

View 3 Images The veteran politician died at her isolated home in Devon on July 8, police believe (Image: DevonLive)

Ann Widdecombe's family issues new statement after man charged with murder READ MORE :

Ann Widdecombe died after being hit on head 21 times with hammer, court hears as man appears on murder charge READ MORE :

On Thursday, Ms Widdecombe's family issued a statement announcing that a private funeral service will be held "in the coming weeks", "limited to those closest to Ann". They added: "A more public memorial will follow later in the year, the details of which will be released in due course." .

A Buckfast Abbey spokesperson today confirmed to the Mirror their statement relates to the private funeral service. They did not comment on when it is likely to take place.

Ms Widdecombe was found dead in her home in Haytor, Devon, eight miles from the church site, which includes a working Benedictine monastery, on July 9 - around 24 hours after police believe she died.

Police charged Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, South Yorks, with the murder of the former MP on Monday. He appeared in court where it was alleged Ms Widdecombe died after being hit with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch. A provisional trial date has been set for June 2027.

The hearing at Westminster Magistrates Court heard Ms Widdecombe was also tipped out of her chair and had her wallet taken during the attack before she was found the next day with head injuries at her remote bungalow on the edge of Dartmoor National Park.

View 3 Images Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, has been charged with Ms Widdecombe's murder

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the alarm was raised when Ms Widdecombe failed to appear for a video interview on Channel 5’s Matt Allwright show that lunchtime.

Producers tried to contact her over the next 24 hours before a gardener was asked to check on her, the court heard.

Article continues below

At an inquest in Exeter on Tuesday, Coroner Philip Spinney read a statement, which said: “Ms Widdecombe was located within her property. She was found to be unresponsive and with visible injuries. The precise cause of death is yet to be established.”

News.title: Second man killed in Huyton crash pictured as family pay tribute to son with 'heart of gold'
News.content:
Second man killed in Huyton crash pictured as family pay tribute to son with 'heart of gold'

The family of 23-year-old sports psychology student Ben Dooley have paid tribute to their beloved son after he was killed along with three other men following a collision on Liverpool Road on Friday

View 2 Images Demi Lea paid a heartfelt tribute to her brother Ben Dooley (Image: Supplied/Demi Lea)

A heartbroken family has paid tribute to a beloved son who died in a car crash in Merseyside alongside three other men.

‌



Ben Dooley, 23, tragically lost his life in the crash on Liverpool Road on Friday, July 24. Police said they were called to reports of a black Cupra crashed into a lamppost just before 2am. Four men, all in their 20s were pronounced dead at the scene, the force later confirmed.

‌



A 27-year-old man, a passenger in the car, was taken to hospital where he is believed to be in a stable condition, the Liverpool Echo reports. Ben's sister today shared tributes to the sports psychology student who loved playing football, paddle and darts and "lit up every room he was in".

‌



The keen gym-goer also enjoyed holidaying with family and going to festivals with his friends, she said.

In a heartbreaking tribute Ben’s mum Kerry said: “My son, my world, my best friend. It was me and you always. My life is ripped apart and I don’t know how I will do life without you. We did everything together.

"I’m waiting for you to walk through the door and say 'you ok mum?'. You were the kindest person I knew with a heart of gold. Do anything for anyone. Loved by everyone who met you. I can’t describe how much I will miss you, it hurts so much. Fly high my baby boy. I love you.”

‌



Ben's sister Demi issued a moving tribute saying: "Ben my little brother, my one and only sibling, the one who always gave me advice and looked out for me, the most caring, kindest person in the world , my heart is broken.

"Feels like a terrible dream, I miss you so much already, the laughs we had and all the memories I will cherish forever. Love you my brother till we meet again."

Demi said Ben was the heart of the family which included Roy, nephew Frankie, nan and grandad, nan Lorraine, uncle Kev, Deana, Georgia, Lucas and younger brother and sister Shay and Chloe.

‌



View 2 Images Craig Brady, 26, pictured with his older sister Kelsey Brady, has been named as one of the crash victims (Image: Kelsey Brady)

The first victim of the crash to be identified was Craig Brady, 26. He was from a large family and had seven siblings as well as two kids of his own, Phoebe, 5, and Archie, 3, with his partner Ellie Jones. His heartbroken older sister, Kelsey Brady said the family is struggling to come to terms with his death.

The 29-year-old, from Dovecot, said: "He was my best mate. He was two years younger than me. It was just me and him growing up until the rest were born, so I don't know life without him."

Article continues below

She continued: "He was amazing. He was a big man about 6ft 2 but he was just like a teddy bear. He really was the most loving person ever. His girlfriend is absolutely distraught. I think she still thinks he’s coming home. She doesn’t believe it.”

News.title: Nearly half of graduates who took out student loan would not do so again
News.content:
Nearly half of graduates who took out student loan would not do so again

EXCLUSIVE: Research by Obsurvant found only half felt properly informed when they chose to go, while just 54% felt their time at school had prepared them for big financial decisions

View 2 Images Research by Obsurvant found only half felt properly informed when they chose to go (Image: PA)

Nearly half of graduates who took out a student loan would not do so if they had their time again, new polling has revealed.

‌



Research by Obsurvant found only half felt properly informed when they chose to go, while just 54% felt their time at university had prepared them for big financial decisions.

‌



The data also found confidence with numbers was the single biggest factor shaping how informed students felt, with 72% of those who felt “strongly confident” about maths saying they felt informed about the long-term cost of their loan, compared to 21% who were unconfident.

‌



Universities can currently charge a maximum yearly tuition fee of £9,535 for standard full-time courses. Last year the Government announced tuition fees will increase in line with inflation for the next two years, meaning fees are on course to be closer to £10,000.

Earlier this year the National Union of Students (NUS) likened the Government to a "loan shark" as students were "mis-sold mortgage-sized debts that politicians can raise repayments on at the drop of a hat".

Andy Burnham's Chancellor faces huge student loan demand to stop graduate misery READ MORE :

UK's biggest student landlord forced to react as young people stay at home READ MORE :

View 2 Images Universities can currently charge a maximum yearly tuition fee of £9,535 for standard full-time courses (Image: Getty)

‌



Lord Agnew, former Treasury minister and Chair of the Numeracy for Life Committee, said: "Nearly half of borrowers now say they wish they had never taken out their student loan, and confidence with numbers is the clearest reason why: those let down by their school maths were far more likely to be in the dark about the true cost of their debt.

“That is the Innumeracy Tax: a charge levied not on income or spending, but on the people least equipped to spot it, paid in decades of repayments they never understood. This is not a theoretical problem.

“Each September, another wave of eighteen-year-olds puts their name to the biggest financial commitment of their young lives, without ever having been shown how to weigh up what it will actually cost them.

‌



“For some, the gamble pays off. But far too many find themselves, a few years on, saddled with repayments stretching towards retirement and a qualification that has not opened the doors they were told it would."

It comes amid controversy over how student loans in England are sold to teenagers. Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert, has repeatedly described Plan 2 student loans as a “breach of contract”.

Graduates who took out a student loan between September 2012 and July 2023 pay back 9% of everything they earn over £29,385.

Article continues below

This threshold will now be frozen from 2027 until 2030, instead of being uprated annually in line with earnings as was promised when Plan 2 loans were first announced in 2010.

News.title: Police looking for biker after man 'exposes himself' in Bradford
News.content:
Police looking for biker after man 'exposes himself' in Bradford

West Yorkshire Police released CCTV pictures of a motorbike rider they wish to speak to following an incident of exposure which is reported to have occurred on Wilson Road, Wyke in Bradford

View 2 Images Police are looking for a biker after a man exposed himself in Bradford (Image: West Yorkshire Police)

Police are hunting a motorcyclist after a man exposed himself in broad daylight in Bradford.

Cops are looking to speak with the biker as part of an ongoing investigation, they said, following the incident on Wilson Road, Wyke, on the southern outskirts of the city.

West Yorkshire Police have released several CCTV images of a motorcyclist who they are looking for following the incident.

The force has now appealed for the public’s help in tracking down the biker. It follows an incident of exposure which is reported to have occurred at 4.50pm on Sunday, July 12, Yorkshire Live reports.

View 2 Images The incident of exposure is reported to have occurred on Wilson Road, Wyke

Article continues below

The man is wearing a helmet in the images, but police hope that someone may recognise him from his general build, clothing, and bike.

The motorcyclist, or anyone with information about his identity, is asked to contact Bradford Adult Safeguarding online or by calling 101, quoting crime reference 13260396146.

News.title: 'Really scary' Derbyshire wildfire burns for more than a MONTH as UK firefighters 'pushed to near limits'
News.content:
'Really scary' Derbyshire wildfire burns for more than a MONTH as UK firefighters 'pushed to near limits'

The Tintwistle Moor fire has burned across Derbyshire's Peak District and was declared a major incident on July 13, leading to firefighters being drafted in to help from across the country

View 3 Images Firefighters have been drafted from across the country to help deal with the fire (Image: Men Media)

A major wildfire has continued to rage near Glossop in Derbyshire, pushing the nation's firefighters to their limits.

‌



The Tintwistle Moor fire has burned some 1,630 in the Derbyshire's Peak District since it began on June 24. It was declared a major incident on July 13 with firefighters being drafted across the country to help contain the monster blaze.

‌



But the sheer scale of the fire has pushed firefighters to their limits and has been a huge drain on resources. Clive Stanbrook, the deputy chief officer for Derbyshire Fire and Rescue Service described the operation as being "complex and challenging".

‌



Firefighters said the scale of the fire led crews to divide the affected area into sectors, namely Didsbury Sector, Crowden Sector, Arnfield Sector, and Featherbed Moss Sector.

View 3 Images The monster blaze has burned some 1,630 in the Peak District (Image: Men Media)

‌



Essex explosion hurls photographer into door and blows in studio roof as fertiliser blast causes mayhem READ MORE :

"Around 65 firefighters from Derbyshire and across the UK, supported by partner organisations including the Fire Operations Group, are actively supporting the response to the Tintwistle Moor wildfire, with many more being rotated and mobilised when required," Stanbrook told the BBC. "Thanks to their hard work, and the support of many colleagues behind the scenes, significant progress has been made."

Dr Kirsten Lees, an environmental sciences lecturer, who specialises in zero carbon at the University of Derby told the BBC that Tintwistle is one of the biggest wildfires seen in England and there is no sign it is ending soon. She added: "Honestly, it's upsetting and it's really scary... My estimate is that it is about the size of a small town. As this is not out yet, we don't know how much bigger it's going to get."

View 3 Images The fire has raged for more than a month (Image: Men Media)

Article continues below

Rob Kenning, a ranger team manager for the Peak District National Park Authority, said it had been trialling having a seasonal ranger to patrol in the evenings in a bid to prevent wildfires in areas likely to attract tourists in the summer months. He said council officers have started to fine people £1,000 who use barbeques in areas of the Peak District.

But there are other areas in the country that are experiencing massive wildfires. The Fire Brigades Union said some 40,000 hectares have been burned in the past year across 1,000 incidents.

In 2026, fire and rescue services in England and Wales have responded to 342 wildfires up to July 6, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council. The Fire Brigades Union has since urged the government to convene a summit to build resilience to further fires and to recruit 5,000 more firefighters across the country.

News.title: Europe wildfire declared emergency with 270,000 people evacuated and fire closing in on Bordeaux
News.content:
Europe wildfire declared emergency with 270,000 people evacuated and fire closing in on Bordeaux

Some 270,000 people have been forced to evacuate parts of Western France and central Spain - while a major incident has been declared in the Cairngorms National Park

View 7 Images Clouds of smoke descend on a campsite in Biscarrosse, south-west France

British holidaymakers have described running for their lives just yards from a raging wildfire.

‌



The terrifying scenes come as 270,000 people have been forced to flee as blazes continue to rip through parts of Southern Europe. Fire crews on Saturday were braced to drop fire-busting chemicals from a cargo plane in the Gironde region in Western France, where an inferno has been roaring since Wednesday.

‌



And with the wind direction shifting, officials fear the flames are moving dangerously close to the nearby city of Bordeaux. Authorities have ordered people between the fire and the city to evacuate, including from parts of western suburbs and other towns and villages. The French military have been drafted in to help and the Spanish government has declared a national emergency.

‌



View 7 Images Firefighters deployed to battle a wildfire spreading in Lege-Cap-Ferret, south-western France (Image: DAMIEN REMBERT/HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Among those caught up was Brit David Morton and his family, who came within 500 yards of the main fire in Cap Ferret peninsula.

He said: “The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point. Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula. We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car.”

‌



View 7 Images David Morton and his family on holiday in France

Zac Morrison, 21, described similarly dramatic scenes. We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door – it was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything,” said Zac, from London. “Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead – there’s people on the beach here with their suitcases. I’ve heard about houses burning in just an hour, it’s scary but sadly people here are getting used to it.”

Other Brits have moved to different areas in France to continue their hols. Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born. He said: “You wouldn’t believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 10pm.

‌



View 7 Images Flames approach a house with a swimming pool in Spain (Image: Getty Images)

While the wildfires show no sign of slowing, the Foreign Office last night chose not to impose warings against travel to France or Spain. France’s minister for international partnerships Éléonore Caroit told tourists: “You have entire areas that are fine, you’re seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.

“I’m in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans. But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening.”

‌



View 7 Images Exactly where is most likely to see wildfires in Europe (Image: Forest-fire.emergency)

In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging. But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles west of the Spanish capital. The city’s regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso said it was the “worst fire in the history of the region.”

View 7 Images Dozens of firefighters set up their equipment on a support line between villages around Bordeaux (Image: Astrid Lagougne/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Successive heatwaves with record-shattering temperatures have turned forests and scrublands into tinderboxes. Fires have burned 130,000 hectares of forest already this year in Spain, an area the size of Rome.

Other European nations are stepping into help, with Italy, Greece, the Netherlands, Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic and Slovakia already providing water-dumping planes and helicopters to the Spanish and French fire fronts.

View 7 Images A fire breaks out in a forest about 80km west of Madrid (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Things are burning closer to home too, as emergency services continue to battle a blaze in the Cairngorms National Park. The fire has now been declared a major incident, and smoke could be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen.

Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney said it is “essential people avoid the affected areas,” adding: “The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least. Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed.”

Wildfires right now

News.title: 'We are going to get Britain believing again - and bring back hope'
News.content:
'We are going to get Britain believing again - and bring back hope'

'Whether someone gets the chance to get back on their feet says something about who we are, it says something about the country we’re trying to build', Prime Minister Andy Burnham writes

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said he is used to people telling him things can't be done (Image: Lauren Hurley / No 10 Downing Street)

I’m used to people telling me things can’t be done. They said it about reopening the Hillsborough inquiry. They said it about re-regulating buses in Manchester. And now they’re saying it about taking power out of Westminster too.

‌



I’m sure I’ll keep hearing it. But if I’ve learnt anything from my time in politics, it’s that “it can’t be done” is usually just another way of saying “we’ve stopped trying”. And this week we’ve shown what’s possible when we don’t accept that as an answer.

‌



Our work started where it should: rough sleeping. On day one, we committed to ending it. Not reducing it. Not managing it. Ending it. Because government after government has treated it like some fact of life – something you just step around rather than solve.

‌



I won’t have that. Yes, there will always be people who fall on hard times. Life doesn’t always go to plan. But whether someone gets the chance to get back on their feet says something about who we are. It says something about the country we’re trying to build.

Andy Burnham urged to create dedicated homeless unit in Downing Street to end rough sleeping READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham inside No 10 North on the opening day (Image: Christopher Furlong/PA Wire)

I want Britain to be a country where nobody is written off. Where everyone is treated with respect no matter who they are or what they’ve been through. And where the government doesn’t avoid a problem because it’s difficult, but rolls up its sleeves and gets to work.

‌



Care of people. That’s what drove every decision I made as Mayor. And it’ll drive every choice I make as your Prime Minister.

We’re bringing that same attitude to the cost of living. Because, for too many families, life has become a constant calculation. Can we afford to put the heating on? Can we make that journey into town? Can we stretch things to the end of the month?

I want people to stop worrying and start feeling hopeful about what’s coming next. I want them to start to believe in Britain again. But I can't ask people to dream about the future when they’re struggling to make life work.

‌



So I’m making it a priority to give families a bit of breathing space. That’s what cutting VAT on electricity bills and capping bus fares at £2 is all about. It’s the first step in taking some of that pressure off people’s shoulders. It’s about giving people a moment to lift their head up and look forward again.

It’s a start. But I know it’s only that. Our job won’t be done until people aren’t just living - but living well. And that will take time and more than any one policy. In fact, it will take more than just Westminster.

Lasting change will only come when we stop tinkering with the system and accepting it’s broken. I’m not here to shift a few things round in Whitehall. We’ve tried that – and it doesn’t work. I’m here to shift power completely. I’m here to make sure that this is a country built to drive growth in every postcode.

‌



This is why one of my first decisions was to open No10 North. This is about rebalancing decision-making in Britain and bringing regeneration and reindustrialisation to every part of it. I want all places to have the power to improve - just as we have seen happen in Greater Manchester. I want all towns to be able to lift their high streets and feel proud of them again.

This is the thinking behind cutting business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues. Those businesses have had a tough time – and they deserve a bit of relief. But they’re also pillars of our communities. They bring us together – in good times and bad. And if we’re serious about rebuilding our towns, we have to get serious about the places that hold them together too.

It’s only been a week. But we’ve done two tax cuts. Lowered bills and fares. Shifted power. Backed our communities. And got on with the job.

Article continues below

I’m not pretending we’ve solved Britain’s problems. Far from it. But this week is a reminder that the government can make people’s lives that little bit easier. That politics can work for the people. And that we don’t have to settle for what others say is and isn’t possible.

Of course, there will still be those who say it can’t be done.

But we proved them wrong in Manchester. And we’re going to prove them wrong again on a bigger scale. We are going to get Britain believing again - and bring back hope.

News.title: Andy Burnham vows to build a Britain where 'nobody is written off'
News.content:
Andy Burnham vows to build a Britain where 'nobody is written off'

EXCLUSIVE: The former Greater Manchester Mayor claimed he was used to being told things can’t be done, and that the era of Government’s giving up trying to solve the issues impacting people was over

View 2 Images The PM wants to build a Britain where nobody is written off (Image: Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty v)

Andy Burnham has vowed to build a country where “nobody is written off” and everyone is treated with respect.

‌



The new PM swooped into power on Monday, and immediately moved to cut business rates for pubs, bring in a £2 cap on bus fares, and slash VAT on energy bills.

‌



In a pledge to go further, the former Greater Manchester Mayor claimed he was used to being told things can’t be done, and that the era of Government’s giving up trying to solve the issues impacting people was over.

‌



Writing for this newspaper, Mr Burnham claimed this week had shown how politicians could make lives a “little bit easier”, but that his job won’t be done until people aren’t just living, but “living well".

Andy Burnham urged to create dedicated homeless unit in Downing Street to end rough sleeping READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham wants to go further and faster on the big issues (Image: Ryan Jenkinson/PA Wire)

He said: "Life doesn’t always go to plan. But whether someone gets the chance to get back on their feet says something about who we are. It says something about the country we’re trying to build.

‌



“I want Britain to be a country where nobody is written off. Where everyone is treated with respect no matter who they are or what they’ve been through. And where the government doesn’t avoid a problem because it’s difficult, but rolls up its sleeves and gets to work.

“I want people to stop worrying and start feeling hopeful about what’s coming next. I want them to start to believe in Britain again. But I can't ask people to dream about the future when they’re struggling to make life work.

"Of course, there will still be those who say it can’t be done.

‌



"But we proved them wrong in Manchester. And we’re going to prove them wrong again on a bigger scale. We are going to get Britain believing again - and bring back hope."

In his first address outside Downing Street, Mr Burnham used his speech to promise an end to rough sleeping, and is expected to make a string of policy announcements in the coming weeks, including on social care.

Mr Burnham has tasked his new Cabinet with “getting that cost of living down”, and said he wants to give give voters breathing space.

Article continues below

A Downing Street source said: “He is constantly guided by the public mood, and what he thinks the public will want to do when he’s presented those challenges.

“His superpower is his ability to have his finger on the pulse, and know where people are on stuff.

“It’s been a whirlwind of a week, everybody has put an absolute shift in, but it’s felt like a joy to do it.”

News.title: Police investigate donations by Tice company to Reform UK
News.content:
Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.

Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of Â£250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election, when Tice was party chairman.

Tice has said the money was given to his firm by Fiona Cottrell, a significant donor to Reform UK and mother of a convicted fraudster with close links to Nigel Farage.

Tice said: "This is the first I have heard of it - if true why are the Met Police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?"

Earlier this month, the Times newspaper, external revealed that two donations given directly by Fiona Cottrell to Reform UK in May 2024 were being investigated by the Metropolitan Police.

That investigation relates to legislation governing elections, which bans concealing or disguising donations derived from an "impermissible" donor, or the use of "false" information about a donation including the amount or the identity of the donor.

The BBC has asked Fiona Cottrell for comment.

News.title: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape fires
News.content:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

News.title: Cairngorm residents say wildfire response 'too slow'
News.content:
People living in the Cairngorms have criticised the handling of a wildfire that has been burning for 10 days.

Residents were evacuated on Friday night after a change in weather sparked fears the blaze was moving towards the village of Nethy Bridge and a major incident was declared.

But locals said the move came too late, and that the Scottish government had been slow in scaling up the response to the incident.

The Cabinet Secretary for Justice, Neil Gray, said: "Throughout this significant incident, the government and the emergency services have given everything to ensuring that the fire is being addressed."

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg goes behind the scenes with Andy Burnham in his first week as PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has just completed his first week as prime minister, with new policy decisions being made and the much discussed No 10 North taking centre stage.

The BBC's Laura Kuenssberg met Burnham for his first sit-down interview since taking charge and got an exclusive behind the scenes look at the new Manchester office.

Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview will be available across BBC News on Sunday.

News.title: Sean McCann, Madeleine's brother, makes Commonwealths final
News.content:
Sean McCann - the younger brother of Madeleine McCann - qualified for Saturday's 400m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games by coming through his morning heat in Glasgow.

With parents Kate and Gerry in the stands, McCann finished fourth in his heat and crept into the final as the last of the eight qualifiers at his first major championships.

"I am buzzing," the 21-year-old said. "It wasn't really an expectation coming in given how strong the field was but delighted to see I have made it."

McCann, a chemical engineering student at Loughborough University where he trains, grew up in England but qualifies for Scotland through his father.

News.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous: What you had to say about wedding rule changes
News.content:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

News.title: How the mystery of dead animals dumped in villages led to a hidden world of illegal hunts
News.content:
On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

News.title: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenas
News.content:
Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.

At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.

But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.

At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.

Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.

"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.

"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."

The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.

"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.

"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' over Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
A major incident has been declared by emergency services as they continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

Some residents of the village of Nethy Bridge have been evacuated as a precaution.

But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The Scottish government said a fire break had been established around Nethy Bridge overnight and new fire breaks were being constructed.

First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience committee early on Saturday, said additional police and fire service resources were being deployed to assist with the evacuation.

He said that it was "essential people avoid the affected areas."

Swinney continued: "The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least.

"Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed."

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

News.title: Twenty firefighters taken to hospital after explosion in Essex
News.content:
Twenty firefighters were taken to hospital after a blaze ripped through an industrial unit and spread to a fertiliser store, triggering a major explosion.

The fire service declared a major incident on Friday, as more than 100 firefighters tackled the flames at Highlands Farm, near the village of Rettendon, Essex.

Three fire engines and two fire service cars were destroyed in the blaze.

Speaking at a media conference on Saturday, Rick Hylton, Essex's chief fire officer, praised the "remarkable professionalism, courage and commitment" of the fire crews.

News.title: Six men arrested over fatal stabbing in south London
News.content:
Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

Police were called at 04:37 BST following reports of a man attending hospital with a stab wound. He later died in hospital, the force said.

The incident is believed to have taken place around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street.

Police said four of the suspects also attended hospital with stab wounds and are continuing to receive treatment, although their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.

Alongside the four men in hospital â three aged 22 and one 24 â officers also arrested two further men, aged 27 and 23, at the hospital on suspicion of murder. They remain in police custody.

The Met said it understood the fatally injured man was stabbed at about 04:20. It added that officers were carrying out inquiries in and around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street to establish the full circumstances around the incident.

Det Ch Insp Sarah Lee, who is leading the investigation, said those in the area would continue to notice an increased police presence throughout Saturday.

The family of the man who died have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Supt Mark Gallacher, a policing lead for the area, described the incident as "tragic".

"We understand that this will cause concern among the local community and specialist detectives are doing everything possible to determine what has happened," he added.

The Met urged witnesses or people with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting reference 1474/25July.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
News.content:
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, AÃ©dÃ©n Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," AÃ©dÃ©n said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

News.title: Murder arrests after teen dies in Luton stabbing
News.content:
Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton.

Officers were called to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

The 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, said Bedfordshire Police.

One of the teenage boys, initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder, remains in police custody. The second boy is in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.

In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today".

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.

Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.

He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.

An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area.

"We would also like to remind the public to not share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for family involved, and also form a vital part of our police investigation," he said.

Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, also asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.

In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in.

"A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."

Raja urged the community to come together.

News.title: Letters by pre-Smiths Morrissey set for auction
News.content:
Letters written by a young Morrissey before he formed The Smiths are to go to auction where they are expected to sell for Â£22,000.

The archive of letters, written to Birmingham pen friend, Simon Pitt, who would go on to become the city's poet laureate, by the singer between the ages of 14 and 20, includes one in which Morrissey says "my ambition is to be a rock 'n' roll star or an actor, or a writer".

Another letter dated a number of weeks later adds: "I always said I was a genius, but nobody listened."

The letters, written between 1974 and 1979, are expected to fetch a combined Â£22,000 estimate when they go on sale in London.

News.title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
News.content:
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.

However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.

As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.

However, it may only be a temporary break.

Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.

Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.

This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.

They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

News.title: Horror fall overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths
News.content:
A sickening fall for England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

News.content:

More than 280,000 people have been forced to flee their homes as devastating wildfires rage across central Spain and southwestern France.

High winds have left firefighters struggling to battle flames as Spain declared a national emergency, with multiple fires merging outside Madrid.

France has deployed its army, with hundreds of soldiers joining efforts to contain the flames, which have ripped through a record 98,000 hectares since January.

On Saturday, authorities ordered the evacuation of large parts of Bordeaux’s suburbs, including the areas of Le Haillan, Eysines ​and Merignac.

“The fires ‌which are hitting our country have reached a level that has never ​been seen before,” French ‌prime minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Saturday.

Madrid’s regional president, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, said it was the “worst fire in the history of the region” and that conditions had been made worse by a combination of high temperatures, wind, and the merging of a number of fires.

open image in gallery Firefighters near Lacanau, southwestern France ( AP )

European Union countries have sent helicopters, planes and ground teams. These include 40 personnel from a Romanian forest fire team, two Portuguese and two Swedish Air Tractor planes, four helicopters – including two from Germany, one from the Czech Republic and one from Slovakia – and from Switzerland, four light helicopters and 30 ground personnel.

“Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a post on X.

Residents forced to evacuate have described apocalyptic scenes as they left their homes behind.

Marion Girault-Rime was awoken at around 4am on Friday by an emergency alert on her phone that instructed every citizen of the wealthy resort town of Lege-Cap Ferret to evacuate immediately.

She grabbed underwear and toothbrushes and, along with her daughter Mahau and boyfriend Tony, rushed to the car. “Luckily, my husband and son were not at home,” she said.

open image in gallery Marion Girault-Rime was forced to flee her home in the town of Lege-Cap Ferret ( Marion Girault-Rime/Quatre Histoires )

It was not long until they were overwhelmed by the smell of smoke as they joined hundreds of other cars fleeing the area.

Ms Girault-Rime was left speechless as cinders blew across the windscreen as though it was “raining ash”, with bright red flames erupting and a towering pillar of black smoke. The scene was “frightening and spectacular”, the 53-year-old told The Independent.

Colonel Romain Moutard, the deputy director of the Landes fire and rescue service, said the fire was “apocalyptic” and described the situation as “Dante-esque” as the flames spread.

The length of the final stage of the Tour de France has been shortened to allow police officers to be redeployed to battle the raging wildfires. The race’s final stage on Sunday will be reduced in length by a third, the Paris police department said, in an extraordinary measure that underscores the gravity of the fires.

The UK government is advising citizens in Spain to avoid travelling through affected areas of Madrid and Avila, while those in France are being told to follow the advice of local authorities. Prospective holidaymakers are advised to check with their accommodation or travel provider before making the journey.

A French foreign minister urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

open image in gallery Firefighters from Spain’s military emergencies unit battle flames in El Tiemblo, 80km west of Madrid ( AFP/Getty )

Wildfires are also affecting parts of Scotland, with a major incident declared in the Cairngorms national park.

More than 500 firefighters have been tackling the blaze, which has raged for the past 10 days and forced locals from their homes in the remote region.

Residents of Nethy Bridge, a Scottish village facing evacuation, are “frustrated” that the fire has not yet been brought under control.

“A lot of people are upset, angry and frustrated at the ongoing situation, because the Scottish government said a week ago [on Wednesday] that they had enough resources to deal with it, and they said on Thursday that the fire was contained,” said Sandy McCook, chair of the Nethy Bridge and Vicinity Community Council.

“My argument with that is, if you said the fire was contained and you had enough resources last Wednesday and Thursday, why are we still fighting it 10 days later, and it’s still running out of control? It is still not controlled in any way, shape or form.”

Mr McCook said that residents of the Cairngorms village could see large plumes of smoke from the wildfire on Friday before they were evacuated. He added: “Apocalyptic is the word for the pall of smoke that was on the go yesterday.”

open image in gallery Smoke rises from the wildfire in the Cairngorms national park on Saturday ( PA )

Scotland’s first minister John Swinney has said that the Cairngorms national park wildfire is still a “very serious situation”.

“Residents, businesses and people staying in the affected areas will understandably be very worried,” he added. “My thoughts are with them and I thank them for their understanding.

“With the fire changing to be in the direction of Nethy Bridge yesterday afternoon, a precautionary evacuation was put in place, and a fire break was successfully established overnight to protect the village.

“Police officers visited all properties in Nethy Bridge, and officers are in the village today to support residents.

“The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again, and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least. Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire, and new fire breaks constructed.”

The first minister said such situations can change “very quickly and dramatically”, reflecting the challenges faced by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Services and other responders.

Don’t count on a Pamela Anderson cameo in the Baywatch reboot.

Anderson, 59, rose to fame playing C.J. Parker on the 1990s series. A reboot in the works from Fox is slated to star Stephen Amell, Shay Mitchell and Brooks Nader.

When asked by Deadline if she would be making an appearance, Anderson responded: “No one’s reached out to me.”

“I don’t know much about it,” she continued. “I know that they were talking to my sons at some point about producing, but I don’t think they had a meeting of the minds. I’m not sure what happened there, but I wish them well.

Anderson maintained it was a “great job” and she “loved going to work every day on the beach.”

open image in gallery Pamela Anderson starred on ‘Baywatch’ in the 1990s ( Paramount Pictures )

“At the time, it taught me a lot, and it gave me worldwide exposure,” she said. “Everything I’ve done has led me to here, which is a blessing. But I have no plans of going back to Baywatch.”

Prodding further, Deadline asked if Anderson was curious at all about what had become of her Baywatch character. But Anderson said she’s not interested in returning to the past.

“Now is my time to really play with different characters. I don’t want to just fill my time until the end of the year. I have options, and some things I’m thinking about, including some theater again,” she hinted.

“I want to make really bold choices. I want to surprise people. I want to surprise myself. And so I’m trying to do things I haven’t done in the past.”

Baywatch first aired in 1989 and went on to become one of the most-watched television series in the world.

The original series starred David Hasselhoff and featured dozens of stars during its 12-year run, including Anderson, Jeremy Jackson, Michael Newman, Gregory Alan Williams, Nicole Eggert, Carmen Electra, and more.

open image in gallery Pamela Anderson has shared thoughts on the forthcoming ‘Baywatch’ reboot ( AFP/Getty )

The show was most recently revived as a movie in 2017, starring Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Zac Efron, and Alexandra Daddario.

The Baywatch reboot will be co-produced by Fox Entertainment and Fremantle, and will run for 12 episodes during the 2026-2027 broadcast season. Burn Notice creator Matt Nix will serve as showrunner.

In a statement to Variety, Michael Thorn, President of Fox Television Network, said: “In its first run, Baywatch defined an entire era of beach life and elevated lifeguards to an iconic status. Now, with our partners at Fremantle, this television juggernaut is set for a modern-day comeback.

“Together, Fox and Fremantle, along with Matt Nix and original co-creator Greg Bonann, will bring the California dream to a whole new generation of fans with fresh stories, rising stars and all the spectacle that make the Baywatch franchise a global sensation.”

News.title: Joshua vs Prenga LIVE: Start time, undercard and fight updates as ‘AJ’ warms up for Tyson Fury showdown
News.content:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury is officially signed – but what's the catch?

Anthony Joshua will fight Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia tonight, in a warm-up for his long-awaited clash with Tyson Fury.

Heavyweight star Joshua takes on Albanian unknown Prenga at Jeddah Superdome, one day after Fury’s bizarre, non-televised warm-up against Mariusz Wach in Thailand – which the “Gypsy King” won via seventh-round TKO.

Joshua, 36, last fought in December, stopping YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in six rounds, 10 days before surviving a fatal car crash in Nigeria, which claimed the lives of two of his teammates.

Should Joshua win here, he will share a ring with fellow Briton Fury later this year, potentially at Wembley Stadium in November – provided the ring walks begin at 2am GMT, according to Saudi matchmaker Turki Alalshikh.

It was a result known for two weeks, ever since Tadej Pogacar raised his arms atop the Tourmalet and smiled at the heavens, seizing the yellow jersey on stage six. It was a piece of history drafted long before the peloton reached the slopes of Alpe d’Huez on this final weekend.

Pogacar had increased his lead with victories on stage 10 and 14, and again at the Alpe’s summit on Friday. On Saturday, the Tour de France returned to Alpe d’Huez via the rarely used eastern back route, the Col de Sarenne. And although Pogacar couldn’t catch the breakaway to claim another stage, his name was already inscribed beside a new feat.

When he completes the race in Paris on Sunday, Pogacar will officially join an elite club of riders – Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain – to have won five yellow jerseys, leaving Chris Froome alone on four. At 27, Pogacar is the youngest to reach the tally, and on this evidence it would take something extraordinary – a freak injury, chronic boredom, perhaps an early retirement to take up stoneware pottery or tend to a smallholding – to prevent him winning a record-setting sixth and several more beyond.

This backdoor run up the Alpe was officially the queen stage of the 2026 Tour, featuring 5,000m of elevation gain over four Tour behemoths: the Croix de Fer, the Col du Telegraphe, the Col du Galibier and finally the Col de Sarenne. Pogacar led the hunt of the breakaway up the brutal hors categorie Sarenne, but the 3min 30sec gap was too much. A wild and often chaotic day of racing was won by Ecuador’s Richard Carapaz, wearing polka dots, who held off the chasers to claim his second stage in three days. It capped an impressive final week by Carapaz, who won the combativity award on four days and secured his place as King of the Mountains.

open image in gallery Tadej Pogacar celebrates wining stage 19 of the Tour de France ( AP )

Yet stage 19, a day earlier, was Pogacar’s trophy moment in the Alps, up the famous 21 hairpins of the Tour’s most iconic climb, the leaders winding through thick layers of giddy fans inches from their faces. Pogacar scaled the Alpe in 35min 27sec, breaking a 29-year-old record. France’s Lenny Martinez of Bahrain Victorious pushed him to the end but lost by six seconds and beat his handlebars in frustration.

Martinez got closer than most. Pogacar was able to pick stage wins almost at will, adding five to his collection here. Pogacar now has 26 career stage victories at the Tour, nine behind record-holder Mark Cavendish. A mark set by a prolific sprinter is being hauled in by a mountain monster.

There are still new frontiers of grand tour racing to breach. Pogacar is yet to win the Vuelta a Espana because he’s raced it only once, when he finished third in 2019. He is still five wins behind Merckx’s total of 11 grand tour titles, although the Spanish race could yet be added to his palmares by the end of the year.

But like so many of his rides, Pogacar is already out on his own as the greatest road cyclist of all time. Merckx admitted as much two years ago and the Slovenian has only got stronger, quicker, more dominant.

His consistency remains astonishing. Pogacar has started nine grand tours and finished all of them on the podium. From his first victory in one of cycling’s five Monument races, winning Liege-Bastogne-Liege in 2021, he has not finished outside the top five in any of the subsequent 21 races, crashing out only once and winning 13 times. Merckx has 19 Monument wins, another record that once seemed unfathomable and is now vulnerable.

But for all the numbers, records and statistics, perhaps it is Pogacar’s relationship with Jonas Vingegaard that feels particularly telling. Three years ago, Vingegaard crushed his rival in their mouthwatering Tour de France head-to-head, proving too strong in the high mountains to win the Tour by seven-and-a-half minutes. “I’m dead,” Pogacar famously said after a chastening stage-17 defeat in the Alps.

It was Vingegaard’s second successive yellow jersey, and it drew the pair level on two Tours each. For all Pogacar’s obvious superpowers, it seemed hard to picture how he might ever be able to withstand Vingegaard’s extreme strength on hot days at altitude, up in the clouds where Pogacar would sometimes wilt.

Does their rivalry even exist now? “Pogacar v Vingegaard” has its own Wikipedia page and it hasn’t had a fresh entry for two years. When Vingegaard crashed out on stage 15 of this race, Pogacar bemoaned the loss of his “friend”, the unintended subtext being that the quiet frost between two fierce opponents had long since thawed. What was meant to be a historic rivalry is now historical.

open image in gallery Tadej Pogacar crosses the finish line of stage 20 with teammate Isaac Del Toro ( Reuters )

There are no contenders to Pogacar’s crown. Remco Evenepoel finished this stage 20 in second place, which is where he will end the Tour on Sunday. The Belgian has transformed himself into an elite rider in the high mountains over the past two years and produced an outstanding performance in this Tour, yet he will still finish seven minutes behind the yellow jersey.

So Pogacar can spend a truncated stage 21 in Paris soaking in the moment after three hard weeks in the saddle, before considering what’s next. He may go for the missing Vuelta crown later this summer, before chasing a third successive world road-race title in Montreal in September. There are still mountains left to conquer, if Pogacar has the will to conquer them. And it is hard to imagine how anyone stops him.

News.title: Donald Trump tells reporters he’ll run for president again at White House correspondents’ dinner: ‘I’m gonna do it’
News.content:
Donald Trump hinted he will run for president again during a speech at the White House correspondents’ dinner on Friday (24 July).

Trump told reporters: “I'm pleased to announce my intention to, and this is somewhat of a scoop, my intention to run for a fourth term as president of the United States."

He then brought out a "Trump 2028" red cap and put it on.

Trump has continually made comments hinting at a third term in office, but an amendment to the Constitution prohibits anyone from serving for more than two terms.

Dawn French has issued a strongly worded plea urging people to “stop body shaming” apparently in response to comments surrounding Marie-France van Heel, the wife of prime minister Andy Burnham.

French, 68, shared a video of herself on Instagram on Friday (24 July), in which she hit out at “bullying” in regards to comments about a woman who she does not name.

The Vicar of Dibley star began: “So, a woman… a human normal woman standing there and all you can talk about is her dress and her body.”

“How dare you body shame her?” she continued. “This is a bright woman who speaks lots of languages; she’s run businesses; she’s faced challenges you wouldn’t even begin to imagine. You wouldn’t have the f***ing courage for it.”

“Stop it! Stop bullying people! It’s a human being with a human body!” she concluded.

French did not mince her words in the caption for her video either, writing: “STOP BODY SHAMING PEOPLE YOU UTTER C***SHRIMPS!!!”

The actor’s comments seem to be in response to the online conversation surrounding van Heel’s appearance after she joined her husband, the newly appointed prime minister, at Buckingham Palace for his meeting with King Charles.

Van Heel, known as Frankie, wore a pastel dress by British label Victoria Beckham for the occasion, sparking some comments about her appearance that have been described as “sexist” and “shameful”.

“I am HORRIFIED by the vitriol Andy Burnham’s wife is being subjected too,” one person commented on French’s Instagram post. Another added: “Seriously?? Am I right in thinking she's talking about the new prime ministers wife?! If so, Dawn is so right.”

Thousands of others also commented their support, including celebrities such as Paloma Faith, who wrote “Love you Dawn!” and Suranne Jones who added love heart emojis.

Both Vicky Pattinson and Bodyguard star Keeley Hawes commented several hand-clapping emojis.

Britain's newly appointed Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, and his wife, Marie-France van Heel, leave Buckingham Palace in London after an audience with King Charles ( Reuters )

Van Heel – who grew up in the Netherlands and Belgium – met Burnham while the two were studying at the University of Cambridge. They got married in 2000 and share a son, Jimmy, and two daughters, Rosie and Annie.

Having worked in marketing and strategy for several years, Van Heel was involved in the logo designs for the BBC and England Rugby.

Race organisers have shortened the finale of the Tour de France in Paris on Sunday, after security forces were redeployed away from the capital to help battle wildfires near Bordeaux.

The Tour de France traditionally finishes with a processional ride to the Champs-Elysees, where the winner of the yellow jersey is crowned.

The event draws tens of thousands of spectators to Paris, but security personnel initially planned to protect the race have now been sent south to support overwhelmed fire services.

It means the route will be reduced from 133km to 89km.

"As numerous wildfires are currently affecting ⁠France, particularly the ‌Gironde region, emergency services are fully mobilised to combat the blazes, while internal security ‌forces are working to secure ‌the affected areas and protect the population," the Paris police and the event's organisers said in ⁠a joint statement.

"In light of this, the Interior Ministry has decided to redeploy a portion of the internal security forces initially mobilised to ensure security for the final stage of the Tour de France, ‌in order to reinforce the response efforts in the areas affected by ‌the wildfires."

Fiirefighters spray water in a burning forest in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region ( AP )

Wildfires in Spain and south-west France, fanned by high winds, have led to widespread evacuation orders in and around Bordeaux, the country’s ninth-largest city. Nearly 200,000 people have been told to leave their homes across France and a further 73,000 in Spain.

“We expect a fight that will be long and very difficult,” said French interior minister Laurent Nunez, who added the government would “reorganise our response so we can fight from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux”.

The route alteration will not affect the result of the race’s general classification, after Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar effectively secured a record-equalling fifth yellow jersey on Saturday. Sunday’s stage 21 is a truce, contested only by a sprint finish, and will not change the overall standings.

News.title: Lewis Hamilton hit with another penalty in blow to Hungarian GP hopes
News.content:
Lewis Hamilton’s hopes of significantly denting Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead were dealt a blow after he was given a three-place grid penalty for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix.

Hamilton looked to be the man to beat heading into qualifying at the Hungaroring and was on course for a record 10th pole position here before a messy final few minutes cost him.

Ferrari looked well placed to end Mercedes’s run of having taken pole position for every grand prix this season. Instead, defending champion Lando Norris snuck in and took a superb pole for McLaren with a lap of 1min 17.207sec.

A poor final lap from Hamilton was compounded by a grid penalty for impeding the McLaren of Oscar Piastri, meaning the seven-time champion will start fourth for the race at one of his most favoured circuits. The only consolation was that Antonelli was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. The Italian will start seventh while Charles Leclerc, Hamilton’s team-mate, will be alongside Norris on the front row.

Heading into the final runs in Q3, Hamilton was 0.101sec ahead of Norris, but did not improve his time. Yet Norris, who was fastest in Q1 and Q2, and was the last man across the line in Q3, had no problem, beating Hamilton’s time by 0.012sec.

Hamilton was critical of his Ferrari team for sending him out first, a decision he said “shocked” him.

“I don’t know why we went first, that was a bit of a shock to me and I definitely wouldn’t have chosen to go first,” Hamilton said. “I had a clean out-lap and when I started my lap and already in turn one I had a snap [of oversteer], I was already a tenth down. The last lap was the worst lap of all... we clearly had the car to be on pole.”

Worse was on the way for Hamilton. The stewards later confirmed the three-place grid penalty to add to the disappointment of missing out on pole.

Replays showed a frustrated Piastri gesturing to Hamilton for blocking him at turn one, ruining the Australian’s final flying lap. Hamilton said he was unaware that Piastri was there, which was proved by video evidence that showed how much he impeded the McLaren. It would have been an easy decision for the stewards to make.

Newcastle will welcome Liverpool, with whom Keegan enjoyed success in the 1970s, to St James’ Park for their Premier League opener, and the two sides are in talks over a suitable pre-match tribute. Flowers, messages and mementos have been laid outside Newcastle’s ground since Keegan’s death on Monday, including a heartfelt message penned by fellow club legend Alan Shearer, which read: “I hope you realised how much you meant, to me, to this club, to everyone. Thank you does not seem enough. Rest In Peace Boss. Alan Shearer.”

With regards to the football, there is an acceptance among Newcastle supporters that, having finished 12th in the Premier League last season and lost Anthony Gordon, Kieran Trippier and Sandro Tonali, this is a summer of transition. The uncertainty surrounding the future of £100m-rated club captain Bruno Guimarães, who is on the radar of Arsenal, will be a concern; Newcastle will be keen to avoid a repeat of the furore that circled Alexander Isak’s departure last summer. Guimarães will join the team next week following his World Cup exploits with Brazil and is expected to take part in Newcastle’s La Manga training camp, which starts on July 31.

Summer signings Sean Steur and Ewen Jaouen were each handed 45 minutes in the behind-closed-doors victory over Darlington, during which Howe used different XIs for the two halves. Bazoumana Touré – the £50m winger acquired from Hoffenheim – is expected to feature today having returned from his post-World Cup holiday. Yesterday Newcastle announced the arrival of midfielder Aladji Bamba, the France youth international, from Monaco and he was immediately integrated into team training. There is every possibility that he will feature this afternoon. Gateshead this week announced two signings of their own, as Luke Supyk, the New Zealand Under-20 forward, agreed a two-year deal having scored three goals in pre-season as a trialist. Defender Jack Robinson also joined the club.

Kick-off is at 12.30pm.

News.title: How to choose a sports bra, with advice from a netball player, bra fitter and scientist
News.content:
How do you tell if a sports bra is the wrong size?

One of the biggest mistakes shoppers make is assuming that if a sports bra feels tight, that’s enough. In reality, support comes from the right fit rather than simply compressing your chest.

Cardwell advises thoroughly testing a sports bra by moving in it in the same way as you will during the sport you will be doing. “Your breasts don’t just move up and down,” she says. “They move all around – circles, up, down, left, right. We want to try and restrict that as much as possible, but not to the extreme where you’re not able to breathe.”

What is a high impact sports bra?

High-impact sports bras are designed for activities where your breasts experience the greatest movement, such as running, HIIT, tennis and netball. Their job is to minimise breast movement in every direction, helping reduce discomfort while allowing you to move more efficiently.

To measure how high-impact a sports bra is, Wakefield-Scurr asks women to run in a laboratory, both without a bra and while wearing different sports bras. “For a bra to be classed as high support, it has to reduce breast movement above certain thresholds,” she says. “If your breasts move 10 centimetres without a bra and five centimetres in a sports bra, that bra has reduced breast movement by 50 per cent.”

In the lab, Wakefield-Scurr and her team found that “if you run in low support compared with high support, you reduce your stride length by four centimetres. Four centimetres might not sound like a lot, but over the course of a marathon, those four centimetres add up to around a mile.” This proves that wearing a high-support bra doesn’t just keep you comfortable, but it can improve your athletic performance.

Cardwell, who wears a double G cup, says high-impact support has improved dramatically in recent years. “There has been a lot more research into high-impact sports bras, especially for larger-chested women.” She also warns against assuming that every sports bra offers the same level of support. “If it’s the same material as a smaller cup size, it’s probably not going to be sufficient for someone like me with double Gs.”

How often should you replace your sports bra?

There’s no set rule for replacing a sports bra, according to Wakefield-Scurr. This is because its lifespan depends more on how you care for it than how often you wear it. “The lifespan of a sports bra is affected more by how you wash and dry it than by how often you wear it,” she says. In one of her team’s studies, support dropped by around a third after 25 washes. “Always follow the washing instructions,” she advises. “You’d be surprised how many sports bras should be hand washed or washed at a lower temperature.”

Looking after your sports bra properly will help it last longer, but no bra lasts forever. Once the underband loses its elasticity or the support noticeably decreases, it’s time to replace it to ensure you have the right level of support.
