Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It will be possible to be at ringside to watch Tyson Fury box in Thailand this Friday evening and then attend Anthony Joshua’s fight in Saudi Arabia on Saturday night.

The Gypsy King will prove that by flying from Bangkok to Riyadh soon after his encounter with the veteran Mariusz Wach in time to see AJ take on somebody called Kristian Prenga.

It is safe to presume that precious few, if any, of their respective thousands of fans will join Fury on that journey or pitch up at either occasion. And not only because many of them will have sacrificed a year or two’s wages, perhaps their mortgages, maybe their marriages on England’s ill-fated World Cup expedition.

Even the rich boys on tour are likely to jib at forking out another small fortune to attend distant events which are fights in name only. Joshua’s flight booking gives the game away, as does the choice of venues. No capital cities this time. Fury goes through the motions in the notorious Thai beach resort of Pattaya. Joshua at Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah-on-sea.

Of course these are by way of preparation for them fighting each other in that forever awaited box-office boomer later this year. But to be honest these match-ups are not so much warm-ups as water-treaders. These opponents would be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners.

Describing Poland’s Mariusz Wach as a ring veteran is actually an understatement of his decline since he went into a world heavyweight title fight against Wladimir Klitschko as 27-0 unbeaten challenger. He not only lost that night in Germany 14 years ago but failed a drugs test which interrupted for two years his descent into today’s 39 wins, 13 defeats record.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

Tyson Fury is fighting Mariusz Wach in Bangkok on Friday as he prepares to secure a long-awaited bout with Joshua

The longer he drags on, as he approaches his 46th birthday, the more he becomes a useful punch-bag, given his masochistic capacity to absorb punches for several rounds. A painful service he has provided to a number of British heavyweights, Dillian Whyte, Frazer Clarke and Hughie Fury among them. This is so patently a mismatch that it is not being televised anywhere in the world, but being saved by Netflix to help promote Fury v Joshua when that finally comes around,

Two years ago Wach was flattened in as many rounds by our world heavyweight champion-in-waiting Moses Itauma. That mercifully swift ending made for more comfortable viewing than some of the pointless beatings he has taken down the years. Make it quick, Tyson.

Kristian Prenga is a virtually unknown entity outside his native Albania. He has passed almost equally unnoticed on undercards mostly around New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia and across the Canadian border since he emigrated to the US.

At least he is ten years younger than Wach and has 20 knock-out wins on his record against one points defeat. Not that you are likely to recognise any of the names on that dance card. Try Joey Dawejko, Aldo Callendar, Tim Chemelli, Willie Jake Jr, or the only man to beat him Giovanni Auriemma. Me neither. Most of them appear to have other jobs, such as barmen, bouncers or cab drivers.

Prenga, a pleasant enough feller, made the right noises at his London press conference: ‘A J and his team have made a mistake. They’ve overlooked my knock-out record. They’ve forgotten that he can no longer take a big punch like mine. Get ready for the world-wide shock which will change my life forever.’

He seems not to have noted that AJ is a former Olympic gold medallist and two-time world heavyweight champion. Nor that he is stepping into an altogether higher realm. Nor that Joshua is highly motivated emotionally by this being his first fight since his two close friends and team members were killed in a car crash in Africa which he was lucky to survive. ‘This is for them,’ he says. Get it done early, AJ. before he has a chance to land.

Fury is set to fly from Bangkok to Saudi Arabia to watch Joshua a day after his own fight

Then you can invite Fury to join you in the ring – ‘but don’t forget Tyson I’m the landlord for this one’ – so they can start the big sell.

November is the likely month for Fury v Joshua 1. Wembley the stadium of choice but only if Brent Council agree to lift their usual 11 pm curfew and permit it to be transmitted live to the American TV audience at somewhere between 2 am and 4 am London Sunday time.

So enormous will be the difference from this weekend that Fury is about to entertain no more than a thousand or so locals in a small, screened-off hall. He is donating the revenue from those tickets to good causes in Thailand, of which he has become fond as a training camp. It will be charity all-round. What with Wach and Prenga picking up probably the biggest purses of their lives for their roles as fall guys. But what if the inconceivable did happen?

Not only would the gigantic pay-days of Fury’s and Joshua’s last hurrah go down the drain but at least one or maybe both their careers would be terminated.

Don’t dare mention it.

*Fury v Wach this Friday night will be for private screening only.

*Joshua v Prenga will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view this Saturday night

*Fury v Joshua is expected to be televised live to Netflix subscribers in the early hours one Sunday morning in November

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua refuses to talk about Tyson Fury clash ahead of comeback fight against Kristian Prenga - with bout versus the Gypsy King on the cards if both stars win this weekend
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua shut down talk of Tyson Fury and insisted there is 'no future' beyond Saturday night unless he first gets the job done against Kristian Prenga in Jeddah.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain showdown with Fury is edging ever closer, with both heavyweights taking interim bouts this weekend before an expected blockbuster collision later this year.

Fury boxes Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday before Joshua makes his return against the heavy-hitting Albanian less than 24 hours later.

But despite the frenzy surrounding what could finally become one of British boxing's biggest-ever fights, Joshua made it clear he has no interest in looking past the man standing across the ring from him.

'Look, respect my opponent here,' Joshua said when questions during Thursday's press conference turned towards Fury.

'We don't want to talk about Tyson Fury. Respectfully, I have done all the media that I can about what the future holds but you know our focus is him and his team.

Anthony Joshua (left) is refusing to entertain talk of a clash with Tyson Fury ahead of his comeback fight

'We have been working since January, working hard, keeping my head down, aligned all my stars and I am fully focused.'

Joshua acknowledged the excitement surrounding what could await him if he comes through unscathed, but stressed that those conversations count for nothing unless he delivers in Saudi Arabia.

'I understand there is a big picture. The goal is to conquer the universe, right? But first we must conquer earth. My target is here.'

It is a mindset forged by the toughest period of his life.

Saturday marks Joshua's first appearance since stopping Jake Paul in Miami last December, just days before tragedy struck when close friends Latif 'Latz' Ayodele and Sina Ghami were killed in a car accident in Nigeria.

The devastating loss forced Joshua away from boxing as he grieved, with serious doubts over whether he would ever fight again.

Instead, he eventually returned to training and rebuilt towards what could become the defining final chapter of his career.

Victory over Prenga is expected to pave the way for the fight fans have demanded for more than a decade, but Joshua insists he cannot afford to think beyond the immediate task.

Fury (pictured) and Joshua are expected to clash this year but must first both win this weekend

'When you speak to me about what may lay ahead or I sit down in an office with Eddie (Hearn) and he presents to me what may lay ahead, it is a great opportunity for me to understand where this checkpoint takes me and what it leads me on to,' Joshua said.

'The reality of the matter is there is no universe, there is no future unless I get past this checkpoint on Saturday night.'

Prenga arrives in Jeddah with 20 knockouts to his name, although the Albanian has never shared the ring with an opponent anywhere near Joshua's calibre.

For the 35-year-old, however, Saturday represents the opportunity he has spent a lifetime chasing.

'I work all my life for this, I waited all my life for this and I hope I am going to show the world on Saturday who I am,' Prenga said.

Sports.title: 'I never considered walking away': ANTHONY JOSHUA opens up on his return to boxing in wake of car crash tragedy that killed two of his best friends - and reveals how the power of prayer spurred him on
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua never considered walking away.

Not after the darkest chapter of his life. Not after the unimaginable tragedy that left the boxing world reeling and forced him to confront grief far greater than any defeat inside the ring. And certainly not now, as he prepares to step through the ropes for the first time since the car accident that changed everything.

The crash near Lagos, Nigeria, late last year claimed the lives of Joshua's childhood friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, both 36. The pair had been part of his inner circle for decades, with Ghami serving as his strength coach and Ayodele as his personal trainer.

On Saturday night, Joshua returns to the ring in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, against Kristian Prenga. It is, in many ways, the beginning of a new chapter.

It is his second fight under Oleksandr Usyk's team, but the first after a full training camp together and the first real opportunity to showcase the technical improvements those around him insist have transformed his game. And, perhaps most importantly, it represents the first step towards the blockbuster showdown with Tyson Fury that British boxing has craved for years.

But before any of that, Joshua had to decide whether he even wanted to fight again.

That decision was never really a decision at all.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

He beat Jake Paul in Miami in December, but within days had lost two friends in a car crash

'I never considered walking away, because boxing is my purpose,' Joshua explains ahead of his comeback. 'It's not just about competing. Boxing is therapeutic as well. It gives me purpose.

'As fighters, that's what it gives us. When I'm boxing, I know I'm where I'm supposed to be. It's where I'm most comfortable.

'It gives me direction in life, and that's why I never really thought about walking away. I'm content. This is where I belong.'

Joshua speaks calmly. There is no bravado, no attempt to create headlines. Instead, there is a noticeable sense of perspective from a man who has spent the past year processing an experience no person should ever have to endure.

He is careful when discussing loss, and even more careful not to make himself the focus of it.

'Everyone deals with it differently,' he says. 'For me, I have to put my own emotions to one side because I focus on the parents.

'My emotions can come later, but I look at what the mums and dads are going through because that's what must be hardest.

'I don't make it about me. I make it about them. You have to keep your own emotions under control. That's not how everyone deals with it, but it's the best way for me. I need to be a good soldier. At the end of the day, it's not about me. It's much bigger than me.'

The 36-year-old says he never intended to walk away from boxing because it is his purpose

Daily Mail Sport's Charlotte Daly caught up with Joshua ahead of his return fight

Another source of strength has come from an unlikely place.

Joshua's move to train alongside former undisputed heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk has inevitably led to questions about technical improvements, but the biggest lesson he has taken from the Ukrainian has nothing to do with slipping punches or throwing combinations.

'The importance of prayer,' Joshua says without hesitation while speaking to The Daily Mail in Jeddah. 'Even if you're not deeply religious or don't follow one particular faith, prayer is important. It's something you can take into every training camp.'

Inside Usyk's camp, Joshua insists every aspect of his game has evolved, but one lesson stands above the rest.

'We'd be here all day talking about everything they've added to my game.

'The biggest thing is my relationship with hard work. You can be in one environment and think you're working hard, then you go into another environment and realise what you thought was hard actually isn't hard enough. It isn't good enough.

'So it's really changed my relationship with hard work. I want more from myself. I've put myself in an environment where I know I'll get more out of boxing because I've given more of myself to boxing. These guys push me harder than I was ever pushed before.'

Those working closest to Joshua believe his defence has improved dramatically since arriving in camp. Watching him spar, they see a more patient, more rounded heavyweight than the explosive Olympic champion who first burst onto the scene over a decade ago.

Joshua pictured moments after the tragic crash took place on a major road outside Lagos

Joshua pictured with friends Latif Ayodele (centre) and Sina Ghami who both died in the crash

Saturday offers the first glimpse of whether those improvements translate under the bright lights.

If Joshua comes through against Prenga, attention will inevitably turn to Fury.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain has flirted with becoming reality for years before collapsing at the negotiating table. Now, with both men rebuilding, it feels closer than ever.

Joshua knows Fury will be watching.

Asked what he wants his rival to think after seeing him back in action, Joshua smiles before delivering an answer that perfectly captures the confidence still burning beneath his measured exterior.

'This guy is a f***ing killer. He's a beast. He's strong. He's quick. He's got good footwork. He's got good defence and it's gonna be hard work trying to beat this guy. That's what I'd want him to think.'

Yet for all the excitement surrounding a potential meeting with Fury, Joshua refuses to place it above the moments that have already defined his career.

'It's a huge fight, but it's not for a world title, if I'm being completely honest,' he says.

Sina Ghami had worked with Joshua for years as his S&C coach and sports rehabilitation specialist, while Latif 'Latz' Ayodele became his PT after years of friendship

'It's a great achievement if I beat someone like Tyson Fury, but for me, nothing compares to becoming a world champion.

'You can beat great fighters, but it's different when you're beating them to become a world champion.'

In an era where some of boxing's biggest stars openly question the value of championship belts, Joshua remains unapologetically old school.

He points to changing financial realities, with fighters now earning fortunes outside the traditional title picture, but believes the sport's history still matters.

'There's a lot of talk nowadays about fighters saying belts don't matter anymore,' he says. 'People's attitudes are changing because there are different opportunities now. But personally, the heritage and history of boxing still means everything to me. You can't beat becoming a world champion, in my opinion...

'Unless someone dangles a big enough carrot in front of me... then f*** the belts.'

It draws a laugh, but the message is clear.

For now, Fury can wait. So can championship ambitions.

Joshua's focus is fixed solely on Prenga and proving that, after everything he has been through, he is still exactly where he believes he belongs.

Back in the ring. Back with purpose. And determined that the next chapter of his career is defined not by the tragedy behind him, but by the fights still to come.

Sports.title: Hamilton slapped with grid drop for impeding Piastri in F1 Hungarian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton has been handed a three-place grid drop for impeding McLaren driver Oscar Piastri in Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix qualifying.

Towards the end of the final Q3 shootout, Hamilton was driving slowly on the main straight while Piastri was approaching behind him on a flying lap.

Unaware the Australian was approaching, Hamilton stuck to the racing line, forcing Piastri to take avoiding action and abort his final flying lap. Piastri sarcastically gave Hamilton a thumbs-up from the cockpit, while a confused Hamilton asked his race engineer why he hadn't been told the McLaren was approaching.

The FIA stewards handed the seven-time world champion a standard three-place grid drop, meaning Hamilton will drop from second to fifth on Sunday's starting grid. As a result, Charles Leclerc, Kimi Antonelli and Piastri will all move up a position on the grid.

"At the approach to Turn 1, Car 44 was travelling at a significantly reduced speed on the racing line while Car 81 was approaching on a push lap," the stewards wrote in their verdict.

"The driver of Car 44 explained that he had just completed a fast lap and did not receive the team's radio message regarding the approaching Car 81 until the latter was already in close proximity. He further stated that, due to the positioning of his car on the track, Car 81 was not visible in his mirrors.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

"Car 81, which was on a push lap, was forced to take avoiding action by running wide and being obliged to abort the lap.

"Having examined the available evidence, the Stewards determined that Car 44 unnecessarily impeded Car 81 during qualifying."

Antonelli is still awaiting his own verdict on allegedly infringing a yellow flag at the end of his final qualifying lap as he passed the stationary Red Bull of Max Verstappen.

"It was pretty bad," Piastri said. "I saw him from the start line, expecting him to get out of the way and I watched him basically all the way up until I nearly hit him. So, yeah, a shame."

Sports.title: Russell to undergo Mercedes engine change but avoids F1 Hungarian GP grid drop
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver George Russell will take a fresh V6 engine for the Hungarian GP following a water leak in qualifying, but will keep his seventh place on the grid.

Russell qualified a distant seventh at the Hungaroring after both he and team-mate Kimi Antonelli looked adrift in qualifying, with Mercedes struggling to keep its tyre temperatures under control.

Russell's second lap was ruined after he crossed the kerbs at the exit of Turn 4, with the impact from the vibrations causing a water leak inside the Mercedes power unit.

Team principal Toto Wolff says Russell's engine was "done", with Mercedes having to replace his power unit for Sunday's grand prix.

Mercedes provided further details in a subsequent statement. "During George’s final lap in Q3, we detected a loss of water pressure on his car and instructed him to stop as a precaution once he had completed the lap.

"Following further inspection, we have elected to change his power unit ahead of tomorrow’s race, moving to his fourth unit of the season and thus within his season allocation."

Russell's fourth internal combustion engine is the final one allowed before incurring grid penalties, moving onto the same number of engines as team-mate Antonelli. Both drivers will therefore likely face a grid drop sometime after the summer break.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

But as Mercedes is replacing a damaged component with one of the same specification, Russell avoids a pitlane start and gets to keep his seventh place on the starting grid. "We had a water leak, hit a bump in Turn 4," Russell explained. "The lap was feeling good until then and then suddenly the lap wasn't. I didn't think much of it, and the team told me the water was spraying over my tyres.

"As soon as we saw it in the data, the water leak, suddenly my tyre temperatures got really cold on the rear. So, I don't think much more, top three definitely not possible, but maybe a few positions higher would have been there."

Meanwhile team-mate Antonelli, who qualified fourth, is facing a trip to the stewards over alleged speeding under yellows as he passed Max Verstappen's stationary Red Bull during his final qualifying lap.

Reigning world champion Lando Norris handed Mercedes its first grand prix qualifying defeat of the season, taking pole ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc.

However, Hamilton received a three-place grid drop for impeding Norris' McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri in Q3, meaning Antonelli would move up to third if he escapes a punishment of his own.

Sports.title: Verstappen on latest Red Bull woes: "Desperate? I'm already past that stage"
Sports.content:
Qualifying at the Hungaroring turned out to be a disappointing affair for Red Bull. Ahead of the weekend, team principal Laurent Mekies hoped that the energy-rich circuit near Budapest would suit the RB22 slightly better, but reality proved far more difficult than expected.

Verstappen will start Sunday's race from sixth on the grid, while team-mate Isack Hadjar will line up one row further back in eighth. To make matters worse, Verstappen also spun at the final corner, something he believes summed up the entire session.

"The weekend has been difficult in general, but when instead of the tyres degrading, your car is degrading, then you have a big problem. So that's what's happening," Verstappen said.

Verstappen made that clear over the team radio immediately afterwards. Following his spin, he told the team: "The car is just completely broken aerodynamically, it's just getting worse and worse. What a joke. What a joke honestly, what a shit weekend."

"The car became impossible to drive"

Speaking to Dutch media in the paddock, Verstappen explained that the team could see those aerodynamic issues in the data – though he could not yet specify what they were – to the point where the car became "undriveable".

"The car just kept developing more oversteer and all the problems only got worse. I arrived at the final corner and the car just spun again. At one point, the car simply became impossible to drive," he said.

After two crashes caused by the rotating rear wing, things went wrong in Hungary due to an aerodynamic problem

Where Verstappen's previous two crashes were caused by the rotating rear wing, he says the most frustrating aspect is that the issue is different every time: "There's always something different happening. It's difficult for me to make sense of it, because I don't know exactly what the problem was myself.

"But it's clear that something was wrong again, because they already told me during qualifying that something wasn't right in the data and that they could see the aerodynamics deteriorating.

"That's obviously not what you want during qualifying, and by that point you can't even adjust the front wing anymore. Then the whole car is no longer in the right balance."

For Verstappen, that made it particularly difficult to get the car into a good operating window over the course of the race weekend in Budapest.

"Well, that's basically impossible," the four-time world champion replied when asked by Autosport.

"This weekend has been very difficult and qualifying was just completely hopeless. There was absolutely nothing you could do with it."

Verstappen says Red Bull is hit by a different problem every weekend – problems that even the team itself does not always understand

Asked whether it leaves him feeling desperate that Red Bull seems to be facing a different problem every weekend, the Dutchman gave perhaps his most telling answer of the day and, by his own admission, he has already moved beyond desperation.

"No, no, desperate? That word doesn't even exist for me anymore," he said. "I'm already past that stage. We just let it go and try again tomorrow."

Earlier this year, after the Japanese Grand Prix, Verstappen said he had already moved beyond "all disappointment". Now, "desperate" can be added to that list as well.

Sports.title: Alonso explains how the impact of Aston Martin’s upgrades go further than Hungarian GP qualifying breakthrough
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso reckons qualifying at the Hungarian Grand Prix was an “important” boost for the Aston Martin Formula 1 team after his first Q2 appearance in grand prix qualifying in the 2026 campaign.

The two-time F1 world champion took 16th at the Hungaroring to end Aston Martin’s run of five consecutive qualifying sessions occupying the back row, with a deficit of around two seconds.

But round 11 in Budapest marked the Silverstone squad’s first major upgrade of the year, radically changing its AMR26’s chassis with an engine update coming next in Zandvoort.

“It was important,” said Alonso. “Definitely, it was important for everyone in the team as it has been a tough period in both factories.

“Having the deficit that we had in terms of performance in the first half of the year, and this package obviously didn't change many positions, but it changed a lot the momentum of everyone in the factory.

“It's not anymore that we are chasing something that we don't know. We know exactly what we are looking for and we know exactly the targets for the next package or the targets for next year.

“So that's, I think for me, the biggest change of this weekend.”

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

The biggest positive for the Spaniard is that he’s managed to complete a clean weekend up to now, while qualifying ahead of Haas, Williams and Cadillac by at least one tenth.

“When you bring a new car, you always believe that it is important to have the correlation right and you deliver what you expect to deliver,” the 44-year-old added.

“Even if it's what we expected, I think it was important to have it and not have a nasty surprise.

“The way the car drives, we just gain load and overall grip on the corners. Maybe a little bit more consistent to drive, so corner by corner, an entry meets an exit of the corner, the car is a little bit more forgiving, so it's a little bit easier to drive.

“The previous car we had, it was trickier to drive.”

But the weekend has not gone as well for Alonso’s team-mate Lance Stroll, who on Friday spun off at Turn 2 during first practice with a rear suspension failure, causing him to miss FP2.

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

On Saturday, he eventually qualified 20th, ahead of both Cadillacs, and although he acknowledged Aston’s progress, Stroll was still left frustrated by the current weaknesses.

“Better, for sure,” said the Canadian. ”I think we're missing a lot on engine. So, yeah, we have to find more power. We're definitely much better on grip level, so we just need to find more power.

“The car didn't turn in Turn 12. I checked. I think we had a 10km/h tailwind and it just went straight into the gravel. So, annoying, because I think we could have got into Q2 today.”

Sports.title: Antonelli risks grid drop as stewards launch Hungarian GP qualifying investigation
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is set to be investigated by the FIA stewards for a suspected yellow flag rule infringement in qualifying for the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix.

Antonelli took fourth on the grid at the Hungaroring as Mercedes was beaten by both McLaren's polesitter Lando Norris and the two Ferraris.

But the championship leader is at risk of starting further down after being summoned to the stewards' office for allegedly infringing F1's yellow flag rules.

On his final qualifying run, Antonelli caught yellow flags in the final corner - where Red Bull's Max Verstappen was stationary in the runoff area after a spin.

Antonelli did improve his final sector time to take fourth, though, with the stewards now investigating if the Italian had lifted enough to respect the yellow flags.

Antonelli had complained over a lack of grip as both he and team-mate George Russell were unable to keep Mercedes' 2026 pole streak intact, the Silver Arrows suffering their first grand prix qualifying defeat of the year.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Russell could only manage seventh on the grid and then ground to a halt on the in-lap with a water leak.

Elsewhere, Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton faces a likely grip drop for impeding McLaren's Oscar Piastri in Turn 1. Hamilton had qualified second, just 0.012s behind polesitter Norris, and ahead of team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Sports.title: Hamilton under investigation by stewards over impeding Piastri in Hungarian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
The FIA stewards have summoned Lewis Hamilton regarding an incident involving the Ferrari driver and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri in Q3 at Formula 1’s Hungarian Grand Prix.

Piastri lay fifth following his first run in Q3 and failed to improve on his last attempt after finding a slow Hamilton on the racing line in Turn 1, now known as Piquet Corner.

“Fuck me, man,” the Australian grumbled on the radio, showing his fist to the Ferrari driver on the approach to Turn 2 – coincidentally now named Hamilton Corner.

As it happens, the Briton was told “Piastri pushing” by race engineer Carlo Santi as soon as he crossed the finish line to conclude his flying lap, but this was followed by “yellow flag, yellow flag”, due to Max Verstappen’s spin in Turn 14 – Szisz Corner – taking centre stage in their conversation.

Then the McLaren racer was baulked by a confused Hamilton, who inquired: “Was Piastri on a lap, or…?”

Santi eventually admitted to being “caught by the yellow flag”.

“It was pretty bad,” commented Piastri, who did qualify fifth after all.

“I saw him from the start line and kind of watched him, expecting him to get out of the way, and I watched him basically all the way up until I nearly hit him. So, yeah, a shame.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“Even without that, it's not been easy for sure this weekend for me. I think missing FP1 definitely had a bit more of an impact than I thought it would because the track conditions have been pretty different to what we've been used to.

“In saying that, you know, today the conditions have been quite a lot different to yesterday, but it's just been difficult to catch up. And I felt like with every lap through qualifying I was slowly getting there and, you know, I felt like I needed that second lap in Q3 more than most weekends, and to not be able to do it was quite frustrating.”

Hamilton was surprised to be in a position to be impeding anyone as he didn’t expect any of his rivals to start their final attempt after he had finished his.

“I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming,” he said. “I thought everyone came out behind me, I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap, and I think Charles was the car that was behind me when I left the pitlane, so as far as I was aware. So yeah, crazy, because it had been clean and obviously it wasn't intentional.”

Pole position eluded Hamilton by 0.012s as Lando Norris edged ahead, so a potential three-place penalty would drop him down to fifth – although that would be a switch from the notoriously dirty side of the grid to the cleaner one.

“Congratulations to Lando, he did a great lap,” the seven-time world champion said. “I felt solid throughout qualifying, but for some reason we went out first, which I don't think was the right call. And the grip wasn't there for either Charles or I. We were quickest throughout, so it's definitely one that got away.”

Sports.title: F1 Hungarian GP: Norris trumps Hamilton to pole by 0.012s, Verstappen spins
Sports.content:
Reigning Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris claimed his first pole of the 2026 season at the Hungarian Grand Prix, beating Lewis Hamilton by 0.012s, as Mercedes suffered its first grand prix qualifying loss of the year.

Norris romped to a 1m17.207s lap in the final moments of qualifying to overcome Hamilton and take his first pole since last year's Las Vegas GP.

As track temperatures approached 50C, the challenge was to keep the tyres alive until the end of the lap, especially for the Hungaroring's twisty yet slippery final sector.

Heading into the decisive Q3 shootout, all the frontrunners had kept at least two fresh sets of Pirelli's softest C5 tyres for the occasion, with Hamilton leading Norris and Charles Leclerc after the first of two runs. Hamilton set a 1m17.219s to dip a tenth below Norris' time, the McLaren man losing time with a huge slide out of the final corner, with Leclerc another tenth in arrears.

Mercedes was conspicuous in its absence as the erstwhile dominant team appeared to struggle for car balance across both cars on the bump and windy Hungaroring. Kimi Antonelli was fourth after the first set of runs ahead of Oscar Piastri, with George Russell split by the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar. But neither team appeared to be a threat to either Ferrari or McLaren.

The decisive Q3 run confirmed as much, and the tricky conditions made it tough for anyone to find additional gains. Neither Hamilton and Leclerc did, but Norris went purple in sector two and then executed a much cleaner final sector to pip Hamilton by 0.012s. It was enough for a first grand prix pole for Norris as the reigning world champion, with the Briton having also taken a sprint pole in Miami.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Hamilton and Leclerc had to settle for second and third respectively, although Hamilton is set to face the stewards for impeding Piastri and is likely to be penalised. Championship leader Antonelli did improve on his final flyer but could only manage fourth, catching yellows in the final corner for a spin by Verstappen. The stewards will also investigate if the Italian lifted sufficiently for the yellow flag.

In the second McLaren Piastri had been on the back foot all weekend compared to Norris and was fifth, having to abort his final lap due to Hamilton's impeding in Turn 1, while Verstappen could only manage sixth as a result of his spin on his second run.

In the second McLaren Piastri had been on the back foot all weekend compared to Norris and was fifth, while Verstappen could only manage sixth as a result of his spin on his second run..

Russell also caught yellows as Verstappen returned to the circuit, but had not been on a better second lap anyway. Hadjar was eighth, with midfielders Arvid Lindblad and Nico Hulkenberg impressing to take ninth and 10th respectively.

Hamilton initially claimed the top of the Q2 timesheets with a 1m17.931s. The Briton enjoyed a 0.247s gap to Antonelli, who complained of a complete lack of grip, suggesting Mercedes was "doing something wrong with tyres".

Norris ended up quickest from Leclerc and Hamilton with a 1m17.456s, while Hadjar recovered from a spin on his first flyer to go fourth as all the other frontrunners also comfortably advanced to Q3.

Fernando Alonso was the surprise package of Q2 as he and Aston Martin finally broke into Q2 thanks to their all-new AMR26 for Hungary. Alonso set his Q2 laps earlier than the rest of the pack to avoid the traffic, but 16th was the best the two-time F1 world champion could muster.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Of the midfield runners Lindblad impressed in seventh and Hulkenberg snagged the final Q3 spot in 10th. That dumped out the second Racing Bulls car of Liam Lawson, who complained of an undriveable car.

Alpine pairing Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto was also eliminated, as was Gabriel Bortoleto and Haas man Esteban Ocon, although the latter did snap a streak of defeats against his team-mate Oliver Bearman.

Norris led Q1 with a 1m18.277s on softs ahead of Verstappen and Antonelli. Ferrari had enough confidence to try and advance on mediums, with Hamilton's 1m18.730s lap good for fourth.

At the rear of the field all eyes were on Aston Martin and its much-vaunted B-spec, and whether or not the Silverstone squad's mid-season revamp would be enough to escape the rear of the grid. Following encouraging signs in free practice, Alonso confirmed Aston has worked itself into F1's midfield, squeezing through at the expense of Haas' Bearman, who rued a "horrible" car balance.

Aston's leap forward also lifted it over fellow struggler Williams, aided by the Hungaroring not being a power-sensitive circuit where Honda's deficit compared to the likes of Mercedes and Ferrari is masked. But Williams was also particularly poor in its own right, with Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon 18th and 19th as the latter was baffled by the constantly changing balance on the FW48.

Behind Lance Stroll in 20th, newcomer Cadillac was the slowest team on the grid with Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez departing from the back row on Sunday.

Sports.title: F1 Hungarian GP: Norris beats Hamilton to top final practice
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Lando Norris has led a three-team fight to top final practice at Formula 1's Hungarian Grand Prix, setting up an intriguing qualifying session in Budapest.

Norris' late 1m18.939s flyer was just over a tenth quicker than Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli on the twisty Hungaroring.

FP3's opening phase was quiet as drivers kept their powder dry for qualifying runs towards the end of the session, when the track would be in its most representative condition for qualifying.

After 16 minutes McLaren's Oscar Piastri was the first driver to dip below the 1m20s barrier on softs before team-mate Norris clocked a 1m19.062s to set the early target, with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar splitting the two McLarens.

Sergio Perez caused a red flag after 20 minutes when he ground to a halt with a smoking rear end of his Cadillac, which appeared to originate from the brakes, a recurring weakness for F1's newest competitor.

On the restart halfway through the one-hour session, Ferrari and Mercedes both set chase for Norris' benchmark. George Russell came closest but still shipped two tenths, while Leclerc was another tenth in arrears. Hamilton did find enough time in sectors one and three to pip Norris by a mere 0.009s as the four top teams were all covered by three tenths ahead of the final set of qualifying simulations.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Liam Fabre

Leclerc had a much cleaner lap on his second attempt and clocked a 1m18.668s, with Antonelli moving up to second. The Italian asked his team to check for potential floor damage after a wild ride over the Turn 4 kerbs. But while the team said it "saw something on the aero" data, it didn't prevent Antonelli from going quicker still with a 1m18.254s effort.

Norris swiftly responded with a 1m18.206s lap, half a tenth up, briefly being bested by Hamilton before Norris reclaimed the lead with a 1m17.939s tour. But with Hamilton and Antonelli just one tenth in arrears, qualifying at the Hungaroring is shaping up to be a closely contested affair.

Leclerc was fourth after going wide in Turn 1 on his last attempt, followed by Piastri, who saw his lap ruined by cutting the Turn 6 chicane. Russell was six tenths behind in sixth, trailed by Red Bull duo Verstappen and Hadjar, neither of which sounded particularly impressed by the RB22's handling on the Mogyorod circuit's many bumps.

Nico Hulkenberg led Audi team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto as the German veteran rounded out the top 10, the German manufacturer appearing to gain the upper hand this weekend in F1 2026's tight midfield battle.

Alongside Perez, Arvid Lindblad was the other driver hit with mechanical trouble. The British Racing Bulls rookie missed most of the session due to a power unit change, but left the garage right at the end to take 13th.

Sports.title: Antonelli under investigation for two separate incidents in qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
World championship leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli is under investigation for two separate incidents after qualifying for the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Antonelli originally qualified fourth on the grid for Sunday’s race. However the two investigations could have a bearing on his starting position.

The stewards have summoned Antonelli for failing to slow sufficiently when he passed yellow flags at the end of Q3, which were shown due to Max Verstappen’s spin.

At the Austrian Grand Prix last month, Antonelli backed off more than he needed to for yellow flags. Team mate George Russell, who did not slow down as much for the same incident, took pole position for that race.

Afterwards Antonelli admitted he had made a “mistake” by slowing down too much for the yellow flags, having thought he saw a double flag warning rather than a single.

The stewards are also investigating Antonelli for failing to comply with the maximum time between the two Safety Car lines during qualifying. He has been summoned to meet them at 6:15pm and 6:25pm local time respectively for the two investigations.

Sports.title: Verstappen blames ‘car degradation’ after latest spin in qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says he feels Red Bull are suffering from “car degradation” after spinning out at the end of qualifying.

The four-times world champion lost control of his car in the last corner on his final lap in qualifying, leaving him sixth on the grid.

“The whole weekend has been tough but in qualifying especially the car is just degrading,” said Verstappen after qualifying. “We don’t have tyre deg, we have car degradation.

“I really can’t make anything out of it, it’s just really, really tough. The car suddenly just started oversteering a lot and honestly every lap that I did in qualifying just was worse and worse.”

Verstappen said the lack of consistency in the problems the team are facing makes them difficult to solve.

“We keep having different problems all the time and that’s probably the biggest issue at the moment,” he said. “There’s always something else that arises and that’s not good.”

Today’s qualifying session is the third time in the last four rounds Verstappen has spun in a competitive sessions. He crashed in Q3 at the Red Bull Ring and spun out in the final laps of the British Grand Prix.

After qualifying Verstappen told his team: “The car is just completely broken aerodynamically.”

“It’s just getting worse and worse, what a joke. What a joke. What a shit weekend.”

Team principal Laurent Mekies consoled Verstappen, telling him it was “Super difficult out there Max” and “we know what you feel, we’ll try and fix what we can fix for tomorrow.”

“I’m sorry, it’s just for me it’s just completely undriveable, really,” Verstappen replied. “It’s really, really bad. The degradation in qualifying is massive. There’s already a problem and then it’s really undriveable.”

Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache admitted “the drivers were not happy with the balance” after qualifying.

“The grip is very low, it’s dusty and very bumpy,” he explained. “The massive change in the wind in the afternoon made it even more complicated and it was a tough session for the drivers. We have to run the car quite stiff here and that leads to a similar feeling to the ground effect cars of the last generation.”

“When the cars are on the edge, like they are for everyone, then the smallest perturbation can upset things,” he added. “On a more positive note, we ran the new iteration of the rear wing here all day without any issue.”

Sports.title: Hamilton demoted to fifth on grid for impeding Piastri | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has been given a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri at the end of qualifying.

Piastri caught Hamilton at turn one as the McLaren driver began his final flying run. After being held up by the Ferrari, Piastri backed off and gestured at his rival – Hamilton gave an apologetic wave in reaction.

Hamilton had the quickest time in the session and was preparing to begin his final run when he had his encounter with Piastri. He admitted afterwards his concern over the incident affected his final lap.

The stewards subsequently summoned both drivers over the incident. They ruled Hamilton received a late warning about Piastri from his team and should have left him space.

Hamilton said he did not have enough time to react to the warning Piastri was behind him. “I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming,” he said.

“I thought everyone was on an out-lap. Everyone came out behind me. I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap.

“Charles, I think, was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So it’s crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn’t intentional.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Hamilton’s three-place grid drop moves him from second on the grid to fifth. His team mate Charles Leclerc takes his place on the front row.

The stewards’ verdict on Hamilton

The stewards heard from the driver of car 44 (Lewis Hamilton), the driver of car 81 (Oscar Piastri), team representatives and reviewed video, telemetry, team radio and in-car video evidence. At the approach to turn one, car 44 was travelling at a significantly reduced speed on the racing line while car 81 was approaching on a push lap. The driver of car 44 explained that he had just completed a fast lap and did not receive the team’s radio message regarding the approaching car 81 until the latter was already in close proximity. He further stated that, due to the positioning of his car on the track, car 81 was not visible in his mirrors. Car 81, which was on a push lap, was forced to take avoiding action by running wide and being obliged to abort the lap. Having examined the available evidence, the stewards determined that car 44 unnecessarily impeded car 81 during qualifying. In accordance with the FIA F1 Regulations and the established penalty guidelines for this type of infringement in qualifying, the stewards impose a three-place grid penalty on the driver of car 44.

Sports.title: Norris snatches pole position off Hamilton, Antonelli under investigation | 2026 Hungarian GP qualifying report
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed his first pole position as reigning world champion with a superb final lap in qualifying at the Hungaroring.

The McLaren driver was one of few people to improve on their final runs in Q3. Lewis Hamilton held provisional pole position after the first runs but failed to find any further time, allowing Norris to pip him by just 0.012 seconds.

Hamilton therefore fell to second on the grid ahead of Charles Leclerc. Andrea Kimi Antonelli had to settle for fourth place despite beginning his final lap well – he encountered yellow flags at the final corner.

The yellow flags were caused by Max Verstappen, who had his third significant spin in the last four weekends. As in Austria, it occured late in qualifying, the Red Bull driver spinning at the final corner.

Verstappen’s spin also obliged George Russell to slow down. The Mercedes driver then came to a stop at turn one immediately after finishing his final lap. Verstappen and Russell will line up immediately behind Oscar Piastri. The McLaren driver and Hamilton are under investigation for a potential impeding incident.

Isack Hadjar rebounded from a spin in Q2 to claim eighth on the grid ahead of Arvid Lindblad and Nico Hulkenberg. Antonelli also had a drama in Q2 as his first flying lap was deleted as he cut the inside of turn seven, and the decision came so late he had already committed to starting his final run on a used set of tyres. Nonetheless, he pulled out a quick enough time on old rubber to reach the top 10.

However as the session came to an end race control announced Antonelli was under investigation for a potential yellow flag infringement.

Aston Martin’s upgraded car proved quick enough for the team to earn their first fully-merited participation in the second round of qualifying this year (Fernando Alonso have reached SQ2 in Montreal, but not participated in it, after crashing). He did his final run in Q2 early, however, and ended up 16th.

Liam Lawson failed to join his team mate in the final 10, saying the Racing Bulls was difficulty to drive. He took 11th ahead of the Alpines. Gabriel Bortoleto, 14th, lost his first attempt to a track limits infringement like Antonelli.

Alonso reached Q2 at the expense of Oliver Bearman, who had been less happy with the balance of the Haas than his team mate after sitting out first practice. The dejected Williams pair also fell at the first hurdle.

Lance Stroll, whose Friday was badly disrupted by a suspension failure, ended up half a second behind Alonso in 20th place. The Cadillac drivers occupied the back row.

Sports.title: Norris heads Hamilton in final practice at the Hungaring | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris denied Ferrari a sweep of all three practice sessions for the Hungarian Grand Prix, setting the fastest time of the weekend so far in his McLaren.

With the soft tyres surprisingly proving resilient enough to yield two competitive times, Norris lowered the benchmark to a 1’17.939. That ensured he came out on top after a spate of runs by the drivers from the leading teams.

Norris displaced Lewis Hamilton from the top of the times by a tenth of a second, the Ferrari driver enjoying a strong run through the final sector. There was almost nothing to choose between him and Andrea Kimi Antonelli in third.

Charles Leclerc put his Ferrari fourth while Oscar Piastri and George Russell were each almost half a second slower than their respective team mates.

The Red Bull drivers did not look especially happy with their cars, Isack Hadjar branding his “undriveable” after a mistake at turn 12. Max Verstappen was the quickest of the pair, albeit seven-tenths of a second off Norris.

Liam Lawson took ninth for Racing Bulls but his team mate Arvid Lindblad missed most of the session with a technical problem. He emerged from the pits just in time for a single flying run. The Audi drivers completed the top half of the field.

Sergio Perez failed to set a time as he came to a stop immediately after leaving the pits. The Cadillac driver’s rear brakes were smoking alarmingly, prompting race control to red-flag the session.

Without that, the Williams drivers might have ended the session slowest of all. Valtteri Bottas outpaced his former team’s drivers and the upgraded Aston Martins were ahead of all four.

Fernando Alonso ended practice just under two-and-a-half seconds off the pace, but set his time early in the session, indicating there could be more pace in the heavily revised AMR26. The team had a fright early in the session, however, when Alonso caught his team mate at turn 12, who did not seem to realise he was there, provoking a worrying near-miss.

Sports.title: Russell’s Spa software fault was also present on Antonelli’s car – Mercedes | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The software fault Mercedes blamed for George Russell’s power deployment problems at Spa was present on both cars, the team has confirmed.

Russell furiously complained about the lack of power he suffered when several cars overtook him on the first lap of the race. He retired when he tangled with Lewis Hamilton at turn five.

Mercedes later confirmed Russell suffered a lack of power due to a problem with the software which manages the energy deployment. However the team’s deputy technical director Simone Resta said the same software was used on other Mercedes-powered cars including that of Russell’s team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who won the race.

“The software is the same for all the cars,” he said, “it was there in every car, but it affected George more than Kimi.”

Resta suggested differences between the drivers’ power units could have contributed to Russell’s problems.

“We also need to bear in mind that, when comparing their performance in the last few races, Kimi was on a fresher power unit, which is, of course, always a bit better than quite a used power unit. That will change in the next races when we start to have a fresher power unit on George’s side.

“So, there’s a bit of everything. There’s a bit of software, but there’s also Kimi being out of phase with George’s programme. You sum up everything when you look at the final result.”

Mercedes are hopeful the problem has been solved for this weekend’s race, and believe it is less likely to recur due to the nature of the Hungaroring, which has far shorter acceleration zones than Spa. Resta said Russell’s feedback had been useful in tackling the problem.

“He has been really good at understanding and highlighting things to us,” said Resta. “We have finally been able to identify the solution and put a fix in place for this race. So, thanks to George for having done that for us, for the team.

“Of course, he’s quite pleased that we’ve been able to get to the bottom of it and sort it out. It has been good teamwork. It wasn’t the easiest thing. As I said, with the new regulations, there are still a lot of things to learn. But it’s a step forward.”

Sports.title: Edgar Berlanga Rejects Steven Butler’s Knockout Threat
Sports.content:
Berlanga dismissed Butler’s knockout prediction, saying experience and ring IQ will decide Sunday’s super middleweight main event in New York.

Edgar Berlanga has dismissed Steven Butler’s confidence ahead of Sunday’s fight, insisting punching power alone will not be enough to beat him. Berlanga says his experience and ring IQ will be the difference when they meet in the super middleweight main event at Madison Square Garden.

Butler recently vowed to hurt Berlanga if the opportunity presents itself. Berlanga, however, doesn’t believe his opponent’s aggressive approach will carry him through the fight.

Looking at the matchup, Berlanga made it clear he expects his boxing ability to make the difference.

“That don’t win fights. You know that. What wins fights is IQ. We got 10 rounds. That’s 30 minutes of fighting with me in the ring. At this point, all that don’t mean nothing,” said Berlanga to Fighthype. “You got a guy that has experience the way I do and the IQ and everything. You got all the punching power in the world, but you’re up there with an elite fighter now. So, it’s going to be a different story.”

Berlanga has built much of his career on knockout victories, but his latest comments suggest he expects Sunday’s contest to demand more than power. Rather than trading punches with Butler, he believes his ring IQ will give him the edge as the fight develops.

The super middleweight matchup headlines Zuffa Boxing’s card at the Theater at Madison Square Garden. Both fighters have predicted victory. Butler has promised to capitalize on any opening, while Berlanga remains confident his boxing ability will be enough to secure the win.

Berlanga has spent years hunting knockouts instead of trying to outbox opponents. His latest remarks suggest he expects to beat Butler with ring IQ rather than power. If that’s the plan, Sunday could reveal a different version of Berlanga, because he has rarely relied on that approach during his professional career.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs. Kristian Prenga Live Results and Fight Updates

Anthony Joshua steps back into the ring this afternoon in Saudi Arabia, taking on Kristian Prenga in a heavyweight bout expected to serve as the final stop before a proposed clash with Tyson Fury later this year.

Event Details

Location: Superdome in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia

Undercard results

Oleksandr Khyzhniak stopped Lenny Patrach in the second round after breaking him down with relentless pressure and heavy punching in their light heavyweight bout. Patrach entered the fight unbeaten but had no answer for Khyzhniak’s nonstop attack, prompting the referee to wave it off. The victory improved the Olympic gold medalist to 2-0 with two knockouts as he continued his impressive start in the professional ranks.

Ziyad Almaayouf overcame an early knockdown to earn a unanimous decision over Frank Lucian Mango in their welterweight bout. Almaayouf recovered well, landed the more effective punches over the later rounds, and gradually separated himself on the scorecards. Mango made him work throughout the contest and kept the action competitive until the final bell. The victory lifted Almaayouf to 8-1-1 and marked a successful return to the win column in front of the Saudi fans.

Mikie Tallon stopped Orlando Pino at 1:31 of the opening round after a blistering start in their flyweight bout. Tallon immediately forced the action, hurting Pino with heavy shots before putting him down to bring the contest to an early finish. The quick stoppage moved Tallon to 15-0 and provided another emphatic knockout for the unbeaten English prospect. It also stood as one of the fastest finishes of the card, drawing a loud reaction from the crowd.

Mohammed Alakel stopped Lydon Chircop at 2:02 of the fifth round in their scheduled six-round lightweight bout after breaking him down with sustained pressure and body punching. Alakel scored multiple knockdowns during the contest as Chircop struggled to deal with the Saudi prospect’s pace and accuracy. The referee stepped in during the fifth round after another damaging sequence, giving Alakel the TKO victory. Alakel celebrated the win with a backflip in the ring following the stoppage.

Sultan Almohammed stopped Efren Besalduch at 2:41 of the third round after a one-sided performance in their featherweight bout. Almohammed floored Besalduch twice in the third with accurate combinations and punishing body shots that steadily broke him down. Besalduch beat the count after the first knockdown but was overwhelmed by another sustained attack, forcing the referee to halt the contest. The victory kept Almohammed unbeaten and provided another early stoppage for the Saudi crowd.

Omar Hikal outboxed Brian Castellano over four rounds to earn a unanimous decision by scores of 40-35 on all three cards in their super middleweight bout. Hikal controlled the fight with the sharper jab, higher work rate, and cleaner combinations, preventing Castellano from building any sustained offense. Castellano had a few competitive moments but spent most of the contest trying to keep pace with Hikal’s steady pressure. The victory improved Hikal to 2-0 as the Egyptian prospect continued his strong start in the professional ranks.

Mohamed Mabrouk Yehya boxed his way to a clear unanimous decision over Bryan Zapata in their four-round super lightweight bout. Mabrouk landed consistently from the opening bell and kept Zapata from finding any lasting success. Zapata remained durable throughout but was unable to change the direction of the fight. Sports.title: Tyson Fury Makes Sudden U-Turn to Attend Anthony Joshua Fight in Jeddah
Sports.content:
Hours after saying he would stay away, Fury confirmed he will travel to Jeddah, predicted a Joshua knockout and sent another X-rated message to his British rival.

Tyson Fury has changed course and confirmed he will attend Anthony Joshua’s heavyweight fight with Kristian Prenga in Jeddah on Saturday. The decision sets up another face-to-face moment as anticipation builds for their proposed November showdown.

The change came just hours after Fury had indicated he would not make the trip. Instead, he confirmed he intends to be ringside. He also backed Joshua to finish Prenga inside the distance.

When the interviewer brought up the possibility of skipping the event, Fury changed course.

Q: “Tomorrow you’re definitely not going to Jeddah, right?”

Tyson Fury: “Yeah, I’m going” saiid to the Stomping Ground.

Q: “What are you expecting from Anthony Joshua versus Christian Prenga tomorrow?”

Tyson Fury: “A knockout.”

Q: “I will interview Anthony Joshua after his fight tomorrow, provided he wins. Would you have a message that I can tell him from you directly?”

Tyson Fury: “Go and suck my big Gypsy balls. Tell him that. And he’s getting chinned.”

The seven-round outing with Wach gave the former heavyweight champion exactly the kind of work he wanted before returning for a bigger event. The trip to Jeddah also creates another face-to-face moment as speculation continues about a long-awaited meeting between the two British heavyweights.

He also made it clear he has no intention of sitting idle while waiting for a deal with Joshua. Inactivity, he believes, only gives opponents a better chance, and he intends to keep fighting if their proposed meeting is pushed into next year.

“I could have sat down and done nothing for two years. Why would I want to do that to give people more chance to beat me? If the fight’s going to be postponed for next year, I’m going to fight again and again and again. Of course I am,” said Fury.

Sports.title: Terence Crawford Predicts Vintage Errol Spence Jr. Against Tim Tszyu
Sports.content:
The former rival expects Spence to rebuild his offense behind the jab and disciplined pressure instead of chasing an early finish.

Terence Crawford expects Errol Spence Jr. to rely on the same jab, pressure and ring control that defined his championship run when he faces Tim Tszyu. Crawford also believes Tszyu’s difficulties with southpaws create a favorable tactical matchup for the former unified champion.

“I think Errol, you know, he’s going to come out and try to show something that we haven’t seen in a while. You know, go back to the old Errol working behind a jab, working behind, you know, smart pressure and breaking them down. I think that’s what we’ll see. I don’t think we’ll see a reckless Errol come tomorrow,” said Crawford to Fight Hub TV. “They got tailor-made styles for each other. You know, I don’t think Tim Tszyu is good with southpaws. Errol not going to have to search for him and he’s not going to have to search for Errol. So, it’s going to make for an exciting fight.”

Crawford’s comments go beyond picking a winner. He described the approach he believes Spence will use against Tszyu, with the jab laying the foundation before gradually applying pressure. It is the same formula that carried Spence through much of his championship run.

That prediction also suggests Crawford doesn’t expect Spence to chase an early finish or abandon his fundamentals after such a long break. Instead, he sees patience and disciplined pressure as the path to success.

Crawford also likes the stylistic matchup. He believes Tszyu’s difficulties against left-handed opponents play into Spence’s strengths, giving the former unified champion a chance to establish his offense from the opening rounds.

Fight night will reveal if that version of Spence still exists after three years away. Crawford believes fans are about to see the fighter who built his reputation behind a sharp jab and steady pressure rather than someone trying to force the action.

Sports.title: James J. Jeffries Stuns Bob Fitzsimmons With Epic Comeback Knockout
Sports.content:
After losing much of the fight and battling through broken bones and heavy bleeding, Jeffries retained the heavyweight championship with an eighth-round knockout in San Francisco.

James J. Jeffries looked beaten for seven rounds before producing one of boxing’s most dramatic heavyweight title finishes, knocking out Bob Fitzsimmons in the eighth round on July 25, 1902. The comeback preserved Jeffries’ championship and became one of the defining victories of the early heavyweight era.

The scheduled 20-round rematch carried enormous significance. Jeffries was making the fifth defense of the heavyweight championship he had taken from Fitzsimmons three years earlier with an 11th-round knockout at Coney Island. Many believed the rematch would determine if the younger, physically imposing Jeffries or the aging master boxer still ruled the sport.

Jeffries entered the ring as roughly a 10-4 betting favorite thanks largely to his overwhelming physical advantages. “The Boilermaker” weighed about 219 pounds, nearly 50 pounds heavier than the 172-pound Fitzsimmons, who was approaching 40 years old. Despite giving away tremendous size and more than a decade in age, “Ruby Robert” remained one of boxing’s most feared punchers and the leading challenger for the championship.

The fight drew a gate of $31,880, with ticket prices ranging from $5 to $20. Jeffries collected a purse of $14,346, while Fitzsimmons earned $9,564. The San Francisco Athletic Club cleared roughly $7,970 after expenses, including a $500 payment to referee Eddie Graney. The octagonal Arena seated approximately 8,000 to 10,000 spectators, with nearly every seat occupied for the heavyweight championship rematch.

For seven rounds, Fitzsimmons boxed brilliantly. Using superior footwork and sharp punching, he repeatedly beat the champion to the target. By the second round, Jeffries’ nose had been broken. Deep cuts surrounded both eyes. Blood streamed down the champion’s face. Fitzsimmons kept landing clean combinations against the larger man. Jeffries refused to wilt.

Fighting from his trademark crouch, he absorbed punishment while waiting for his chance. Although badly swollen and nearly blinded by blood, the champion remained dangerous because of his durability and punching power.

The ending came suddenly in the eighth round. After another exchange, Fitzsimmons momentarily lowered his guard and spoke to Jeffries. Contemporary reports differ on exactly what was said. Some believed Fitzsimmons taunted the champion. Others believed exhaustion prompted him to invite Jeffries to throw his best punch.

Only one opening was needed. Jeffries fired a crushing right hand to the body before a devastating left hook crashed into Fitzsimmons’ jaw. The former champion collapsed and was counted out, giving Jeffries a knockout victory despite appearing to have lost nearly every round.

Although victorious, Jeffries looked like the beaten man. His face was grotesquely swollen and badly cut, while Fitzsimmons showed comparatively little visible damage. Observers remarked that anyone seeing the two fighters afterward would likely have guessed the wrong winner.

The bout briefly generated whispers that the knockout had been staged, but those claims quickly disappeared. Fitzsimmons dismissed any suggestion of wrongdoing, saying Jeffries had won fairly and that “to the best man belongs the laurels.” Jeffries, peering through swollen eyes, returned the respect by calling Fitzsimmons “the most dangerous man alive” and later described him as the greatest fighter of his weight.

Referee Eddie Graney also rejected the rumors, praising the contest as nearly flawless with no fouls or questionable tactics. Veteran boxing writer George Siler reached the same conclusion, crediting Jeffries’ extraordinary stamina for carrying him through the punishment before delivering the decisive finish.

The victory extended Jeffries’ reign as heavyweight champion. He successfully defended the title two more times before retiring in 1905 without losing the championship in the ring. His lone career defeat came five years later after returning from retirement to challenge Jack Johnson.

Fitzsimmons also added another remarkable chapter to his career. Rather than retire, he moved down in weight and became boxing’s first three-division world champion by capturing the light heavyweight championship.

Few heavyweight title fights have produced such a dramatic reversal. After absorbing seven rounds of punishment, Jeffries needed only one opening to preserve his championship and cement one of the most memorable victories of his career.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Says Stephen Fulton’s Career Is Over After Weight Miss
Sports.content:
Bradley accused the former two-division champion of wasting his talent after a second straight failure to make weight forced the Liam Wilson fight to be canceled.

Tim Bradley launched a fierce attack on Stephen Fulton after the former champion failed to make weight for a second consecutive fight, leading to the cancellation of his scheduled bout with Liam Wilson. Bradley said Fulton’s repeated problems on the scales have cost him opportunities and could bring his career to an abrupt end.

“This don’t make no damn sense. Serious, Stephen Fulton, what the hell going on, bro? Every time he in training camp, this dude. This is career suicide. The man can’t stop eating. That’s the problem. I don’t get it. All that money you’ve left on the table. All that talent you got,” said Bradley on his channel.

The cancellation marked the second consecutive fight in which Fulton was unable to make the contracted weight. Earlier this week, the bout had already been changed from a WBA super featherweight title eliminator to a 133-pound catchweight after his camp requested the adjustment. The fight was eventually scrapped after Friday’s official weigh-in.

Bradley argued that Fulton is wasting the ability that once made him one of boxing’s top fighters.

“You waste your damn talent. You should be ashamed of yourself, man. I don’t see how you can live with yourself,” Bradley said.

Bradley closed by questioning Fulton’s future in the sport, saying the latest episode may cost him future opportunities.

“Career is over, player. Ain’t nobody gonna spend and waste no money on your ass no more, bro. You on a vacation now,” said Bradlet.

He also criticized the Sydney card as a whole after the cancellation removed another featured bout from the undercard, leaving Tim Tszyu’s clash with Errol Spence Jr. as the only matchup he was eager to watch.

Ghana News.title: Mid-Year Budget Review: What happened to the GH¢40m promise to Ghana’s creative industry?
Ghana News.content:
Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson

When Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson presented the 2026 Budget last November, Ghana's creative industry finally had reason to celebrate.

For years, practitioners had called for dedicated public financing to unlock the sector's enormous economic potential. Government responded by announcing two flagship interventions, a GH¢20 million Film Fund and a GH¢20 million Creative Arts Fund.

Together, they represented a GH¢40 million commitment to an industry that contributes to employment, tourism, exports and Ghana's cultural identity, yet has long struggled with limited access to financing.

Eight months later, the Mid-Year Fiscal Policy Review has arrived. Parliament has been updated on the implementation of numerous government programmes. Yet, conspicuously absent from the Finance Minister's statement is any mention of the two funds promised to the creative sector.

That silence should concern everyone who believes Ghana's creative economy deserves more than political recognition.

The Missing GH¢40 Million

The Mid-Year Review provides updates on funding and implementation for several flagship initiatives, including the Big Push Programme, the National Apprenticeship Programme, Youth Employment interventions, MahamaCares and even preparations for Ghana's participation in the FIFA World Cup.

But when it comes to the Film Fund and the Creative Arts Fund, there is nothing. There is no disclosure on whether any allocations have been released.

For an industry that has waited decades for structured public investment, that omission is significant.

Interestingly, just days after the Mid-Year Budget Review, President John Dramani Mahama, while receiving farewell calls from the outgoing Swiss Ambassador and Australian High Commissioner, disclosed that the GH¢20 million Film Fund had already been disbursed and that industry stakeholders were determining how the money should be invested.

He also reaffirmed that another GH¢20 million had been allocated to the Creative Arts Fund to support practitioners across the wider sector.

That announcement offers reassurance that the commitment has not been abandoned.

However, it also raises important questions.

If the funds have indeed been released, why were they omitted from the Mid-Year Fiscal Policy Review? Why has there been no formal public update on their implementation, governance arrangements or disbursement mechanisms?

For an industry that has consistently called for transparency and accountability, those questions deserve answers.

Beyond the promised funds, the Mid-Year Review offers little that directly advances Ghana's creative economy.

This is despite mounting evidence globally that the creative economy is not merely a cultural asset but an economic one.

Across Africa, countries are investing in film production, music exports, animation, gaming and digital storytelling as engines of growth. Ghana cannot afford to remain on the sidelines.

One of the few policies likely to affect the creative industry is government's intention to apply VAT to foreign digital platforms serving Ghanaian consumers. At first glance, this appears to be a tax administration measure. But its implications extend far beyond revenue collection.

If implemented, important questions arise. Will streaming platforms absorb the additional tax? Will subscription prices increase for Ghanaian consumers? Will higher costs reduce demand for digital entertainment? How might this affect Ghanaian creators who earn royalties and advertising income through these platforms?

These questions remain unanswered, but they are likely to shape the future economics of Ghana's digital creative ecosystem.

Not everything in the Mid-Year Review is disappointing for creatives.

Government's decision to extend the zero-rating of VAT on locally manufactured textiles until 2028 is welcome news for Ghana's fashion industry.

Textile producers, garment manufacturers and fashion designers stand to benefit from lower production costs and improved competitiveness.

Equally important is the increase in the VAT registration threshold.

Many smaller creative businesses including production houses, photographers, event organisers, designers, agencies and independent studios, may no longer be required to register for VAT.

Reducing compliance costs could allow many of these businesses to reinvest more resources into growth.

While these measures were not designed specifically for the creative economy, they nevertheless provide some indirect relief.

The broader issue is not simply whether the GH¢40 million exists. It is whether Ghana is prepared to treat the creative economy as a strategic pillar of national development rather than an occasional campaign promise. Successive governments have acknowledged the sector's enormous potential. Studies have shown that creative industries generate employment, stimulate tourism, preserve cultural heritage, drive innovation and contribute significantly to GDP in countries that invest in them.

Yet public policy often treats the sector as an afterthought. The Film Fund and Creative Arts Fund present an opportunity to change that narrative.

If managed transparently, they could help finance local film productions, strengthen music exports, support theatre and publishing, expand digital content creation and provide seed capital for creative entrepreneurs.

But transparency matters just as much as funding.

Industry stakeholders deserve to know how the funds will be governed, who qualifies for support, how applications will be assessed and what accountability mechanisms will ensure the resources reach practitioners rather than becoming another political initiative that fades with time.

The promise has been made. Now the industry deserves implementation, transparency and results.

The author, Kenneth Awotwe Darko is a multimedia journalist with interests in climate change, sustainability, arts and culture.
