About 20 years ago, P.E.I. farmer Rose Viaene watched her husband David take their tractor out into their farm fields and destroy their garlic crop — an act of defiance born out of frustration with Canada's large grocery chains.

Viaene said before then, their garlic was sold across Atlantic Canada, including at Sobeys and Real Canadian Superstore. But that relationship changed when grocery retailers began importing cheaper garlic from China.

The large retailers were still open to buying garlic from the farmers, but Viaene said the offer was too low — just 50 cents per pound when it cost the farm $7 per pound to produce.

"We were at the mercy of the big corporates or the buyers at that time," Viaene explained.

But rather than take the offer and eat the loss, the couple refused.

"Hell no, we're not going to do it," she recalled deciding. "We're not going to let them make the money and us go see the bank again for another winter to support us. No, we weren't going to do that."

Trisha, left, and Rose Viaene run the Riverview Country Market in Charlottetown. About 20 years ago, Rose and her husband David decided to destroy their garlic crop rather than sell it to Canadian grocery giants for a paltry price. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)

Jenn Pfenning, president of the National Farmers Union, said that same frustration the Vianaes felt toward Canada's large grocery retailers "is repeated multiple times a day, every day across the country."

"The concentration of power with such a small number of organizations in terms of retail food space really means that there is no farmer in Canada who actually has the weight to balance the power that they hold," Pfenning said. "And [the retailers] really do dictate extremely effectively what a product can be sold for."

The Carney government's national food security strategy, which acknowledges that 75 per cent of Canada's grocery sales are made by just five retail chains , is trying to both empower farmers and cut into grocery consolidation by pledging a 10-year, $1-billion fund to establish as many as 40 local food hubs across the country.

While experts acknowledge this proposal can help wrest control from large grocery chains, some doubt it will help Canadian consumers reduce their food bills.

WATCH | PM lays out goals of the new food security strategy: Carney announces $3B food security strategy | Duration 1:28 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new $3-billion national food security strategy to combat issues in the Canadian food system in Toronto on Thursday.

Ann Higgs, who runs a food hub called Growers Station in Charlottetown, told CBC's The House that clients including restaurants, community groups and small grocers can submit orders to the hub, which then informs local farmers what they need to pack.

Growers Station then picks up the packages and distributes the food to its clients.

According to Higgs, food hubs like hers help smaller farmers who may be priced out of running larger operations due to land costs grow their businesses and establish closer relationships with local customers.

"We grow when our farmers grow, we improve when our farmers improve, and as a food hub we can do those unique things with the mid- and small-size farmers that the large grocers cannot," Higgs said.

Among Growers Station's clients is Krunal Patel, who runs Crapaud General Store on P.E.I.'s South Shore, about 30 kilometres from Charlottetown.

Krunal Patel runs Crapaud General Store P.E.I.'s South Shore area. He told The House that he gets fresh producers from Growers Station, but he still needs to buy dry goods from wholesalers that are owned by Canada's grocery giants — his competition. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)

Patel bought the store in 2020, achieving a lifelong dream. Growers Station provides him with fresh produce, but he still needs to buy dry goods from wholesalers like TRA Atlantic, which is owned by Sobeys — his competition.

He told The House that in order to get a good price, small businesses like his have to purchase in bulk, but that's more food than his customers need.

"Not only the price, [but] I need to think about the [sell-by date] as well because as a small store, I won't be able to sell that many. So if [food] expires, I'm not going to get credit or anything," Patel explained.

In a statement, Loblaw told CBC it has "built multi-generational relationships with growers and suppliers in P.E.I. and across Canada which we greatly value."

"When sourcing products we need to always balance both the importance of our relationships and supporting local businesses with a range of factors including affordability for Canadians, available capacity, and assortment. It's a responsibility we take very seriously," the statement said.

Could food hubs help lower grocery prices?

Although a push for more food hubs across Canada will provide smaller grocers with extra avenues to get fresh produce, allowing them to be more competitive, University of Guelph food economist Mike von Massow told The House it's "not going to reduce our grocery bills by a whole bunch."

"It provides resilience and it's a very good thing to do, but I think if we depend on it to lower grocery prices we are bound to be disappointed," von Massow said.

According to von Massow, groceries are more expensive in Canada right now because of issues with the supply chain, such as poor growing conditions in Mexico that have driven up tomato prices.

WATCH | Competition Bureau says Canadian grocery industry needs more players: Fixing Canada's grocery prices problem: the Competition Bureau's plan | About That | Duration 9:27 Canada's Competition Bureau says the problem with grocery prices is a lack of competition. Andrew Chang breaks down what led to the concentration in the industry, and proposes possible solutions to diversify the market.

Von Massow said he doesn't believe it's a case of "greedflation" or price gouging in Canada, but he said the extra funding in the government's food strategy to strengthen the Competition Bureau is worthwhile.

"I'm reasonably sure it's not going to reduce prices a whole bunch, but it should increase our confidence that we're not being gouged at the grocery store," he said.

Asked why the federal government is investing so much money into a food hub proposal that some experts doubt will cut grocery bills, Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald told The House that part of the strategy is supporting critical infrastructure.

"I think it's important that we try to do more here at home," he said.

Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food Heath MacDonald rises during question period in the House of Commons in Ottawa on June 16. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Giving people more places to shop opens the market, which drives price fluctuations, MacDonald said.

"I think having that opportunity to put more products locally on the shelf with less transportation costs, being able to create those hubs in regions that presently don't have them ... will drive competition. And when you drive competition you drive price, and you drive the price down," he added.

Today, Rose Viaene and her daughter Trisha run the Riverview Country Market in Charlottetown, a year-round farmers' market that features local produce and other goods.

The market has had its ups and downs, but Viaene and her daughter said it remains competitive by focusing on local success instead of profit.

"If you're successful, we're successful, too. And that's the whole part of how we need to work together and come together," Trisha Viaene said. "If Canada's moving in the right direction, it is supporting these small local stores, giving us the ability to compete with these bigger stores."

World.title: What’s life like under wildfire alert? For Kimberley, B.C., residents, it’s part prep, part wait and see
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There's no end in sight to an evacuation alert for residents of Kimberley, B.C., as a wildfire continues to rage nearby. The community's mayor says all they can do is pack essential belongings, keep businesses running, and wait.

Facing a weeks-long wildfire evacuation alert, how does daily life in Kimberley carry on?

An old evacuation checklist is still pinned to Jerry Shepit’s refrigerator in Kimberley, B.C.

One line tells him to bring a radio and “lots of coins for the payphone.”

“No payphones now,” the 86-year-old said, amused by how much emergency advice has changed.

Shepit moved to Kimberley in 1975, when it was still a mining town. He worked at the Sullivan Mine until it closed in 2001 and stayed in the community.

Over 51 years, he has renovated his house and filled it with memories.

“Even though it’s an old house, it’s quite a treasure to me,” he said.

On July 19, the entire city of Kimberley was placed under evacuation alert because of the out-of-control Matthew Creek wildfire burning about 10 kilometres west of the city.

Jerry Shepit moved to Kimberley in 1975, when it was still a mining town. He worked at the Sullivan Mine until it closed in 2001 and stayed in the community. (Amber Wang/CBC)

The alert has left more than 9,000 people in the East Kootenay community suspended between ordinary life and the possibility of an emergency.

Residents must be ready to go on short notice.

'Your home is your castle'

Shepit describes himself as old-fashioned when it comes to technology. He doesn't go online and rarely uses the smartphone his family gave him, so he only learned about the evacuation alert when a family member called his landline.

“That was quite a surprise, actually, because I didn’t see any smoke in town or anything like that,” he said.

If he has to leave, medication will be the first thing he packs. He is less certain about where he would go.

Looking around his home, Shepit glanced at a handmade Christmas gift from his grandson.

That, he said, would have to come with him too.

“Your home is your castle,” he said. “I hope it’s still standing when it’s all over.”

An old evacuation checklist is still pinned to Jerry Shepit’s refrigerator. One line tells him to bring a radio and 'lots of coins for the payphone.' The 86-year-old is amused by how much emergency advice has changed. (Amber Wang/CBC)

Keeping the doors open

In downtown Kimberley, Angela Symes is keeping Black Dog Cycle & Ski open while preparing for the possibility of leaving.

She owns the business with her husband and a business partner, and said the alert has already led to cancellations.

“We live surrounded by a beautiful mountain range, and with that comes this type of threat,” she said.

If the alert becomes an order, Symes said the store and everything inside it would be left as it is.

“I believe things are things. As long as everybody I love is safe, that’s all I’m concerned about."

Angela Symes, co-owner of Black Dog Cycle & Ski in downtown Kimberley, says the evacuation alert has already led to cancellations, though the business remains open. (Amber Wang/CBC)

Leaving, but not evacuating

For Doug and Dawn Bryant, leaving Kimberley was already part of the plan.

The couple had been preparing to drive their RV to Alberta to visit family when the alert was issued.

It didn't change their destination, but it changed what they packed.

They added wills, financial documents, heritage jewellery and other irreplaceable belongings to what Doug described as “virtually a house on wheels.”

“We don’t consider ourselves being evacuees at this point in time,” Doug said. “It’s only an alert. There’s no order yet.”

Still, leaving carried a new uncertainty.

Doug and Dawn Bryant were already preparing to travel to Alberta in their RV when the alert was issued. They added important documents, jewellery and other irreplaceable belongings before leaving Kimberley. (Amber Wang/CBC)

“It definitely is in the back of our mind that we may not be able to get back,” Doug said.

As of Friday afternoon , the citywide alert linked to the Matthew Creek wildfire remained in effect, along with a separate alert covering 66 properties along St. Mary Lake Road.

The wildfire had grown from an estimated 567 hectares on July 19 to 869 hectares by Friday.

Kimberley Mayor Don McCormick said wind and weather conditions would help determine how long the alert remains in place.

“You can never predict how long this is going to last,” he said. “I suspect this will be measured in probably weeks, not days.”

For now, life in Kimberley continues, but leaving has become part of the calculation of an ordinary day.

World.title: Mushroom farmers concerned about U.S. tariffs, market shares
World.content:
Some Canadian mushroom farmers are raising concerns over how the latest American tariffs on the product could impact their sales on both sides of the border.

On July 14, the United States government announced plans to slap an 8.26 per cent anti-dumping tariff on Canadian mushrooms following a U.S. Department of Commerce probe into whether Canadian mushroom growers are selling fairly.

Mushrooms Canada, formerly the Canadian Mushrooms Growers Association, confirmed to CBC News that the U.S. began collecting these duties on July 17.

The latest tariff follows a previous 2.84 per cent tariff announced in May.

Some of the mushroom growers who don’t export to the U.S. worry bigger companies who do will now look to increase the amount of product they sell in Canada.

“What’s going to happen is that there’s going to be an oversupply within Canada.… It’s going to drive that price point down, which is going to hurt the farms even more,” said Mike Medeiros, a partner with Carleton Mushroom Farms.

The Carleton Place, Ont.,-based company produces roughly 136,000 kilograms of fresh mushrooms a week. Medeiros said the company currently only ships within Canada, supplying major retailers like Costco and Loblaws.

Possible production reduction

Mushrooms Canada said Canadian fresh mushrooms make up roughly 20 per cent of the American market.

“As a result of Canadians doing well [in] the American market because of our higher quality … That’s why we have some upset mushroom growers in the U.S.,” said Mushrooms Canada CEO Ryan Koeslag.

Some Canadian mushroom exporters say their American customers are generally willing to eat increased costs, for now.

“The last bit, we passed everything to the customers. So they initially accepted it, and our orders are a little bit lower,” said Agnesh Marsonia, general director of Champag Mushrooms.

“We’ve heard rumblings about some of our customers talking to American farms to transition over, but they haven’t told us anything yet.”

Champag near Montreal produces nearly 62,000 kilograms of mushrooms per week and ships roughly 40 per cent to the U.S.

Marsonia said he predicts Champag and other exporters would scale back production to not to saturate the Canadian market and drive down its price of mushrooms.

WATCH | The local mushroom market and U.S. tariffs: Eastern Ontario mushroom farmers worry about new U.S. tariffs | Duration 1:53 Last week, the U.S. introduced a new eight per cent tariff on Canadian mushroom imports, on top of a previous three per cent tariff. Some Canadian growers are worried about how that will affect their businesses. The CBC’s Liam Baker reports.

The U.S.-based group that petitioned the commerce department to launch the investigation, Fresh Mushrooms Fair Trade Coalition, claims Canadian growers are unfairly subsidized in part due to government sales tax exemptions.

Mushrooms Canada counters that farm products on both sides of the border benefit from tax exemptions.

Currently, its CEO Koeslag said he thinks there will still be a demand for Canadian mushrooms in the United States, but the higher costs could result in lower demand there and cut into farm profits.

That's despite what these growers describe as Canada's wide adaptation of Dutch growing methods that encourage a hardier mushroom that's grown faster.

Medeiros largely credits the heightened quality of Canadian mushrooms to Dutch growing methods, involving aluminum shelving like the ones shown here. He says the shelving allows the mushrooms to cultivate in four week harvest cycles. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

While Canada's consumption of mushrooms may have decreased in recent years, Koeslag said eastern Ontario remains an important area for cultivation, largely due to nearby Quebec's strong appetite for them.

Still, Koeslag said he predicts the costs of mushrooms to increase in the U.S. in coming years, mainly because of tariffs, causing trickle-down effects that could threaten smaller farms.

“Anytime we see some kind of a big shift in the market demand, there could be implications at the local markets and the local producer,” Koeslag said.

“We could definitely use [a] price increase in our industry,” said Medeiros in Carleton Place.

“With inflation over the past five to six years, we’ve been absorbing all that, so our margins have eroded.”

Mushrooms Canada is appealing both tariffs to the U.S. Department of Commerce, which is expected to make a final determination on both tariffs in the fall.

Canadian fresh mushrooms were also not included in the latest 50 per cent tariffs proposed by the U.S. government on Monday.

World.title: How the peaceful hobby of puzzling turned into an international competition of speed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Inside a Georgetown, Ont., community centre, Adam Gray emptied a 500-piece puzzle onto the table. But he wasn't settling in for a leisurely evening — he was about to race the clock, and a handful of competitors.

Gray had always been told he was a fast puzzler, so when he discovered videos of people speed puzzling during the COVID-19 pandemic, he decided to give it a shot.

By 2023, he was competing in Canada's first-ever national speed puzzling competition.

"This is where I was going to find out, OK, am I actually kind of good at this or was I just kind of kidding myself,” said the Guelph, Ont., resident.

Gray, who is part of a growing global community of speed puzzlers, is currently ranked 10th in Canada, according to the not-for-profit Canadian Jigsaw Puzzle Association (CJPA). He’s completed over 400 jigsaw puzzles this year alone, and can finish a 500-piece puzzle in under an hour.

The concept of speed puzzling is simple: get a puzzle — often 500 pieces — and see how fast you can put it together. Times vary widely depending on the puzzle's image, but the world's best speed puzzlers can typically finish a 500-piece puzzle in under an hour.

Adam Gray works to complete a 500-piece puzzle in the finals of Canadian Nationals. Gray says he's done 400 puzzles so far this year. (Cory Haslam/CJPA)

While many people discovered speed puzzling during the pandemic, competition organizer Amanda Belanger says its popularity stems from a desire to get away from screens. It also has a very low entry point, as all it requires is a puzzle, a table, and some time.

"It's become more of a social activity, where I think formerly it was a lot more of an individualized activity," said Belanger, president of CJPA, which has a Facebook group that's grown to nearly 5,000 people.

"Most people that I've talked to, they now have friends that they puzzle with on a regular basis."

More opportunities to compete

Abby Conklin started speed puzzling two years ago, competing at home with her extended family. She and her family enjoyed it so much that they did some research and found there were competitions they could enter.

"We went to our first one in Quebec and we loved it and we've been doing it ever since," said Conklin, 24, who lives in Fredericton.

Conklin attended her first national competition earlier this year, where she competed individually, with a partner, and as part of a team.

The Canadian Jigsaw Puzzle Association hosts national events each year. There were so many participants this year that the event was moved to a hockey rink. (Cory Haslam/CJPA)

"I think I did three puzzles back to back with, like, maybe 15 minute breaks in between," said Conklin. "I was mentally exhausted. But after every puzzle, I'd go outside to get some sun, and then I'd be like, yeah, I'm ready for the next one. I just want to keep going."

Belanger says the competition has come a long way since that first event in a community hall in 2023. For this year’s national event, which also took place in Georgetown, they had to rent a hockey rink in order to accommodate the nearly 1,000 people who signed up.

In addition to national competitions and virtual events, CJPA is hosting six regional events across Canada this year, including in Winnipeg, Calgary and Sackville, N.S., up from three the previous year.

"I think after this year, what we said is we need to grow our leadership team a little bit," Belanger said. "It's been exciting. It's been a big passion project."

The inaugural World Jigsaw Puzzle Championship was held in 2019, bringing together 200 individual competitors, 200 pairs, and 86 teams. While the pandemic delayed the next event until 2022, interest in speed puzzling surged during those months of lockdowns and isolation.

At the most recent world championship in 2025 — which is hosted in Valladolid, Spain — approximately 960 individuals, 640 pairs and 270 teams competed. Weronika Huptas, the reigning world champion from Poland, finished the final 500-piece puzzle in just under 40 minutes. Megan Sloka, the Canadian champ, finished the same puzzle in just over 51 minutes.

A group of four work on a 1,000-piece puzzle at Canadian Nationals in 2026. (Cory Haslam/CJPA)

There are more international competitions coming onto the scene. In 2027, Toronto will welcome some of the best puzzlers in the world as it hosts the 2027 World Series.

"This also shows how the sport is changing. There's different types of competitions that are popping up around the world, and there's so many opportunities to be a part of it," said Gray, who will compete at the event.

Ravensburger, one of the world's biggest puzzle brands, is also leveraging growing Canadian interest, designing new Canadiana puzzles specifically to debut at national competitions, including a scene from Charlottetown and a busy outdoor rink.

When Abby Conklin first started speed puzzling with family members, she didn't realize there were organized competitions. (Cory Haslam/CJPA)

Practice, practice, practice

Gray, who gives tips to first-time speed puzzlers on his YouTube channel, says there are a few ways to improve your puzzling time.

He suggests playing background music to keep you focused, and finding a comfortable place to puzzle. He recommends doing the border of the puzzle first, and then finding sections to work on one at a time.

Belanger says to practise flipping pieces, and try using both hands to do so.

"I think just doing as many puzzles as you can," she said, suggesting puzzlers branch out to different brands and styles of puzzles to ensure you're ready for anything. "You never know what might come up at a competition."

If you're intrigued by speed puzzling, Gray says to look for events in your local community, or just buy a puzzle, get out a stopwatch, and see how you do. There are websites where you can see how your time compares to other people around the world.

"You're seeing a lot of people give it a go. And that's what's really fun about speed puzzling. Really, anyone can do it."

Conklin hopes she can one day place in the top 10 at nationals, but even if she doesn't make that mark, she still enjoys the activity.

"It's like organizing all these pieces to make a beautiful image, just there's something so satisfying about it," said Conklin. "The fast thing … it just happens."

World.title: Canadian intern at NATO military headquarters in Belgium faces spying charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium has been arrested on spying charges, Belgian prosecutors said Saturday.

"She is suspected of spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.

The woman was as an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in the Belgian city of Mons, it said. The prosecutor's office described her as a Canadian national of Chinese origin, but didn't name or provide more details of her identity. They did not specify the third country or criminal organization to which she's allegedly linked.

CBC News has reached out to Public Safety Canada and Belgium's Federal Public Prosecutor's Office for more information.

Home, workplace searched

SHAPE is NATO's top military headquarters, the base of Allied Command Operations, which is responsible for planning and carrying out all operations of the 32-member transatlantic security alliance.

LISTEN | Canada's relationship with NATO: Just Asking 59:35 Footing the NATO bill: What Canada’s growing defence budget actually buys you Canada went to this week’s NATO summit in Turkey with a promise to spend 5 percent of its GDP in defence by 2035. But what does NATO, and Canada’s military strategy, really mean for everyday Canadian life? Lieutenant General the Honorable Andrew Leslie is a retired commander of the Canadian Army and former MP. Alexander Lanoszka is an associate professor in the department of political science at the University of Waterloo.

The suspect had come to the attention of SHAPE’s security services, which reported her to Belgian intelligence officials, according to the statement.

Investigators searched the suspect's home and her workplace at SHAPE, and she was placed under arrest on Friday.

A SHAPE spokesperson said there was no indication that NATO or SHAPE operational readiness, command and control arrangements or ongoing tasks had been affected.

"SHAPE continues to fulfil its responsibilities without interruption."

The prosecutor's office said it would make no further comment as investigations continued.

World.title: He spent years playing and coaching hockey alongside Russians. Then Putin invaded Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Oleksandr Matviychuk sifts through a stack of hockey medals hanging in his Kyiv apartment, the 51-year-old proudly shows off one earned during his decade playing for Ukraine's national team starting in 1999.

His eyes are then drawn to a medal he earned during the five seasons he played in Russia's Kontinental Hockey League between 1998 and 2003.

Back then, Russians were his teammates and some of his fiercest competitors on the ice. Now, he struggles to even think about facing off against them again. Anger blurs his ability to envision it.

"It's tough to imagine going in the same ring with them," he said, speaking to CBC News a few hours after Russian ballistic missiles killed at least 28 people in an attack on the Kyiv area in the early hours of July 6.

"They just tried to kill my people. Why should I feel anything different?"

Matviychuk shows off some of the hockey medals he won during his career as an elite player and coach. He spent five seasons playing in Russia, including in Moscow and St. Petersburg. (Vitalli Virchenko/CBC)

Off the ice and onto the front

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, the decades Matviychuk spent playing and coaching hockey came to an abrupt end once he signed up to fight.

Then, in June 2025, his time at the front ended violently after he was shot in the face while trying to help evacuate a group of Ukrainian soldiers who had been surrounded by Russian forces.

At one point, he said, doctors weren't sure he was going to live. But more than a year and nearly a dozen surgeries later, his face has been largely reconstructed.

A surgical team operates on Matviychuk in June 2026. During this surgery, plastic surgeons focused on the area around his upper lip. (Vitalii Virchenko/CBC)

Matviychuk now spends most of his time at his dacha, or rural cottage, valuing the quiet time by himself. He doesn't like venturing outside because of the way people look at him. Even though Ukrainians are now used to seeing people scarred by the violence of war, he says, some still can't help but stare.

"I don't like them feeling sorry for me," he said. "I don't like it. I prefer to stay at home and do not enjoy going out."

At one time, hockey took Matviychuk all over the world, including to North Bay, Ont., where he spent two seasons, between 1994 and 1996, playing in the Ontario Hockey League. He fondly remembers tournaments in Calgary and points out a novelty hockey stick in his apartment that was signed by other players after a youth tournament.

WATCH | 'I don't like them feeling sorry for me,' says soldier disfigured by war: Ukrainian hockey player injured in war longs to return to game he loves | Duration 2:38 After trading in his hockey skates for a military uniform, Oleksandr Matviychuk sustained severe injuries on the battlefield. The former Ukrainian national team player is now undergoing reconstructive surgery in Kyiv and longs to return the game he loves.

Matviychuk had taken a Ukrainian youth team to a tournament in Belarus just a few days before Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the start of what he called a "special military operation." He remembers many of the parents were concerned about the trip because of repeated warnings from the U.S. that Russia was poised to invade Ukraine.

Matviychuk assured them everything would be fine, convinced Russia wouldn't invade. When it did, he started reaching out to the Russian players he still kept in touch with.

"Most of the Russians … they kind of act like … that bird that's hiding its head in the sand, just saying, 'No, no it's not happening …. We're not doing anything,'" he said. "Some guys were saying, 'Please don't go fight. You'll get killed.'"

Matviychuk playing for Ukraine in a 2005 game against Finland at the IIHF Men's World Championship in Innsbruck, Austria. He hasn't been back on the ice since his injury because the cold air could make it harder for him to breathe through his nose. (Jeff Gross/Getty Images)

Around the same time, he said, some of his hockey contacts in Canada offered him a coaching role in Alberta — a pathway to get him out of the country — but he turned it down because he didn't feel right leaving.

Instead, Matviychuk was assigned to Ukraine's military intelligence agency, known by its acronym GUR. He had no prior military experience and didn't know how to shoot a gun, but sports had made him strong and scrappy, and he was used to working as part of a team.

But the analogy only goes so far.

"On ice, when you get blood, you just put a little snow on it, and it stops right away."

War, he says, is much dirtier.

A photo shared on Instagram by Matviychuk's daughter shows her father in Eastern Ukraine before his injury. (Alina Yeroshkina/Instagram)

'The war is not over'

Over the past four years, Matviychuk was sent on missions across Ukraine, including over the border during incursions into Russia. While he couldn't disclose specific details, he spoke of harrowing experiences, ruined villages and nearly impossible missions that sometimes didn't go as planned.

In June 2025, his team was sent to help a group of Ukrainian troops leave an area surrounded by Russians. Their task was to evacuate them and take up new positions. When they arrived, they encountered Russian forces immediately.

"We just had to fight ... as soon as we realized that this was not our guys who [we] were supposed to meet."

The Russian troops started shooting, and one member of Matviychuk's team was killed right away. Four others, including Matviychuk, were severely injured.

"We had one guy who was totally unwounded, and he took care of the rest of the Russians, so we could get out."

Dr. Leylya Omerova, middle, says facial injuries can be especially tough for patients' mental state because it can make them insecure when they go out in public. (Vitalii Virchenko/CBC)

Shot in the face and arm, Matviychuk applied his own tourniquet to his limb to stop the bleeding. He remembers walking himself to an evacuation vehicle while holding his gun, fully aware that his face was "hanging" off.

The next thing he remembers is waking up in a hospital in Dnipro, Ukraine. He was initially treated there before being moved to Kyiv.

"When he came to us, he didn't have a nose — the nose was destroyed," said Leylya Omerova, a Kyiv-based plastic surgeon.

"This kind of injury gives patients not only physical suffering but mental and psychological suffering."

Surgeons reconstructed his nose, jaw and lips, and he has at least one more surgery planned for the fall.

These two images taken my medical staff show how his face was changed over the course of several surgeries. The image on the right was taken near the beginning of his facial reconstruction while the one on the left is more recent (submitted/Dr. Leylya Omerova)

Back at his apartment, he shows off some of the newest medals added to his collection. The awards were given to him for his military service, but he admits he doesn't really know what each one represents.

They aren't like his hockey medals, where the trophies and team pictures hanging on the wall bring back fond memories of competition and camaraderie.

"I want to go back to [hockey], but I don't feel free to do it," he said. "The war is not over."

World.title: Nursing home booze ban inspires Minnesota woman to fight for her right to party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with Anita LeBrun: As It Happens 6:32 Minnesota grandmother wins law change allowing nursing home to serve booze

Anita LeBrun can soon — legally — enjoy a nice glass of pinot grigio served at her assisted living facility. She's earned it, given LeBrun is the reason nursing homes in Minnesota can now serve booze.

"It's just kind of fun when you say, 'Well, today's happy hour,' and with a drink, it just makes it all the better," the 82-year-old grandmother of five told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

LeBrun testified in front of Minnesota lawmakers twice, arguing that laws that prevented assisted living facilities from serving drinks were unreasonable and should be changed.

And those lawmakers agreed, passing what has been coined the "Grandparents' Happy Hour" bill, allowing facilities to serve alcohol to residents and guests at special events without a licence, as long as they notify the state ahead of time.

To celebrate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz even visited LeBrun's assisted living facility, where the two enjoyed a toast following a ceremonial signing of the bill.

"Growing older shouldn't mean giving up the freedoms you've enjoyed your whole life," said Walz in a Facebook post.

Walz, centre, performs the ceremonial signing of the bill while Lebrun, left, watches. (Submitted by Amira Choice Champlin)

Broken booze rules

LeBrun first decided to challenge state legislation after Amira Choice Champlin, the assisted living facility where she lives in Champlin, Minn., was told by local officials that it had broken the rules at an event in April of 2025.

The facility had just finished some renovations, and was going to have a toast with some champagne. But staff were told by the Champlin Police Department that was not allowed.

And that wasn't all. Previously, the facility had served its residents drinks on Tuesdays and Fridays, with a limit of two per person. But the facility was told that also wasn't allowed. Happy hour was over.

It wasn't that alcohol was strictly forbidden. LeBrun and her fellow residents were welcome to partake in their own rooms, with their own booze, and bring a drink to a community event. But with no liquor license, having drinks served by the facility was strictly off limits.

LeBrun spoke in front of state lawmakers twice, arguing for a change to the restriction. (MNHouseInfo/YouTube)

LeBrun would actually purchase wine to share with others, as her two daughters would offer to stop at the liquor store before they came for visits (though someone else had to take care of the beer, she says).

But she says most residents don't have cars, so purchasing their own booze isn't easy. You can take the bus, but LeBrun says it can be hard to get out some days.

"And in the snow, you know Minneapolis is pretty chilly in the winter with lots of snow and ice, so that's very hard too," said LeBrun. "It's hard to bring boxes of wine on the bus."

'Happy hour at the place where we call home'

In testimony, facility executive director Abigail Dahl told lawmakers that getting a permit would bring a lot of cost and red tape, and the permit just didn't fit the facility's situation.

"Assisted living and nursing home dining operations are already operating under a comprehensive public health regulatory framework designed to prevent foodborne illness and protect residents," said Dahl.

"Requiring a liquor license is simply red tape without value. It's duplicative, not protective."

LeBrun says she was nervous to testify before the state legislature. She had never done anything like that before.

So, with her daughters' help, she would practice in front of the mirror.

"Just because we are older, and living in assisted living, doesn't mean we should have fewer freedoms than anyone else," she told the state legislature.

"This amendment is simply putting into law what many people assume is already allowed: happy hour at the place where we call home."

In April the bill was passed with a vote of 129 to one. It was then signed into law by Gov. Walz in July.

LeBrun said she was nervous to speak in front of state lawmakers, but encouragement from her daughters and some prep work in front of a mirror got her through. (Submitted by Amira Choice Champlin)

"This was never just about serving alcohol," said Sara Luehmann, float executive director of Ebenezer, which operates senior housing in the U.S.

"It was about preserving our residents' independence, dignity, and the right to make their own choices … Challenging this restriction was about recognizing that autonomy doesn't end with age, it should be respected and protected throughout every stage of life."

The bill will take effect in August, meaning licensed facilities will be able to serve liquor. And in August, Amira Choice Champlin will be taking advantage of that.

It will be hosting an all-day party to celebrate the new legislation. There will be an Elvis impersonator, live music, all-day food, and — of course — booze.

"After you have just a little glass of wine, you can talk to people, reminisce, and everybody's just more relaxed," said LeBrun.

World.title: Tour de France final stage shortened to redeploy officers as 250,000 flee wildfires in France, Spain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The length of the Tour de France's final stage was cut by the country on Saturday to redeploy officers to battle raging wildfires that forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, including from some the suburbs of the wine region city of Bordeaux.

A specially adapted cargo aircraft was sent to dump flame retardants on a huge blaze raging in the Gironde region of southwestern France.

The Tour de France's last stage on Sunday will be reduced in length by a third, the Paris police department said, an extraordinary measure that underscored the gravity of the fires in southwest France.

The riders will race inside Paris, rather than starting from Thoiry west of the capital, on a circuit of 89 kilometres, down from the 133-kilometre route that had been planned. Part of the race's security detail will instead be used "to reinforce the response efforts in the areas affected by the wildfires," the Paris police department said.

Wildfires in southern Europe this week have displaced more than 250,000 people, including some 70,000 people evacuated in central Spain.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the hulking A400M aircraft will join 18 other water- and retardant-dropping planes and helicopters waging an expected "long and very difficult" battle against the blaze raging in the Gironde region of southwestern France.

With winds expected to shift in a west-to-east direction on Saturday afternoon, potentially driving the fire closer to Bordeaux, fire crews and authorities were digging trenches, using retardants and taking other steps to block it, Nunez said. He said the fire was about 30 kilometres west of the city and lost some of its intensity overnight.

The government mobilized soldiers to join the battle and was rushing in 1.5 million face masks to protect against choking smoke.

WATCH | Thousands flee 'nightmare' wildfires in southwestern France: Thousands flee 'nightmare' wildfires in southwestern France | Duration 2:08 Multiple fast-moving wildfires have forced the evacuation of at least 20,000 in southwestern France, where locals have described the situation as a 'nightmare.'

Authorities ordered people between the fire and Bordeaux to evacuate, including from parts of the city's western suburbs and other towns and villages.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described the fires as unprecedented and said the Gironde blaze became so strong on Friday that it had begun generating its own winds.

"Our priority is clear: protecting human lives," he posted on X, adding that evacuation orders "must be respected without delay."

He said firefighting teams were being reinforced Saturday with the addition of hundreds of soldiers and that breathing masks to filter out smoke particles were being rushed to the Gironde region for those exposed to the clouds of potentially noxious fumes.

Blazes caught authorities off guard

The virulence of the wildfires, fuelled by high temperatures and the long-term effects of climate change, caught fire crews and authorities off guard in both countries.

Firefighters in Spain said the blazes spread so fast and violently that they could not be tackled head on. In France, some people even fled by boat when flames swept through touristic towns on the Atlantic coast.

Dozens of French firefighters have been injured, authorities said, but no deaths were reported in either country despite the scenes of panic as townsfolk fled by car and police went door to door to tell people to leave as large plumes of smoke darkened the skies.

Local people try to stop the wildfire near Lacanau, amongst worsening drought conditions following a heat wave and water shortages across much of France on Saturday. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)

Successive heat waves that hit unusually early and hard this year, baking Europe with record-shattering high temperatures, have turned forests and scrublands into tinderboxes.

Fires have burned 130,000 hectares of forest already this year in Spain, up from an annual average of 100,000 hectares over the past decade, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Saturday as he visited a command post west of Madrid.

He said more favourable weather Saturday offered "a window of opportunity" for fire crews to bring the blazes under control. Madrid's regional government said the fires decreased in intensity as winds and temperatures dropped.

Other European nations were helping, with Italy, Greece, the Netherlands, Portugal, Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia already providing or expected to deploy water-dumping planes and helicopters to the Spanish and French fire fronts.

Wildfire headed toward Bordeaux

Gironde region prefect Sophie Brocas said on Friday night that strong winds from the west were pushing the fire closer to the Bordeaux metropolitan area and that it had grown to "an unprecedented magnitude."

Bordeaux's western suburbs covered by evacuation orders included Le Haillan and parts of Eysines and Mérignac, where the city's airport is located.

The airport said it remained open but that its bus and tram services were suspended.

A member of the Kiat Yack Martial Arts Academy checks his peer for injuries after helping extinguish fire around the academy in the village of El Tiemblo, during wildfires affecting Castile and León province, Spain, on July 24. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

The Gironde blaze broke out Wednesday near the Cap Ferret peninsula on France's Atlantic coast, 60 kilometres from Bordeaux. Bordeaux authorities took in thousands of evacuees, offering them food and shelter in an exhibition centre, and the city's mayor said it could be equipped to welcome as many as 10,000 people if that became necessary.

Evacuation orders were sent with special alerts to mobile phones, instructing people to leave, Brocas said.

"We want everyone to be quickly brought to safety. We must act quickly together."

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Petro to seek court order to annul election of De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro said Tuesday that he will seek a court order to annul the election of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he had gather enough evidence to prove that his successor “was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes.”

“Today we are presenting the body of evidence we have gathered to the representatives elected by the people, and we will file a lawsuit with the courts to annul the elections, as is our duty,” said the outgoing president.

We are not making things up when we say that Abelardo’s government was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes included in the percentage automatically adjusted by algorithms created by private Israeli companies with the endorsement of their genocidal government. President Gustavo Petro

“We are facing not only the imminent rise of fascism in Colombia but also what may be the greatest threat to global democracy since Hitler’s time,” said Petro.

In a response that was broadcast on his social media channels, De la Espriella reiterated that Petro was a “tyrant” who was trying to perpetuate power through a coup d’etat with the help of the leftist runner-up in the election, Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Even before becoming a candidate, I warned you: Petro is a tyrant in the making who seeks to perpetuate himself in power by any means necessary. And today, as the president-elect of all of you, I ratify what I have said for so many years. This is no longer an analysis or an opinion; it is a palpable reality. From the moment nearly 13 million Colombians stood by me to defeat him and his political frontman, Petro and Cepeda began their Plan B to stay in power, no matter what it takes. And they want to do so through a coup d’état. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

The president-elect asked the armed forces “to protect the Constitution and democracy, and to disobey any order that Petro may be giving to the contrary.”

Resistance, dear compatriots. We cannot allow them to snatch away what we achieved at the ballot box in an epic democratic battle this past June 21. Let us resist, for August 7 is near. God, the vote, and democracy have spoken; we are going to defend the Constitution and the rule of law as we must. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella has long claimed that he will extradite his predecessor to the United States.

World.title: De la Espriella suspends Colombia’s transfer of power
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella on Tuesday suspended the transfer of power after President Gustavo Petro accused him of fraud.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said he had “given instructions to the vice president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term.”

I have just given instructions to the president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term, a government that, with its decisions and its conduct, seeks to destroy Colombia. Abelardo de la Espriella

“My duty is to protect the interests of the Nation and guarantee a serious, transparent transition at the service of Colombians, never to legitimize the disaster or the disregard for the constitutional order,” said the president-elect.

In a press conference, Finance Minister German Avila said that he had also suspended cooperation with the transition process in response to comments made by a member of De la Espriella’s team, convicted fraudster Carlos ALonso Lucio, that “undermine the respect, dignity, and decency” of the transition process.

Recent statements by members of the incoming transition committee undermine the respect, dignity, and decency of a process such as the one we are carrying out. These statements were surely made intentionally to hinder the transition process. Accusations and insults have been leveled against the president and his administration, alleging that they are criminals, that they are manipulating the justice system, and that they are seeking to extradite us, among other blunders that have been made. German Avila

“All we have received are insults and disrespect, slander and offenses, and we will not tolerate a single further act of aggression or threat,” said the finance minister.

Avila asked Inspector General Gregorio Eljach to oversee the continuation of the process.

In a post on social media platform X, incoming vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo stressed that his team would continue going through the books to make sure that “those who have betrayed the trust of the Colombian people must answer to the institutions and to history.”

World.title: Universidad de Chile Eliminated by Curicó Unido in Copa Chile Upset

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky
World.content:
The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance. While there is no scientific consensus on its effects, itâs commonly associated with heightened emotions, sleep disturbances, and symbolic transitions.
