World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Brazilian industry estimates nearly half its US exports will face additional tariffs
World.content:
Brazilian industry estimates nearly half its US exports will face additional tariffs

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 12:39 UTC Full article

The study, released on Thursday, details that the new 12.5% rate reaches 4,060 Brazilian products

Some 48.7% of Brazilian exports bound for the United States will be subject to some form of additional tariff following the entry into force of the new forced-labor levy, according to a study by the National Confederation of Industry (CNI), the country's main industrial employers' body.

The study, released on Thursday, details that the new 12.5% rate reaches 4,060 Brazilian products. Of those, 3,985 were already subject to the 25% surcharge in force since Wednesday and will now pay a total of 37.5% to enter the US market. That group accounts for 80.7% of affected exports, some $10.8 billion. Another 75 products, worth $1.6 billion, will be covered only by the new rate. Together, the measure covers $12.4 billion, equivalent to 29.4% of Brazilian sales to that destination.

The new levies stem from the investigation conducted under Section 301 of US trade law, which covered 60 trading partners. In its final determination, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) included Brazil among the countries that, in its assessment, “failed to impose and effectively enforce a ban” on the import of goods produced with forced labor.

The CNI challenged that rationale. According to the confederation, the justifications presented by the USTR do not reflect Brazilian reality, since the country has some of the most advanced legislation to prevent and eradicate forced labor across supply chains, with internationally recognized mechanisms for inspection, accountability, and worker protection.

“It is essential that dialogue between Brazil and the United States be maintained and deepened. At the same time, we need to act quickly to soften the impact on the affected companies,” the body's president, Ricardo Alban, said in a statement, adding that they are holding talks with the federal government and with the most affected sectors to define short-term measures.

The Brazilian government called the tariffs improper and signaled a response. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said the country would not sit lamenting the measure and announced a credit line for the sectors involved.

Brazil ended up in the highest band of the new scheme, while Argentina secured the minimum 10% rate through commitments made in its bilateral agreement with Washington to ban such imports. The tariff round, covering about 99% of US imports, was applied under a different instrument from the levies the Supreme Court struck down in February, when it found the administration had exceeded its authority by invoking an emergency powers law.

World.title: Goldman Sachs cuts Argentina's growth forecast to 2.7% and looks ahead to the elections
World.content:
Goldman Sachs cuts Argentina's growth forecast to 2.7% and looks ahead to the elections

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:22 UTC Full article

Despite the revision, the bank considered that the economy is “expanding at a moderate pace” and maintained a favorable assessment of several aspects of the economic program

Goldman Sachs lowered its growth forecast for Argentina's economy in 2026 from 3% to 2.7% and anticipated a possible contraction in activity during the second quarter, according to a report by the bank. The institution also said economic performance will increasingly be assessed against the presidential elections of October 2027.

The cut followed April and May indicators that came in below expectations. In the first quarter, gross domestic product had grown 0.7% on a seasonally adjusted basis, an improvement the report attributed to the statistical carryover from late 2025 and to March's performance, which offset weaker figures for January and February.

Despite the revision, the bank considered that the economy is “expanding at a moderate pace” and maintained a favorable assessment of several aspects of the economic program. It highlighted the commitment to fiscal balance, reserve accumulation, and an improving trade position: by its calculations, the central bank has bought close to $13 billion so far this year and net reserves have risen by around $6.6 billion. The 12-month trade surplus reached the equivalent of 3.2% of output, with the energy sector accounting for nearly half of the result.

The bank also praised the disinflation process. After the 1.9% recorded in June, it projected that prices will continue to decelerate in the second half and that the year will close near 29%. In its overall assessment it said the country remains “on the right track in terms of macroeconomic policy,” while warning that political and social challenges persist. “The margin for error is narrow,” it said, anticipating greater investor attention on Javier Milei's prospects for reelection.

Goldman Sachs's forecast sits below other recent estimates. Moody's projects growth of 3.4% for 2026 and 3.5% for 2027, while the International Monetary Fund estimates 3.5% this year and 4% next.

The report came days after Moody's raised Argentina's sovereign rating to B3 from Caa1, with a positive outlook, the third upgrade in under three months following those by Fitch and Standard & Poor's. It is the first time in a decade that the three main agencies have aligned their assessments. The central bank exceeded $10 billion in foreign-currency purchases in the first half, meeting the target agreed with the multilateral lender.

Country risk, meanwhile, closed the week at 437 basis points after rising 4.3%, with a session high of 445. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva is scheduled to visit the country next week.

World.title: New US tariff scheme expands Argentine zero-duty lines to 2,212
World.content:
New US tariff scheme expands Argentine zero-duty lines to 2,212

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:14 UTC Full article

Argentina was also placed in the lowest band of the new regime, with an additional 10% tariff, the same rate that previously applied

The new US tariff scheme that took effect on Friday raised to 2,212 the number of Argentine tariff lines that can enter the US market at a 0% rate. To the 1,675 lines already covered by the Reciprocal Trade and Investment Agreement (ARTI), signed on February 5 in Washington, another 537 were added following a review by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

Argentina was also placed in the lowest band of the new regime, with an additional 10% tariff, the same rate that previously applied. Under the criteria published by the USTR, that rate applies to economies that already ban the import of goods produced with forced labor, committed to doing so through a reciprocal trade agreement, or apply a partial regime with that effect. That group also includes Canada, Mexico, India, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, Guatemala, and Honduras, among others. The remaining partners covered received a 12.5% rate.

In Argentina's case, its placement in the lower band rests on the commitments made in the February agreement to ban such imports, even though the domestic regime is not yet in force. The original 1,675 lines, which official estimates suggest would enable exports worth some $1.013 billion, were not affected by the new mechanism. A further 93 country-specific exemptions were added, including jojoba and argan oils, live animals, flowers, cork, timber, and precious stones.

The US Chamber of Commerce in Argentina (AmCham) said the ARTI will begin to be fully implemented and that the measure broadens opportunities for local exports. The Argentine government, for its part, played down the impact of the new regime and prefers to await definitions from Washington before sending the bilateral agreement to Congress for consideration.

Analysts quoted by the Argentine press nonetheless pointed to elements of uncertainty. International relations scholar Julieta Zelicovich said the tariffs work as “a pressure mechanism” that creates a “state of permanent negotiation” with trading partners, and anticipated that the new rules will be challenged in court, as happened with the tariffs issued under the emergency powers law and Section 122. Economist Federico Vaccarezza warned that the agreement lacks a dispute settlement mechanism.

The round covers 60 trading partners accounting for about 99% of US imports and replaces the universal 10% tariff that expired on Friday. Brazil, by contrast, has since Wednesday faced 25% duties issued under the same legal instrument, following a separate investigation.

World.title: Uruguay: nearly half of those polled say the government is falling short of expectations
World.content:
Uruguay: nearly half of those polled say the government is falling short of expectations

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:10 UTC Full article

The same poll put Orsi's approval at 24% and disapproval at 56%, his worst reading since taking office

For 49% of Uruguayans surveyed, Yamandú Orsi's government is performing below the expectations they held at the start of the administration, according to the latest poll by the consultancy Factum, covering the third two-month period of 2026. The study, with fieldwork conducted between June 2 and 20 and released by VTV Noticias, shows a sustained deterioration in perceptions of the government since the beginning of the term.

Among the remaining respondents, 27% consider that the government is performing as they expected and just 1% believe it is exceeding their expectations. Another 22% said they expected nothing from the current administration, and 1% declined to answer.

Comparison with earlier measurements shows the scale of the shift. In the fourth period of 2025, 45% rated the government's performance as equal to or above their expectations, against 30% who placed it below. In the third period of 2026 that relationship reversed: 28% now place it at or above, and nearly half below.

By region, the negative assessment is slightly higher in the country's interior, where 50% consider the government to be falling short of expectations, against 49% in Montevideo. Favorable views, by contrast, are somewhat higher in the capital: 31% of Montevideo residents rate the government as equal to or better than expected, a figure that drops to 25% in the interior.

The most critical age group is the youngest. Among people aged 18 to 33, 50% believe the government is below their expectations and only 18% place it at or above. Those over 62 show the relatively most favorable assessment, with 35% rating the government as equal to or better than expected, though 44% also place it below.

The sharpest differences emerge when 2024 voting is taken into account. Among those who voted for the Frente Amplio, the governing coalition, 52% say the administration is falling short of what they expected, while just 3% say they expected nothing from it.

The expectations measure is not equivalent to an approval rating, as it compares the government's performance with what each person anticipated at the start of the term. On that separate question, the same poll put Orsi's approval at 24% and disapproval at 56%, his worst reading since taking office, with a cumulative drop of 13 points since the first period of the year. The fieldwork coincided with the controversy over the purchase of an official vehicle.

World.title: Trump jokes about a third term at correspondents' dinner, three months after the attack
World.content:
Trump jokes about a third term at correspondents' dinner, three months after the attack

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:06 UTC Full article

The evening was a repeat of the April 25 event, which was interrupted when a man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired near the ballroom

US President Donald Trump joked about the possibility of seeking a third term during his speech at the annual White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, held on Friday in Washington. Toward the end of his roughly hour-long remarks, he put on a hat reading “Trump 2028.” The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution bars a president from serving more than two terms.

The evening was a repeat of the April 25 event, which was interrupted when a man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired near the ballroom. The accused was subdued by officers before reaching the venue and faces charges over the incident. The rescheduled edition was held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel — which Trump owned before his first presidency — with a considerably smaller guest list and heightened security.

“As I said three months ago, the show must go on,” the president said at the outset, in his first appearance as president at an event he had avoided for years. Trump said he had scrapped the harshest passages of the speech he had prepared for April. “That was going to be a doozy,” he said.

Through his remarks he praised part of the press corps and criticized other journalists, while taking swipes at political rivals and public figures, among them hosts Jimmy Kimmel and Jimmy Fallon, Representative Ilhan Omar, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, and musician Bruce Springsteen. Several comments referred to the physical appearance or intellect of those mentioned, and in one case he repeated a claim about a congresswoman that was debunked years ago. NPR judged that some of the remarks flirted with racism.

Much of the humor drew a limited response. According to accounts by CNN and The Washington Post, several jokes were met with silence from the audience. His press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, had previewed the speech as “unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious.”

The association's outgoing president, Weijia Jiang, opened the evening with a reference to the April attack, which she said “tested all of us.” The event also featured the annual journalism awards and a tribute to a Secret Service agent who helped subdue the assailant.

Trump, who has maintained a tense relationship with the press throughout his political career, said he respects most of the correspondents and called his attendance an “honor.” He added that he expects to attend next year's edition, in 2027, though he jokingly made his participation conditional on how the media treat him.

World.title: Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications
World.content:
Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:05 UTC Full article

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations”

Uruguay was placed in the highest band of the new US tariff scheme, with an additional 12.5% levy on its exports to the United States, for not having an explicit ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor. The measure, which took effect on Friday, raises the rate that had applied to the country since February, of 10%.

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations,” given that the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) had announced the start of the investigation in March and released its proposal in June. The Ministry of Economy and Finance confirmed the move from 10% to 12.5%.

The new scheme, applied under Section 301 of US trade law, covers 60 trading partners accounting for about 99% of US imports, and replaces the 10% universal tariff that expired on Friday. Under the USTR's determination, the 12.5% rate applies to economies that have not adopted a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor, did not commit to implementing one through a reciprocal trade agreement, and are not part of the differentiated calculation group, which includes the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Switzerland.

The breakdown leaves Uruguay at a disadvantage relative to several regional partners. Argentina, Ecuador, Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador fell under the lower 10% rate, having adopted restrictions or committed to doing so. Costa Rica, Panama, and the Dominican Republic, by contrast, face 12.5%, as does Uruguay. Brazil, meanwhile, has since Wednesday been subject to 25% tariffs issued under the same legal instrument, following a separate investigation.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in announcing the measure.

The USTR said certain products are exempt, among them raw materials whose higher cost could cause supply shortages in the US market, though it did not publish a detailed list. China does not appear in this scheme, as it is subject to separate and higher tariffs.

The round is part of Donald Trump's administration's effort to rebuild its tariff structure after the Supreme Court struck down in February the tariffs issued under an emergency powers law, finding that the administration had exceeded its authority.

World.title: Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner
World.content:
Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:00 UTC Full article

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts

The six contenders to succeed António Guterres at the head of the United Nations set out their proposals on Thursday in a debate held in the General Assembly Hall, a week before the formal start of the selection process. For nearly two hours they answered questions from diplomats, UN staff, and civil society representatives, in a publicly broadcast session.

The candidates are former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa, Argentina's Rafael Grossi, currently director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, former Guyanese foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, and former Senegalese president Macky Sall. Five of the six come from Latin America and the Caribbean, in line with the regional rotation expectation that favors the region this cycle; Sall is the only African candidate. Guterres leaves office on December 31.

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts. “I would like no one to ask me again where the UN is. That will be my indicator,” Grynspan said when asked what achievements she would hope to show after five years. On Security Council paralysis, she argued that “the blockade of the Security Council is when the job of the secretary-general starts,” citing her role in the deal that allowed grain exports through the Black Sea as a precedent applicable to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

Bachelet stressed the importance of the post's moral authority and said neutrality and independence are essential for all 193 member states to feel represented. Asked how he would act if a permanent Council member waged a war of aggression, Grossi replied that the secretary-general must “dialogue and listen” and approach conflicts realistically, examining their root causes and the situation of the party under attack. Espinosa said the organization is in crisis and must recover its capacity to prevent conflicts, while Sall focused on reforming the international financial architecture and Rodrigues-Birkett defended the scope for action despite the post's lack of executive power.

The format, with no direct exchange between participants, limited the contrast of ideas. According to analyst Richard Gowan, Grossi is the most frequently mentioned front-runner, though he has not locked up the race, and both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett have significant backing. Several capitals have yet to define their positions. The decisive phase begins on July 30, when the fifteen members of the Security Council, five of them with veto power, start their closed-door voting.

World.title: Family of murdered journalist urges Paraguay to comply with Inter-American Court ruling
World.content:
Family of murdered journalist urges Paraguay to comply with Inter-American Court ruling

24th Friday, July 2026 - 06:48 UTC Full article

The family also said it had proposed holding the official act of acknowledgment of responsibility at the site of the killing, a proposal that was not accepted

The widow and children of Paraguayan journalist Santiago Leguizamón, murdered in 1991, have called on the state to fully comply with the ruling in which the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Paraguay responsible for failing to properly investigate the crime. The demand was voiced on Monday at a ceremony beside the monument honoring the broadcaster in Pedro Juan Caballero, on the border with Brazil, convened by the family, the Paraguayan Journalists' Union, and the Human Rights Coordinating Body, with backing from the International Federation of Journalists.

Leguizamón, director of the Mburucuyá radio station, was shot on April 26, 1991, as he left the studio, after receiving threats over his investigations into organized crime along the border. In November 2022, the Inter-American Court declared Paraguay internationally responsible for violating his rights to life and to freedom of expression, as well as his relatives' judicial guarantees.

Among the reparation measures, the court ordered the reopening of the criminal investigation, the advancement of a law protecting journalists and human rights defenders, the strengthening and funding of the Journalists' Safety Roundtable, the creation of a fund for prevention and assistance programs, and the reinstatement for five years of the national journalism prize bearing the broadcaster's name.

“The most important part, the structural one, which concerns public policies to protect journalists, still has not advanced,” said Dante Leguizamón, the journalist's son and executive secretary of the Human Rights Coordinating Body. The family also said it had proposed holding the official act of acknowledgment of responsibility at the site of the killing, a proposal that was not accepted.

For its part, the vice-presidency has convened for July 27 the Public Act of Acknowledgment of International Responsibility in the journalist's memory, and maintains that compliance with the ruling is advancing through the interinstitutional commission that coordinates the implementation of international judgments, in whose meetings the family's representation has taken part.

The bill recommended by the court was submitted to Congress in 2023 by opposition lawmakers. An alternative proposal pushed in 2025 by governing-party legislators, which excludes human rights defenders and concentrates its implementation in the Interior Ministry, was rejected by journalists' unions and remains stalled in committee.

Since the end of Alfredo Stroessner's dictatorship in 1989, 22 journalists have been murdered in Paraguay, nine of them in the border department of Amambay. Only three of those cases have reached a final judicial resolution.

World.title: Postcards from Mexico: On the Cabo San Lucas Marina
World.content:
CABO SAN LUCAS, Baja California Sur, Oct. 25 — It’s quiet and cool off the strip. The abarrotes are just opening, and there’s an old man in a vest up the block pushing a shopping cart full of empty beer cans. That might be mop-up duty from last night’s debauchery, or this morning’s. Stray dogs patrol the streets, trotting from one garbage pile to the next like derelict show ponies. In their glory days, they guarded the now-abandoned buildings that flank the street, too pure for this world with their barbed-wire crowns of thorns.

Baby birds are just waking up, warbling. They were promised a worm, like all early birds, but maybe they’ll settle for the gnats buzzing around my face, plentiful at these hours when it’s still not hot enough for the sun to burn them out of the air midflight.

It doesn’t take much to drown out the noise they make. Every half-minute, buses rattle up the sand-dusted Narciso Mendoza and down the Leona Vicario. As I turn onto Lázaro Cárdenas, I’m presented with a beautiful bouquet of belching tubas courtesy of the music blaring from the back of a black vocho. One doesn’t question who would blast banda music at this hour. “Reveille.” “La 4 x 4.” Same tiger, different stripes.

The soundtrack of the Cabo San Lucas Marina

The playlist in the Cabo San Lucas Marina is different. You might still hear some classics, depending on whose boat you walk by, but the shops and kiosks pander to a different demographic. I still haven’t quite figured out which. Daft Punk begets Murray Head, which begets Katy Perry. Speaking of which, Señor Frog’s is still thriving. Even at this hour, I spot a gringo retiree in board shorts and a tank top loitering in front, presumably curious about hours of operation. He’s in good company.

Along the esplanade, you hear far more English than Spanish. Much of that comes from merchants stumbling through back-of-the-napkin phrases they’ve committed to memory to entice newly arrived tourists to buy their wares. Though I also hear an old woman muttering something to her dog about one of the boats they pass by, so I guess even the dogs here are fluent.

‘A parking lot for yachts’

Along a wall, a line of men wearing Oakleys, long-sleeved shirts and visors sits idly, taking it easy before heading out on whatever excursions they’ll be leading. Nearby, a bored-looking clerk in a dockside store that looks like Cabo’s version of J. Peterman scrolls on his phone, unfazed about the urban sombrero sales quota he’ll need to meet by the end of the day. Even aboard the boats, on the eve of the world’s biggest marlin tournament, local fishermen prattle, hosing down decks and trying to be heard over the dull roar of idling boat engines.

This marina is like a Costco parking lot for yachts, though instead of an associate in a neon vest checking your ID, there’s a tall, wrought-iron gate with an entrance like a cage that only those with a key can get through. I pause to size it up, then look around to see who’s watching. “I could hop that,” I say to myself.

Ethan Jacobs is a freelance writer and writing coach based in Playa del Carmen. He has written extensively in narrative and short fiction formats, and his work has received recognition both domestically and internationally in microfiction, short fiction and narrative essay formats.

World.title: Is Chipotle in Mexico a good or bad idea? A ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast
World.content:
Recently, and with much fanfare, Chipotle opened its first restaurant in Mexico. Perhaps not surprisingly, the opening spurred a polarizing debate and discussion about whether a U.S.-based Mexican restaurant chain would do well in the country. Years ago, Taco Bell entered the country and ultimately left in what was considered a disaster.

So what are the arguments for and against Chipotle coming to Mexico? Is it yet another unwanted assault of American culture on another country? Or is it a welcome sign of competition and choice for Mexicans?

Could it lead to lost business for local Mexican restaurants and reduced “authentic” Mexican food options? Or could it create a standard for the trifecta of affordability, service and quality that Chipotle is known for and oftentimes doesn’t exist in many restaurants today? Or perhaps it’s not that big of a deal, and people should move on?

And finally, what does the choice of a ritzy Monterrey suburb as the first restaurant location in the country tell us?

I will admit that while I have been a very frequent customer of Chipotle in the United States, I have actually eaten very few burritos here in Mexico. And the ones I have had have been very different.

In this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong, George and I talk through the arguments on each side of the debate and offer our own thoughts and opinions. Where do you stand on this issue? Check out the discussion here:

Confidently wrong about Chipotle: Episode 5 - Season 3

Watch this video on YouTube

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: US sanctions more than 50 Jalisco cartel-linked individuals and businesses
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury on Thursday imposed sanctions on 39 Mexican individuals and 16 companies it alleges are linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), calling it “the largest action ever taken” against the notorious crime gang.

The measure targets the leadership of the cartel — designated by President Donald Trump as a foreign terrorist organization — and its illicit financing networks across Mexico.

The Treasury Department said in a statement that the goal of the sanctions is to limit the CJNG’s ability to traffic fentanyl and other drugs into the United States.

Shortly thereafter, Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) reported it had identified “indicators related to possible operations with resources of illicit origin, including cash transactions, acquisition of high-end vehicles, jewelry and real estate,” as well as “international transfers, intensive use of credit and debit cards and transactions using virtual assets.”

As a result of this review, Mexico blocked the accounts of the same 55 individuals and companies sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department.

“The coordinated actions between Mexican and U.S. authorities strengthen mechanisms of international cooperation to prevent abuse of the financial system, combat money laundering and weaken the economic structures of organized crime,” the UIF said.

Among those sanctioned is Juan Carlos González, aka “El Pelón,” identified by U.S. authorities as the new leader of the CJNG following the February death of his stepfather, cartel founder, Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, who was killed in a federal operation.

The U.S. State Department has offered a reward of US $5 million for the capture of González, who holds both Mexican and U.S. citizenship.

Also sanctioned was the network of associates and subordinates linked to Audias Flores Silva, aka El Jardinero, who was arrested by Mexican authorities in April.

The UIF review found “inconsistencies” in tax records involving the accused, saying “they present characteristics of shell companies or with corporate structures of limited or no apparent economic activity.”

A complaint was filed with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the 39 individuals — as well as eight others accused of being part of the same CJNG network — were added to the UIF’s Blocked Persons List (BPL).

The BPL is a public report identifying individuals and legal entities involved in money laundering or terrorist financing. All Mexican individuals and companies are required to immediately suspend any and all acts, operations or services with people or entities on the BPL.

With reports from EFE, Infobae, El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Volaris will be the first Mexico-based airline to offer passengers Starlink satellite Wi-Fi
World.content:
Low-cost airline Volaris will soon become the first Mexican carrier to offer Starlink satellite Wi-Fi on board its flights.

Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network, is known for allowing users to browse the Internet as if they were on the ground. In the sky, users can text, make video calls, listen to music, work remotely, or watch streaming content.

First, we changed the way Mexico flies. Now, we’re changing what flying feels like. The fastest Wi-Fi in the sky is coming aboard with @Starlink Book here: https://t.co/YO6KQwZld5 pic.twitter.com/eL6T5xjTOV — Volaris (@viajaVolaris) July 14, 2026

Starlink’s advantage is that it operates via satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO), much closer to the planet than older systems, shortening data travel distance, cutting response time delay, and using flat smart antennas to track moving connections.

Volaris expects to have Starlink’s Internet available across its entire fleet by 2027. But it has not specified whether access will be free for all passengers, linked to a loyalty program, or have an additional cost.

The rollout will encompass more than 150 Airbus A320 and A321 aircraft, on both domestic and international routes.

This announcement is part of a broader strategy by Indigo Partners — Volaris’s holding company — which also includes JetSMART, Wizz Air, Frontier, and Cebu Pacific. Collectively, these airlines plan to install Starlink on more than a thousand aircraft worldwide.

Unlike other connectivity models, the service won’t be managed by the airline, but directly by Starlink through its own system.

Beyond improving passenger experience, the technology seeks to improve communication between aircraft and ground personnel, anticipate maintenance needs before they become failures and better react to unforeseen events.

Said Volaris head Enrique Beltranera, “The airline’s ultra-low-cost model goes hand in hand with an exceptional travel experience, which continues to evolve in line with our customers’ expectations.”

With reports from Aviación Online and ADN 40

World.title: Trump re-imposes his tariffs, but Mexico gets a pass
World.content:
The U.S. government imposed new tariffs on 80 countries effective on Friday, but Mexico escaped relatively unscathed.

Taxes on Mexican goods replace the 10% duty U.S. President Donald Trump dictated in February after the Supreme Court invalidated the broad-based tariffs he had applied last year. Those original replacement tariffs were valid for only 150 days, prompting Friday’s new levies.

U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer informed President Claudia Sheinbaum of the pending decision during a Thursday morning meeting at the National Palace.

Afterward, Mexican Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard explained that the 10% tariff does not affect approximately 80% of the products Mexico exports to the U.S.

“Mexican products that comply with the terms of the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact (USMCA) will remain tariff-free,” Ebrard said.

The other 20% involved previously established sectoral duties — including those applied to specific non-USMCA goods, steel and vehicles — that were already set at 10% and therefore will essentially be unchanged.

There is a possibility that Mexico could be subject to an “excess capacity” tariff — an obscure provision of a 1930 trade law that applies to countries that “put undue burdens on U.S. imports.” This is likely to be addressed during ongoing USMCA negotiations.

The new U.S. tariffs seek to address what the Trump administration claims are unfair trade practices in an effort to restore some of the rates struck down by the Supreme Court.

The USTR conducted investigations seeking to establish that some countries had failed to take steps to curb forced labor, with the alleged worst offenders now facing a 12.5% tariff rate. However, the forced-labor compliance requirements do not affect Mexico, Ebrard said.

Sheinbaum reiterated this news during her Friday morning press conference.

“All products we exported within the USMCA have zero tariffs, with the exception of steel, some vehicles and products exported outside the treaty,” she said. “Mexico remains exactly the same as we were a week ago.”

The US Trade Representative’s Mexico City agenda

In addition to meeting with Sheinbaum, Greer was in Mexico City to participate in bilateral talks as part of the ongoing review of the USMCA.

Greer and Ebrard discussed topics ranging from steel and aluminum and derivative products, automobiles, economic security, labor, agriculture and electronic payment services.

Sheinbaum said her meeting with Greer served as “an assessment of how far the talks have come, to learn more about what the U.S. is proposing, and to consider the timeline.”

With reports from El Economista, El Financiero and Atlantic Council

World.title: 900 more troops arrive in Mazatlán after a series of targeted attacks
World.content:
A contingent of 900 Mexican Army troops arrived in the early hours of Thursday at the port of Mazatlán, Sinaloa, as part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks in recent weeks.

City Clerk Moisés Ríos Pérez said the newly arrived soldiers bring the total number of troops for the enhanced security operations to more than 1,300.

Ríos explained that the Public Security and Defense Ministries, and other authorities involved in daily security meetings, are working on accommodating the new troops before defining their operational deployment.

“Nine hundred arrived at midnight yesterday; we are struggling to relocate them at the moment,” Ríos told local media. “But we’re hoping that with this new number we can now deploy them throughout the municipality . . . to prevent more [violence].”

The security reinforcement, a joint effort among federal, state and municipal authorities, comes in response to a surge in violence that has marked the start of the summer holiday season in the port city and tourist destination.

Between July 12 and 18, local media reported Mazatlán recorded seven homicides and one femicide, in addition to a shooting and suspected explosive attack on a home. On July 17 and 18 alone, six armed attacks were reported in less than 24 hours, leaving four dead and three wounded. Days later, between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered in less than a day.

Investigations by the State Attorney General’s Office (FGE) are underway to clarify the homicides and to identify the victims and the perpetrators.

The climate of violence stems from the conflict between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel following the arrest and extradition two years ago of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, the former leader of the criminal organization.

Since September 2024, Mazatlán has been the scene of armed attacks, kidnappings, disappearances, and murders.

Some of the new personnel will be stationed in areas such as Germán Evers and Urías, while another group will guard the federal highways leading to Durango and Nayarit. The effort aims to protect both residents and tourists arriving at the destination during peak season.

With reports from Infobae, Noroeste and Los Noticeristas

World.title: Sheinbaum touts improved security perception amid 54% drop in Morelos homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🎤 Cuernavaca cabinet meeting: Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos.

Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos. 📊 Security perception improves: INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December.

INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December. 🚨Temoac mayor murder: Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday.

Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday. 📰 Oaxaca journalist killing: Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family.

Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family. ⚖️ Ruffo arrest not political: Sheinbaum denied persecution claims over ex-Baja California governor Ernesto Ruffo’s arrest, tying it to a 12-month fuel theft probe involving his company, Ingemar.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Cuernavaca, the capital of the state of Morelos, continuing a practice begun in January of holding regional Security Cabinet meetings on the road to highlight local challenges.

Located just south of Mexico City, Morelos is the third-smallest entity in the republic, with a population of just under 2 million residents.

Morelos is grappling with corruption and organized crime challenges, though murder rates have dropped by 54% since Governor Margarita González was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024 (the same day Sheinbaum took office).

Officials credited Plan Morelos — a joint federal-state security strategy implemented in April — and state-level efforts for reducing high-impact crimes across the state.

President touts improving public perception of security

Sheinbaum highlighted improvement in the public perception of security as reflected in the quarterly survey conducted by the national statistics agency INEGI, saying the results indicate that the public is noticing the advancements her government is making.

So far this year, Mexicans’ perception of insecurity dropped in both the first and the second quarter.

INEGI reported that 63.8% of those surveyed felt unsafe in their city in December, while 61.5% said they felt unsafe in March. That number fell to 59.8% in the latest survey.

The president acknowledged that perception sometimes changes gradually, often depending on whether one or one’s family have been victims of a crime.

“But it also depends on what you hear or read,” she said. “The important thing is that we are delivering results … and the population sees that.”

Federal authorities take over two high-profile murder cases

In stark juxtaposition to the public perception survey, Sheinbaum and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch offered updates on the investigations into Wednesday’s shocking murders.

With regard to the murder of Valentín Lavín Moreno, the mayor of Temoac (just 80 kilometers east of Cuernavaca), Harfuch said federal agents are working closely with Morelos prosecutors “to clarify the events and apprehend those responsible.”

Harfuch added that Lavín, who was shot to death in his City Hall office, was under investigation for possible links to two local crime groups. Lavín’s in-laws were arrested on Thursday, accused of having ties to organized crime.

A few hours before the tragic events in Temoac, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot to death in the state of Oaxaca.

Federal prosecutors have taken over the case at the request of the Oaxaca authorities, Harfuch said, declining to elaborate further.

Sheinbaum has directed Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez to meet with Leyva’s family and will also consult with journalists. “We have committed to several meetings in hopes of reassuring them that impunity will not be permitted,” Rodríguez said.

Sheinbaum denies Ruffo arrest linked to politics

In response to a question regarding opposition figures accusing the Sheinbaum administration of political persecution, the president denied that federal prosecutors are targeting political opponents.

Addressing the recent arrest of former Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo — a member of the National Action Party (PAN) — Sheinbaum said Ruffo was ensnared in a 12-month fuel theft investigation in which eight others were arrested.

“[Ruffo] is the primary shareholder [of Ingemar, the company accused of criminal activity], but he was not the ‘target’ … and the investigation is ongoing,” she said, adding that any others found to be involved will be pursued equally.

Sheinbaum said the investigation seeks to prove that Ingemar was illegally importing fuel (and evading taxes) and was fraudulently distributing it. “This has nothing to do with politics,” she said.

With reports from Milenio and Infobae

World.title: El Nigromante Exhibitions in Mexico End Soon—Free Entry
World.content:
San Miguel de Allende · Culture

Key Facts —Three shows. Temporary exhibitions by Ana Thiel, Mauricio Palos, and Jesús Martínez Carrión are in their final weeks. —Closing dates. The shows end on 2 August, 8 August, and 16 August 2026 respectively. —Free admission. Entry to all three exhibitions costs nothing. —Opening hours. Tuesday through Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00. —Permanent murals. Visitors can also see works by Siqueiros, Eleanor Cohen, and Pedro Martínez on the same trip.

Three distinct El Nigromante exhibitions enter their final weeks this August, offering a last chance to see contemporary glasswork, documentary photography, and a century of Mexican illustration inside one of San Miguel de Allende’s most important cultural landmarks.

El Nigromante (Bellas Artes), San Miguel de Allende (Photo: Francisco Navarro Ledesma, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

A Trio Of Shows Nears Its End

The Centro Cultural Ignacio Ramírez “El Nigromante,” operated by Mexico’s Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL), is hosting three temporary summer exhibitions. All three close during August 2026, giving visitors a narrow window to catch them.

The exhibitions span contemporary art, documentary photography, and illustration. Each occupies a distinct gallery space inside the historic former convent on Hernández Macías street.

Ana Thiel’s “Anhelos Compartidos” Closes First

The first to close is “Anhelos compartidos” by Ana Thiel, on view in the Sala de Arte Mexicano. Its final day is Saturday, 2 August 2026.

Thiel is known for her work in glass, a medium she pushes far beyond the decorative. Her pieces explore transparency, fragility, and the layered nature of memory, making the show a quiet but technically striking entry in the summer programme.

Mauricio Palos Documents “Where The Earth Remains”

“Donde la tierra permanece. De la selva a la Luna” by Mauricio Palos closes on 8 August 2026.

The exhibition brings together photography and visual art that traces connections between landscapes, communities, and the marks people leave on the land.

Palos has built a career documenting social and environmental stories across Latin America. This body of work moves from dense jungle to the stark imagery of lunar exploration, offering a meditation on territory and belonging that resonates with San Miguel’s own complex relationship between tradition and change.

Jesús Martínez Carrión: A Century Of Mexican Line

The final El Nigromante exhibitions to close is “Jesús Martínez Carrión. De la ilustración a la caricatura,” ending its run on 16 August 2026.

The show surveys the career of a prolific illustrator and caricaturist whose work spans decades of Mexican publishing.

Martínez Carrión’s line work captures political satire, literary illustration, and social commentary with equal fluency. For visitors interested in Mexico’s rich tradition of graphic arts, this is the standout of the three.

The Permanent Collection: Siqueiros And More

A visit to see the temporary shows also grants access to El Nigromante’s permanent murals, which are worth the trip on their own. The centrepiece is a mural by David Alfaro Siqueiros, one of the titans of Mexican muralism alongside Rivera and Orozco.

Two additional murals round out the permanent route: one by Eleanor Cohen, which includes the well-known scene “Las Lavanderas,” and another by Pedro Martínez. Together they offer a compact but powerful survey of Mexican mural tradition inside a single building.

What This Means For San Miguel’s Cultural Pull

San Miguel de Allende has long traded on its cultural capital as much as its colonial architecture. Free, professionally curated exhibitions at an INBAL-run centre reinforce the city’s position as a genuine arts destination, not merely a picturesque backdrop for destination weddings.

For the large expat and investor community in the city, a thriving cultural scene underpins property values and quality of life. A steady calendar of exhibitions like these signals institutional investment in the arts that goes beyond the private galleries catering to tourist buyers.

Practical Details For A Late-Summer Visit

El Nigromante is located at Hernández Macías 75, in the heart of San Miguel’s historic centre. The centre is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00, and admission to all three temporary exhibitions is free.

Visitors aiming to catch all three should plan their trip before 2 August, when the Thiel show closes first. Those arriving later in the month can still see the Palos and Martínez Carrión exhibitions before they close on 8 August and 16 August respectively.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do the El Nigromante exhibitions close in 2026?

Ana Thiel’s “Anhelos compartidos” closes on 2 August 2026. Mauricio Palos’s “Donde la tierra permanece” closes on 8 August 2026.

Jesús Martínez Carrión’s exhibition closes on 16 August 2026.

Is there an admission fee for the exhibitions at El Nigromante?

No. Entry to all three temporary exhibitions is free of charge.

The centre is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00.

Can I see the Siqueiros mural during the same visit?

Yes. The permanent murals by David Alfaro Siqueiros, Eleanor Cohen, and Pedro Martínez are accessible during regular opening hours alongside the temporary exhibitions, at no extra cost.

World.title: Santiago Winter Weekend: Soup, Coffee & Vinyl, July 25–26
World.content:
LIFE: SANTIAGO DE CHILE

Key Facts —Soup Festival. A free-entry winter soup festival runs Saturday 25 and Sunday 26 July at MUT in Las Condes. —Coffee Expo. ExpoCafé Chile 2026 brings over 170 exhibitors to Espacio Riesco from 24 to 26 July. —Vinyl Fairs. Recurring vinyl record fairs operate at Centro Arte Alameda and Antonella Bar in Las Condes that weekend. —Wine Expo. Expo CAV 2026, with more than 50 Chilean wineries, closes its public day on Saturday 25 July at the same venue. —Snow Options. Valle Nevado, El Colorado and La Parva ski centres sit less than 50 kilometres from the city.

A Santiago winter weekend on 25 and 26 July offers indoor refuge with a free soup festival, a major coffee expo and vinyl record fairs across the city.

Santiago, Chile

Soup takes centre stage at MUT

The Festival de la Sopa sits inside the larger Mercado de Invierno at MUT, Avenida Apoquindo 2730, Las Condes. Entry is free and the event runs from 10:00 to 19:00 on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can expect classic Chilean soups, vegan options and international recipes alongside stalls from local producers. The winter market also features artisanal foods and seasonal products, making it a practical stop for expat families and professionals looking to fill a cold afternoon.

MUT itself has become a draw for the Las Condes business crowd. The mixed-use development houses offices, retail and gastronomy, so the soup festival doubles as a low-commitment weekend outing for residents and visitors already in the financial district.

ExpoCafé Chile 2026 draws the specialty-coffee crowd

ExpoCafé Chile 2026 opens at Espacio Riesco, Avenida El Salto 5000, Huechuraba, from 24 to 26 July. Organisers expect roughly 25,000 attendees and have confirmed more than 170 exhibitors.

The three-day fair covers the full specialty-coffee chain: roasters, baristas, equipment makers and training workshops. For investors tracking Chile’s consumer market, the scale signals how far specialty coffee has moved from niche to mainstream in the capital.

Tastings and talks run throughout the weekend. The event is fully indoors, which matters in a Santiago winter when temperatures routinely drop below 5°C and rain can disrupt outdoor plans.

Vinyl fairs keep Santiago’s analogue music scene alive

No single mega-fair is confirmed exclusively for 25–26 July, but Santiago’s recurring vinyl circuit is active. The Feria del Vinilo at Centro Arte Alameda, Avenida Libertador Bernardo O’Higgins 139, offers free entry and regular weekend programming.

A second option is the Feria Casa Disco at Antonella Bar, Avenida Apoquindo 7709, near the Los Dominicos metro station. Both events combine record sales with music programming, drawing collectors, DJs and curious newcomers.

Vinyl culture in Santiago has grown steadily over the past five years, with dedicated shops and fairs multiplying in Providencia, Ñuñoa and Las Condes. For expats, these fairs are a low-cost way to plug into local cultural life without needing fluent Spanish.

Wine, classical music and Japanese pop culture fill out the Santiago winter weekend

Expo CAV 2026, a wine fair with more than 50 Chilean wineries, closes its public day on Saturday 25 July at Espacio Riesco. That means visitors can pair the coffee expo with a wine tasting in the same venue on the same day.

A free classical-music concert by the Orquesta Sinfónica Juvenil de Puente Alto plays Saturday at 17:00 at Parroquia Santa Filomena, Santa Filomena 315. The programme features Beethoven and Rossini, and the setting is indoors.

For a completely different register, the Rainbow Decora Fest lands at Fundación Cultural Casa de los Diez, Avenida Santa Rosa 179, on Saturday. The event focuses on Japanese Harajuku fashion and Decora style, drawing a young, creative crowd.

Snow and hot springs for those who want to leave the city

Ski centres Valle Nevado, El Colorado and La Parva sit within 50 kilometres of Santiago and are fully operational in late July. Farellones offers a lower-altitude snow-play option for families with young children.

Cajón del Maipo and the Termas de Colina hot springs are reachable in roughly 80 to 90 minutes by car. The combination of snow-capped peaks and thermal pools has made the Cajón a staple day trip for Santiago-based expats and tourists.

Back in the city, ice-skating rinks at Parque Araucano and Parque Bustamante operate throughout the winter in one-hour blocks. The Nievinfest at Ciudad Empresarial adds artificial snow and night-time snow shows for those who prefer a managed winter experience.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the soup festival at MUT free to enter?

Yes. The Festival de la Sopa and the Mercado de Invierno at MUT are both free-entry events.

They run from 10:00 to 19:00 on Saturday 25 and Sunday 26 July at Avenida Apoquindo 2730, Las Condes.

Where is ExpoCafé Chile 2026 and how much does it cost?

ExpoCafé Chile 2026 takes place at Espacio Riesco, Avenida El Salto 5000, Huechuraba, from 24 to 26 July. Ticket prices vary by day and access level; visitors should check the official ExpoCafé Chile channels for current pricing and workshop fees.

Are there vinyl record fairs in Santiago on 25 and 26 July?

Yes. Recurring vinyl fairs operate that weekend at Centro Arte Alameda (Avenida Libertador Bernardo O’Higgins 139) and at Antonella Bar in Las Condes (Avenida Apoquindo 7709).

Both offer free entry and are accessible by metro.

World.title: Italian Restaurant Rooftop Planned for Downtown São Paulo
World.content:
São Paulo Gastronomy

Key Facts —The partnership. Entrepreneur Facundo Guerra and chef Jefferson Rueda are collaborating on a new Italian restaurant in downtown São Paulo. —The location. The venue will occupy the rooftop of Edifício Virgínia, in the city’s historic Centro district. —The concept. Italian cuisine will be filtered through Argentine and Brazilian cultural influences, reflecting Guerra’s dual heritage. —The timeline. Opening is forecast for after next year’s Carnival, placing it roughly in March or April 2026. —Guerra’s debut. This marks Facundo Guerra’s first restaurant project, after building a career around high-profile bars and cultural venues.

A new Italian restaurant downtown São Paulo is taking shape on the rooftop of Edifício Virgínia, bringing together nightlife entrepreneur Facundo Guerra and celebrated chef Jefferson Rueda for a project that deepens the Centro district’s gastronomic revival.

São Paulo dining

A First Restaurant for a Nightlife Impresario

Facundo Guerra has spent years shaping São Paulo’s nocturnal landscape through venues such as Love Cabaret, Bar dos Arcos, and Formosa Hi-Fi. Yet the Italian restaurant downtown São Paulo he is now planning represents a departure: it will be his first proper restaurant.

Guerra was born in Argentina and has long described himself as a paulistano by choice. That dual identity informs the concept, which promises Italian cooking refracted through Argentine and Brazilian sensibilities rather than a straight reproduction of a trattoria.

Jefferson Rueda Brings Culinary Weight to the Italian Restaurant Downtown São Paulo

Jefferson Rueda is one of Brazil’s most recognised chefs, best known for A Casa do Porco, the downtown restaurant that has appeared on Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants list and drawn global attention to São Paulo’s Centro. His portfolio also includes Bar da Dona Onça, Hot Pork, and Sorveteria do Centro.

Rueda is no stranger to Italian cooking. Earlier in his career he explored what he called “ítalo-caipira” cuisine at Attimo and Pomodori, blending Italian technique with ingredients from the São Paulo countryside.

That experience makes him a logical fit for a project that promises Italian food with a South American accent.

Edifício Virgínia and the Centro Revival

The choice of Edifício Virgínia places the Italian restaurant downtown São Paulo squarely within a neighbourhood that has been slowly reclaiming its place on the city’s dining map. A Casa do Porco itself helped prove that a neglected corner of Centro could become a destination, drawing diners from across the metropolitan region.

A rooftop setting adds a layer of ambition. São Paulo’s skyline is vast and often underused from a hospitality standpoint, and a well-executed rooftop venue can command premium pricing while offering an experience that ground-floor restaurants cannot match.

What the Project Signals for São Paulo’s Hospitality Market

São Paulo’s restaurant sector has shown resilience through Brazil’s recent economic cycles, with high-end openings continuing even as broader consumer spending fluctuates. A project pairing Guerra’s brand-building skill with Rueda’s culinary credibility is likely to attract both local food enthusiasts and the international visitors who pass through Latin America’s largest city.

For investors and expats watching Brazil’s consumer market, the venture is a data point suggesting confidence in downtown real estate and in diners’ willingness to spend on experiences. It also reinforces a pattern of established operators doubling down on Centro rather than decamping to the Pinheiros or Jardins neighbourhoods that have dominated recent openings.

What We Still Do Not Know

No official name has been announced for the Italian restaurant downtown São Paulo, and the precise opening date remains vague beyond the “after Carnival” window. That suggests a launch sometime in March or April 2026, though construction and licensing timelines in central São Paulo can shift.

Menu details are also absent from early reports. The broad strokes — Italian cuisine, Argentine and Brazilian cultural references — leave room for anything from handmade pastas with chimichurri to wood-fired dishes that draw on Rueda’s deep knowledge of pork and fire cooking.

The Read-Through for Latin America Watchers

São Paulo’s gastronomy scene functions as a bellwether for discretionary spending and urban regeneration trends across Latin America. When operators of Rueda’s calibre commit to a neighbourhood, property values and ancillary businesses — wine shops, boutique hotels, specialty coffee — tend to follow.

The Guerra-Rueda partnership also illustrates a broader Latin American pattern: the blurring of lines between nightlife, culture, and dining. Guerra’s background in bars and music venues, combined with Rueda’s kitchen, points toward a space that may function as more than a place to eat — a model that has proven durable in cities from Mexico City to Buenos Aires.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Facundo Guerra and Jefferson Rueda’s Italian restaurant open?

The restaurant is forecast to open after next year’s Carnival, which places the likely launch in March or April 2026. No exact date has been confirmed, and construction timelines in downtown São Paulo can shift.

Where exactly is the new Italian restaurant downtown São Paulo located?

The restaurant will occupy the rooftop of Edifício Virgínia, in São Paulo’s Centro district. This is the same general area that houses A Casa do Porco, Jefferson Rueda’s flagship restaurant, which helped transform the neighbourhood into a dining destination.

What kind of food will the Guerra-Rueda restaurant serve?

The concept is Italian cuisine with cultural influences from Argentina and Brazil, reflecting Facundo Guerra’s Argentine heritage and Jefferson Rueda’s experience with Italian-Brazilian cooking. A detailed menu has not yet been released.

World.title: Suriname Picks Zoureena Rijger for Crop Over Festival 2026
World.content:
Caribbean Cultural Diplomacy

Key Facts —The Representative. Zoureena Rijger, Miss Suriname 2009 and a well-known media personality, will represent Suriname at the festival. —The Event. The Barbados Crop Over Festival 2026 runs from 3 to 9 August, culminating in the Grand Kadooment Day parade. —Cultural Lineage. Rijger is the youngest daughter of the late Surinamese singer and composer Lex Rijger, a towering figure in the country’s musical history. —Regional Context. The invitation underscores a quiet push to deepen cultural and tourism links between South America’s Caribbean coast and the island nations. —The Economic Angle. Crop Over is Barbados’s single largest tourism driver, generating significant foreign-exchange inflows each summer.

Suriname’s Zoureena Rijger will carry her country’s colours to the Barbados Crop Over Festival 2026, a move that signals fresh cultural and tourism ambition between the South American nation and the Eastern Caribbean.

Crop Over, Barbados (Photo: Dan, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

A Familiar Face Takes the Regional Stage

Zoureena Rijger is no stranger to the spotlight. She won the Miss Suriname crown in 2009 and has since built a steady career as a media personality in Paramaribo.

Her selection for Crop Over 2026 places a recognisable Surinamese figure inside one of the Caribbean’s most-watched cultural gatherings. Organisers typically invite regional representatives to strengthen the festival’s pan-Caribbean identity.

Rijger also carries a deep musical lineage. She is the youngest daughter of Lex Rijger, the celebrated Surinamese singer and composer whose work shaped the country’s modern sound.

For readers unfamiliar with Suriname’s cultural landscape, Lex Rijger is not simply a nostalgic name. He is widely regarded as a foundational artist who blended Surinamese folk traditions with Caribbean and Latin influences, helping to define a national musical identity in the decades after independence.

That heritage gives Zoureena Rijger’s presence at Crop Over a symbolic weight beyond her own public profile. She arrives not just as a former beauty queen and broadcaster, but as a living link to a revered artistic dynasty.

What the Crop Over Festival 2026 Actually Is

The Barbados Crop Over Festival traces its roots to the 1780s, when plantation workers celebrated the end of the sugar cane harvest. Today it is a multi-week summer spectacle of calypso, soca, masquerade, and street parties.

The 2026 edition is scheduled for 3 to 9 August. The final day, Grand Kadooment, draws tens of thousands of revellers in elaborate costumes for a road march that effectively shuts down the island.

For Barbados, the festival is not merely tradition. It is the anchor of the summer tourism season, filling hotels, villas, and Airbnbs and generating critical foreign-currency revenue.

To understand its scale, it helps to know that Crop Over is not a single event but a season. It typically begins weeks earlier with calypso competitions, folk concerts, and craft markets, building steadily toward the Grand Kadooment climax.

The festival’s modern revival began in the 1970s, and it has since grown into Barbados’s signature cultural export, drawing visitors from across the Caribbean, North America, and Europe.

Suriname’s Quiet Caribbean Play

Suriname sits on South America’s northeastern shoulder, culturally more Caribbean than Latin in its coastal zone. Yet its diplomatic and economic ties have historically tilted toward the Netherlands and its immediate neighbours, Guyana and French Guiana.

Sending a former Miss Suriname to Crop Over is a low-cost, high-visibility gesture. It signals Paramaribo’s interest in weaving itself more tightly into the Eastern Caribbean’s cultural and tourism economy.

For regional investors, these soft-power moves matter. They often precede airlift negotiations, joint marketing agreements, and the kind of people-to-people familiarity that underpins cross-border business.

Suriname’s position is unusual in South America. Dutch is the official language, and the population includes descendants of African slaves, Indian and Javanese indentured labourers, and indigenous communities — a demographic mix that mirrors parts of the English-speaking Caribbean more than it does neighbouring Brazil or Venezuela.

That shared cultural DNA makes festivals like Crop Over a natural bridge. A Surinamese presence on the parade route is not an exotic novelty; it is a reminder of deep, often under-acknowledged, historical connections across the Caribbean Sea.

The Money Behind the Mas

Barbados does not publish a single official revenue figure for Crop Over, but industry estimates place the festival’s direct economic impact in the tens of millions of US dollars annually. Airlines add flights, and spending ripples through hospitality, retail, and transport.

Suriname’s participation carries a modest price tag but offers outsized branding returns. A single well-placed cultural ambassador can generate media coverage across the Caribbean diaspora in North America and Europe.

For expat readers and frontier-market watchers, the takeaway is straightforward: the Caribbean’s cultural economy is integrating, and even small South American players are finding seats at the table.

The diaspora dimension is especially important here. Caribbean festivals function as powerful magnets for emigrant communities, who return home or attend diaspora events abroad, spending on travel, accommodation, and local services in the process.

What to Watch as August 2026 Approaches

The immediate question is whether Rijger’s role will be ceremonial or whether Suriname will mount a fuller presence — a band, a costume section, or a dedicated tourism activation.

Any move toward direct air links between Paramaribo and Bridgetown would be the real signal. Currently, travel between the two capitals requires a connection, usually via Trinidad or Panama.

For now, the announcement puts Suriname on the Crop Over map in a way it has not been before. That alone is worth the cost of a plane ticket and a costume.

Another open question is whether other South American nations with Caribbean coastlines — or significant Afro-Caribbean populations — will follow Suriname’s lead in seeking a formal presence at future editions of the festival.

Observers will also be watching for any joint tourism packages or cultural exchange agreements announced in the weeks surrounding the event, as these would signal that the gesture is part of a longer-term strategy rather than a one-off appearance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Zoureena Rijger and why was she chosen for Crop Over 2026?

Zoureena Rijger is a Surinamese media personality who won the Miss Suriname title in 2009. She is also the daughter of the late musical icon Lex Rijger.

Her public profile and cultural pedigree make her a natural choice to represent Suriname at a major Caribbean festival.

When exactly is the Barbados Crop Over Festival 2026?

The festival is scheduled for 3 to 9 August 2026. The climactic event, Grand Kadooment Day, falls at the end of that window and features the main costumed street parade.

What does Suriname gain from participating in Crop Over?

Participation raises Suriname’s visibility within the Caribbean tourism market and the wider diaspora. It is a soft-power investment that can pave the way for deeper cultural exchange, tourism promotion, and eventually direct air connections between Suriname and Barbados.

World.title: Flamenco Versions of Popular Songs Hit Uruguay’s Intimate Stages
World.content:
Arts & Culture | Uruguay

Key Facts —The Artists. Carmen Pi is a Uruguayan singer and pianist; Gonzalo Franco is a flamenco guitarist and composer. —The Collaboration. They perform live concerts reinterpreting popular Spanish-language songs with flamenco and folk influences. —The Format. Their shows use an intimate voice-and-guitar setup in small venues across Montevideo. —Franco’s Milestone. He released Libre, considered the first flamenco guitar album by a Uruguayan artist. —Pi’s Approach. She is known for cross-genre reworkings, including candombe versions of songs by The Beatles and Sting.

Two Uruguayan musicians are drawing audiences with intimate flamenco versions of popular songs, blending Spanish guitar traditions with Latin American classics in Montevideo’s small venues.

Montevideo, Uruguay
