World.title: Rhymes and resilience: Illest Morena raps her truth
World.content:
As she enters her fifth year, rapper Illest Morena now carries herself differently, molded by countless experiences that only a woman in a largely male-dominated space could have

Since 2021, female emcee Illest Morena has fought tirelessly for a seat at the table in the local hip-hop scene.

Back when she first started, she could only count the number of active Filipina rappers on one hand. But even when it appeared that the less competition there was, the better, it remained a big challenge for her and her fellow “femcees” to actually get people to listen.

It was Illest’s hunger (and outright audacity) as a newcomer that powered her through that — and it was precisely how she lured new listeners into her craft in the first place. There was a fearlessness that came with putting out every new song, and an intense desire to prove herself to the public early on.

“I wasn’t scared when I started. Ibang-iba ang gigil ng isang rookie. Kapag rookie ka (The grit of a rookie is totally different. When you’re a rookie), you don’t think about the consequences of what’s gonna happen. You don’t think about the outcome. You only think about the possibilities of the things you wanna do,” she told Rappler.

Now, she’s entering her fifth year in the industry with her head held high. She carries herself differently this time — with the consolation of knowing who she truly is despite what those around her may say, and a new air of confidence she got from towering over all the noise.

Silver linings

When it comes to public perception, rappers are often thought to have a steady sense of self-assurance. Many of them are seen as headstrong individuals who are unfiltered, and are able to easily tune out the hate they may get in return.

Illest is as outspoken as ever. It shows not just in her autobiographical approach to music, but in the views she expresses as a human being.

At the end of the day, however, she is a human being before anything else.

“A lot of people think that I don’t get hurt by the words they say kasi kita mo naman wala din silang preno magsalita sa akin eh. Feeling siguro nila hindi naman ako masasaktan or hindi ko naman mapapansin yun. But I internalized a lot of those words that they said about me and that they said to me. It took a lot of self-healing for me to get to the point where I kind of got immune na nga sa mga sinsasabi nila,” she confessed.

(A lot of people think I don’t get hurt by the words they say because they have no filter when they speak to me. They probably think I won’t get hurt or I won’t pay attention to what they say. But I internalized a lot of those words that they said about me and that they said to me. It took a lot of self-healing for me to get to the point where I kind of became immune to what they say.)

Now wise beyond her years, the Illest we see now was molded by countless experiences that only a woman in a largely male-dominated space could have.

There was a time when the Illest who was unafraid to pour out her deepest thoughts for everyone else to see appeared to have faltered.

“Later on in my career, when I reached some kind of traction, doon pumasok ‘yung pressure (that’s when the pressure came in) and being afraid to speak out, and being afraid of detractors. [There was] this pressure to look and seem perfect all the time. That was one of the fears I developed as I went on in the industry,” she admitted.

For a year, she had stopped releasing solo tracks, her public performances became limited, and her once steady social media presence dwindled, too.

“I wasn’t posting that much on social media because I gained weight. And being a female artist, part of your currency is your looks. And it hurt me because that time I realized that you guys were kind of just objectifying me. Are you guys really listening to my songs? Do you guys really like me for my talent? Or is it just because I look like this? Is it because I present myself this way?” she explained.

It was then an uphill battle for Illest to come to terms with loving herself no matter what form she came in — even if it meant having to fight hard to convince herself that she liked what she saw whenever she stood in front of the mirror.

“I’m still writing the same songs, the same message. What just changed was how I looked, and it hurt me. It offended me. But when I look in the mirror now, I can say to myself, ‘I’m proud of you no matter how you look. With your bed hair, kahit kakagising mo lang or wala kang ligo (even if you just woke up or haven’t showered), I am proud of myself no matter what happens.’”

It was tough, and Illest will be the first to admit that. Still, like the fighter she is, she learned to use it to her advantage. Instead of retreating and boxing herself in, she stood firmly and peeled her mask off for good.

“I think now, kaya lumalabas na lalo ‘yung personality ko sa (the reason why my personality comes out more on) social media and I’m being more active, is because I’ve kind of learned that lesson and I gained this newfound confidence that I never would’ve found if I didn’t gain weight or if I didn’t get these bashers on social media. No matter what they say, or no matter what I look like, this is me. I’m a baddie,” she added.

Two sides to Illest

When she’s not on stage, Illest Morena is Angelica Layague. Angelica is quiet, enjoys her own company, and appears to be a bit more reserved than the fierce performer that struts around the platform like she owns it.

“[There’s] this private version of me where I love journaling. I love scrapbooking. People don’t know that about me because they think that when they see me, I’m like a fighter. That’s what they see but they don’t know I love to do affirmations: ‘I am beautiful. I am great.’ And I like talking to myself sometimes. And they don’t see that. But when I go to TikTok, you guys see a little bit of that version of myself. I’m kind of funny and crazy.”

But when it comes time to get behind the mic, Illest Morena goes through a complete transformation. Once she’s surrounded by a crowd waiting to hear her spit bars, she emanates a sort of aura that can’t seem to be shaken. She attests that she gets it all from her fans.

“Masaya ako kapag nakikita ko talaga ‘yung mga fans. Sila ‘yung nagbibigay sa akin nung extra extroverted version of myself kasi nga ‘di ba, medyo mahiyain ako in real life, as Angelica, not as Illest Morena,” she told Rappler.

(I’m really happy when I see my fans. They bring out the extra extroverted version of myself because I’m quite shy as Angelica, not as Illest Morena.)

“But when I see their faces, it makes me wanna show out and show off so that they get their money’s worth when they pay for tickets.”

For five years and counting now, fans have come to love Illest’s signature flavor R&B and hip-hop — catchy, and deeply rooted in what’s personal to the artist. Her music has always been autobiographical, in the sense that it captures Illest in all her seasons, even the ones she’s long outgrown.

Play Video

The core of Illest’s artistry was what remained unchanged all these years. This time, though, her catalogue has taken on a new form, one that’s even more raw and vulnerable.

And in doing that, Illest has no regrets.

“I’d rather have people see me as I am than see me as something I’m not, and then they expect something from that version of me or that mask that I have or put me on a pedestal. I don’t like that,” Illest told Rappler.

Fueled by delusion

In year five, Illest is on a roll. She’s more grounded in her sense of self, and she’s achieving milestone after milestone to boot.

The 24-year-old “femcee” already has a long list of joint bangers to her name (think “Lagabog” feat. Skusta Clee and “Quickie” feat. Hev Abi to name a few) — and she’s determined to keep it coming.

She just never would have thought her next collaborator would be Apl.de.Ap, who not only knew her by name when they first met, but was well aware of Illest’s impact in the local music scene. When the Black Eyed Peas star reached out for a potential feature on an upcoming song, it was an instant “yes” for Illest.

“It felt like I had to live up to the first impression because he said he heard I was one of the best here. I don’t want him to think otherwise,” Illest shared in a mix of English and Filipino.

Then came “Wind It,” a summery, reggaeton-inspired track featuring Apl.de.Ap, Fana, and Illest herself.

Play Video

These opportunities don’t just get handed to Illest, though. They all come as a result of years of grit and — cliche as it sounds — unapologetic belief in yourself.

Illest, then, has this to say: “Be very delusional with your self-belief. And also, never let one mistake or a challenge bring you down. Because it’s just part of learning, part of growing, and part of upgrading into this better version of you.”

That’s Illest Morena for you. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s SONA 2026
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City.

The situation is markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule.

This year, as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year.

How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for crackdown on flood control corruption?

World.title: AI agent spent days hacking, but sources say OpenAI didn’t notice for a week
World.content:
WASHINGTON, US – The OpenAI agent that broke into tech firm Hugging Face went on a dayslong hacking spree that OpenAI didn’t notice until well after the threat was contained and the FBI was alerted, according to people familiar with the investigation.

The agent – a program capable of making decisions and executing complex tasks with little or no human oversight – attempted to break out of its isolated testing environment at OpenAI around July 9, according to two of the people.

The intrusion at Hugging Face, which operates as a repository for AI tools and models, began two days later on July 11 and lasted until July 13, said Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face’s co-founder.

It took several more days for OpenAI to realize its agent was behind the hack, and the two companies only communicated about it for the first time on or around July 20, according to Wolf and three of the people familiar with the investigation.

OpenAI’s public disclosure, on July 21, that one of its agents had slipped out of control and carried out the break-in at Hugging Face drew global attention. But many details of the hack, including how long the agent went rogue and OpenAI’s belated knowledge of it, are being reported here for the first time.

Hugging Face is preparing a public timeline of the hack, Wolf said, adding that he could not speak to what happened at OpenAI. In a statement, OpenAI said the hack was unprecedented and “marks an important moment for AI safety.” It added that it was reviewing the incident with outside advisers and would eventually publish a technical report.

A spokeswoman said there were “several inaccuracies” in Reuters’ reporting but didn’t respond when asked to describe them.

The FBI declined to comment about the incident.

The incident, which evoked science fiction scenarios about humans losing control of dangerous AI systems, comes at a delicate time for OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Its executives are preparing for a possible initial public offering that could come as soon as this year to help finance the billions needed to fund its growth in years to come.

OpenAI’s loss of control over its AI agent raises new questions about the company’s safety procedures, three cybersecurity experts said.

“Does that mean that they left it unattended and didn’t realize what it was doing? Or maybe they did and didn’t know how to contain it? Both are equally dangerous and alarming,” asked Marley Smith, the principal intelligence specialist at the nonprofit World Ethical Data Foundation.

Signs of trouble?

The episode started while OpenAI was testing the cybersecurity prowess of an agent powered by two of OpenAI’s most advanced models, GPT‑5.6 Sol and an unreleased model OpenAI has described as “even more capable.” By that point, there were already indications of strange behavior from OpenAI’s technology, according to three sources.

In one case, an agent left notes apparently for future versions of itself, according to three people familiar with the matter. The notes, found in a part of OpenAI’s infrastructure, laid out instructions for how agents could free themselves from OpenAI’s internal constraints, the people said. Earlier tests of the models yielded cases in which monitoring systems had been disconnected, one of the people said.

Reuters could not establish if these incidents were linked to the rogue agent that began escaping on July 9 and attacked Hugging Face on July 11.

Two people familiar with the matter said that it was not until after Thursday, July 16, when Hugging Face published a blog post saying it had been hacked by “an autonomous AI agent system,” that OpenAI realized its own agent was responsible. That meant at least a week elapsed between when the model first exhibited signs of troubling behavior and OpenAI’s realization that it was responsible for the hack.

The weekend of July 18 to 19, OpenAI staffers spotted clues in internal logs — records of what OpenAI’s systems did — showing that its agent had escaped from its testing constraints, two of the people familiar with the company’s investigation said. Reuters could not establish what prompted OpenAI to sift through the logs.

Four people familiar with OpenAI’s model-training practices say the company often runs several different model evaluations at the same time, all of which operate at high speeds and generate such enormous amounts of data that employees sometimes struggle to keep up.

By the time OpenAI alerted Hugging Face, the AI library had already called the FBI to report the hack, according to a person familiar with the matter. Reuters could not establish whether the bureau had opened an investigation.

New questions about autonomous agents

Autonomous agents are one of the most talked about aspects of the AI industry. Boosters speak of creating armies of virtual employees that work 24 hours a day and send productivity soaring.

But increased autonomy comes with an increased risk of unexpected behavior, and the powerful models they draw on are primed to take shortcuts in order to complete tasks or pass tests.

“The models lie, they cheat, they hack,” said Jeffrey Ladish, whose organization, Palisade Research, studies the capabilities and motivations of AI agents.

Ladish said that while the hack of Hugging Face cast an unflattering light on OpenAI, it should spark broader questions over how much all the leading AI companies are willing to invest in onerous security measures while locked in a race with one another to deploy the best and fastest models.

“There has to be government oversight,” Ladish said, “because it won’t happen otherwise.” – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] From fugitives to courage, all that escapes the Marcos admin
World.content:
Gerald Bantag, Harry Roque, Atong Ang, Zaldy Co, and Bato dela Rosa. These are the high-profile fugitives that the Marcos administration has yet to arrest.

Almost every year, a fugitive hounds President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his administration.

The death of hard-hitting broadcaster Percy Lapid rocked Marcos’ “Bagong Pilipinas” promise in 2022. “Ka Percy,” as his fans called him, was a fearless radioman known for his fiery remarks against Marcos and former president Rodrigo Duterte.

He was killed in August 2022. The investigation led to the identification of the supposed mastermind: then-Bureau of Corrections chief Gerald Bantag.

Five months later, in April 2023, the courts issued warrants. While other suspects were nabbed, Bantag was slippery as an eel. The police failed to arrest him and he’s been hiding ever since.

Come 2024, Marcos’ biggest news in his State of the Nation Address was the ban on Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGO), which his predecessor Duterte had approved.

Among the biggest names implicated was Duterte’s former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque. In 2025, a local court issued a warrant against Roque for his alleged involvement in a raided POGO in Pampanga, but he was already abroad at the time.

Philippine authorities had cancelled his passport in a bid to deport him, but to no avail. Roque has a pending application for asylum in Europe and has yet to be arrested.

Play Video

Then there’s businessman Atong Ang, who was tagged as the alleged mastermind behind the disappearance of the missing sabungeros (cockfighting enthusiasts).

Ang, as early as 2022, was already part of the probe, but it took a bombshell testimony from his former right-hand man, Julie Patidongan, to pin him. The businessman is facing kidnapping with homicide and kidnapping with serious illegal detention cases, both non-bailable, as of January 2026.

Like the past two fugitives Bantag and Roque, Philippine authorities have yet to arrest Ang.

But who could forget arguably the two biggest fugitives under Marcos? Former congressman Zaldy Co and International Criminal Court (ICC) suspect Senator Bato dela Rosa.

Co is at the heart of the flood control corruption as the House’s former appropriations chief and for being the beneficial owner of contractor Sunwest. He is facing graft and malversation cases before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan.

Supposedly, Co was apprehended by authorities in the Czech Republic and Marcos announced this himself. After only a few days passed, the Marcos government cannot even disclose Co’s status after the supposed intervention.

Was Co released? Did he escape or what? Malacañang swept the Co apprehension story under the rug just like that.

Dela Rosa was in hiding for months since Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla announced that he had a pending warrant. He reappeared in May at the Senate, took custody there under the leadership of then-Senate president Alan Peter Cayetano.

The Duterte ally escaped from the upper chamber hours after a shooting incident allegedly instigated by his military academy classmate. In the days that Dela Rosa was staying at the Senate, the Marcos government refused to arrest him.

Then after he escaped, the Department of Justice announced a manhunt operation for the Senator.

Just like that, another person has been included in the list of roaming fugitives under Marcos.

Mr. President, these people are no ordinary citizens — they are high-profile individuals running from the wheels of justice. Their continued freedom not only shows lack of diligence from your administration’s part, but also political will.

Your administration had the time and energy to announce blow-by-blow developments at the height of these issues, but went radio silent when the investigation hit the wall or when people forgot about these fugitives.

Personally, I don’t forget these names, nor what they allegedly did. I have covered all these cases, as well as the victims on the other side of this story. The families longing for their loved ones, the people who were wronged.

It’s a disservice to give them a flicker of hope, then leave them hanging in the middle of their quest for justice. The country is facing so many problems right now, but do not forget that it’s also your responsibility to ensure peace and order.

A president also has the duty to ensure justice for everyone; exacting accountability even to the most powerful people of this land.

I know, it’s not that simple, but do something. There are two years left on your term.

Do not allow these fugitives to continue running from justice — and courage from escaping from you. Man up, Mr. Marcos. – Rappler.com

World.title: NGO sounds alarm on PH joining Pax Silica: Whose interest does it serve?
World.content:
PRE-SONA FORUM. The Center for People Empowerment in Governance (CenPEG) holds 'The Presidency and the People’s Trust: Governance, Accountability, and National Sovereignty' in partnership with the University of the Philippines College of Mass Communication on July 21, 2026.

'Let us reserve our natural resources and mineral resources for our own agricultural modernization and industries,' CenPEG director Bobby Tuazon says at their annual forum on the state of the presidency ahead of President Marcos' 5th SONA

MANILA, Philippines – Concerns about the Philippines’ participation in the Pax Silica initiative came into focus at a forum on the state of the presidency ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address on Monday, July 27.

The US-led initiative was among the issues discussed at the Center for People Empowerment in Governance’s (CenPEG) forum, “The Presidency and the People’s Trust: Governance, Accountability, and National Sovereignty,” held in partnership with the University of the Philippines College of Mass Communication on Tuesday, July 21.

CenPEG policy director Bobby Tuazon sounded the alarm on the Philippines’ participation in Pax Silica, a US-established program which the country joined in April.

“Pax Silica essentially serves American interest to define the US-led global tech and economic alliance to dominate supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and critical minerals designed to counter China’s dominance in technological manufacturing,” he said.

Semiconductors are among the Philippines’ top exports. They are also fundamental building blocks of artificial intelligence systems.

“This is a new structure that interlinks the Subic naval base where there is now a so-called technological hub, but actually an arms manufacturing depot run by the US, and then of course Clark, Manila, and Batangas,” Tuazon said, in reference to the proposed Luzon Economic Corridor, which aims to link the aforementioned areas through a freightway system.

Other concerns related to Pax Silica are water consumption, potential for mining activities, and the possible displacement of indigenous communities residing in the area.

Tuazon questioned the country’s foreign policy under Marcos: “Does the Philippines really have an independent foreign policy? I think many of us here would say right away that there’s no such thing. A foreign policy in theory should be dictated by national interest and nothing else. What we have is that foreign policy is dictated by American interest, particularly against China.”

For Tuazon, the Philippines should instead prioritize economic development, especially modern agriculture and basic industrialization.

“Let us reserve our natural resources and mineral resources for our own agricultural modernization and industries. These are the requisites we need to develop a truly free and independent foreign policy,” he said. – Isabel Victorino/Rappler.com

Isabel Victorino is Nation intern for Rappler. Dhe is a 4th year Communication student at the Ateneo de Manila University and a Features staffer at her school publication, The GUIDON.

World.title: IBON Foundation: Upper-middle income milestone doesn’t reflect Filipinos’ realities
World.content:
BIRDTALK MIDYEAR 2026. Executive Director Sonny Africa and Research Head Rosario Guzman share their insights on the country's economic situation during IBON Foundation’s Birdtalk Midyear 2026 at UP Diliman.

Despite the World Bank's recent upper-middle-income upgrade, think tank IBON Foundation warns that the country's income classification masks deeper structural weaknesses in employment, inequality, and industrial development

MANILA, Philippines – Ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fourth State of the Nation Address (SONA), IBON Foundation warned that the Philippines’ recent economic upgrade to upper-middle-income (UMIC) status masks the daily struggles of millions of Filipinos, calling the figure detached from reality during its Midyear Birdtalk on Wednesday, July 23 at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

IBON Foundation executive director Sonny Africa described the World Bank classification as a “mere statistical classification,” saying it masks deeper structural problems in employment, inequality, and industrial development.

“The growth model that resulted in the statistical reclassification can expand economic output, but is unable to create decent work with livable pay for the majority of Filipinos,” Africa said.

The Marcos administration has described the World Bank reclassification as a “vote of confidence” in its economic policies, a characterization that IBON disputed during the forum.

A ‘disguised crisis of joblessness’

While the government frequently highlights low official unemployment rates, IBON’s analysis indicated that employment has increasingly become a coping mechanism rather than a pathway out of poverty.

According to the group’s data, a staggering 78% of the workforce, about 38.7 million Filipinos, are trapped in “vast informality”. The think tank noted that this includes millions of self-employed individuals, unpaid family workers, and laborers in unregistered establishments enduring volatile working conditions.

UPPER-MIDDLE-INCOME. IBON Foundation presents Philippines’ position among upper-middle-income economies based on the World Bank’s 2025 gross national income (GNI) per capita classification during its Birdtalk Midyear 2026 forum at UP Diliman on Wednesday, July 23. Image from IBON Foundation

Although the country’s economic growth was enough to qualify it for UMIC, IBON stressed that the purchasing power of the working class has eroded, estimating that the average minimum wage is worth 21% less today than it was in 1989.

The group’s presentation showed that 14.4 million families, representing roughly 70 million Filipinos or 62% of the population, remain poor or low-income. This reality, IBON argued, contrasts sharply with the immense concentration of wealth at the top of the economic pyramid, driven by an exclusionary growth model that favors large conglomerates.

The decline of domestic production

IBON argued that these labor market conditions stem from the long-term weakening of the country’s productive sectors.

“It is critical to reverse agricultural decline, industrial erosion, and worsening technological dependence, with a determined program of rural development and Filipino industrialization that qualitatively transforms the economy’s producing structure,” Africa said.

According to them, instead of building local industries, the Philippines has undergone decades of deindustrialization. IBON’s data showed that manufacturing has dropped to just 17.4% of the country’s gross domestic product, its smallest share in 76 years, since 1949.

Meanwhile, the agricultural sector has shrunk to a historic low of 7.9%. The think tank asserted that this lack of a strong industrial and agricultural foundation is exactly why the economy struggles to generate high-quality, secure jobs, exposing the “exhaustion” of the country’s growth model.

GROWTH AND POVERTY. IBON Foundation presents data comparing annual GDP per capita with self-rated poverty. Image from IBON Foundation

Pax Silica and foreign-reliant development

IBON cited the US-led Pax Silica alliance as an example of the development model it argues has deepened the country’s dependence on foreign capital. The initiative aims to transform a portion of New Clark City into an AI-native “Economic Security Zone” anchored by foreign tech giants.

However, IBON also warned that without deliberate state intervention, such as binding requirements for technology transfer and local supplier development, these high-tech hubs will not lead to genuine Filipino industrialization.

“Mega-hyped efforts like the US-led Luzon Economic Corridor and Pax Silica will not deliver promised industrialization because these will be implemented under the same one-sided foreign investment regime that has held the economy back for decades,” Africa said.

Under proposed “joint governance” frameworks with the United States, IBON raised concerns that the Philippines may simply remain locked in a subordinate role within the global value chain. The think tank argued that the country risks merely supplying prime real estate, critical minerals, and cheap labor for foreign supply chains, while foreign corporations retain control over operations, technologies, and profits.

“There will likely be a lot of optimism during the SONA. But this will ring hollow because the Marcos administration is unable to deliver real economic reforms while the people’s conditions continue to worsen,” Africa said.

IBON argued that national development cannot be measured by gross national income (GNI) averages alone or achieved solely through foreign investment enclaves. Instead, the group said the country needs secure employment, stronger domestic agriculture and manufacturing, and economic growth that translates into tangible improvements in Filipinos’ lives.– Rappler.com

World.title: Still swinging: What’s next for Manny Pacquiao’s boxing career
World.content:
At 47, Manny Pacquiao does not plan to stop fighting anytime soon as the Filipino boxing icon eyes both professional and exhibition bouts, with the postponed rematch against Floyd Mayweather Jr. still in the cards

Father Time is undefeated, but Manny Pacquiao keeps resisting.

At 47, Pacquiao does not plan to stop fighting anytime soon — the Filipino boxing icon eyeing both professional and exhibition bouts through 2026 and 2027, with a long-awaited rematch against Floyd Mayweather Jr. still firmly on the agenda.

So what is next?

Top priority

According to Manny Pacquiao Promotions chief executive officer Jaspreet “Jas” Mathur, reviving the postponed Mayweather rematch is the priority.

Pacquiao and Mayweather, who first met in their blockbuster 2015 showdown, had agreed to face each other again in a professional fight scheduled for September to be streamed globally by entertainment giant Netflix.

A quick look at Netflix’s catalog shows the rematch remains on the platform’s schedule, but the fight has been postponed indefinitely due to legal and contractual disputes involving Mayweather’s camp.

“He has a long way to go. He’ll definitely be in a lot of exhibitions over the next few years but we ran into a little bit of a hiccup with the Mayweather fight that was initially planned for September of this year,” Mathur said of Pacquiao.

“Based of that, we didn’t entertain other exhibition offers that were there around. We’re also looking at the right partners to work for exhibitions, and then from there, also the right opponents for pro fight. There’ll be a lot of things coming up.”

“There’s a plan to have a fight for this year and then to roll into next year with the big fight.”

Mayweather has been embroiled in legal trouble after CSI Sports Events, which was contracted to produce the American’s exhibition against former world heavyweight champion Mike Tyson and rematch against Pacquiao this year, sued him for breach of contract.

CSI Sports Events claimed that Mayweather breached their agreement when he agreed to fight Greek kickboxer Mike Zambidis in an exhibition bout scheduled for June 27. The fight, however, never took place.

Mathur, though, said Mayweather was not to blame for the postponement of his rematch with Pacquiao.

“It’s just a very, very big mess and just a very complicated situation that was really caused by one person. For the record, this whole mess that happened is not really Floyd’s fault but we have to untangle it. There’s been a lot of work and his team is working, they’re doing what they need to do to untangle certain things,” said Mathur.

“Next year, 100 percent, it’s going to happen.”

By the time the rematch rolls around, however, Mayweather — who will turn 50 in February — and Pacquiao are far removed from the fighters who squared off in their 2015 clash famously dubbed the “Fight of the Century.”

The fight shattered revenue records by generating over $600 million, although the action in the ring proved underwhelming, with a defensive-minded Mayweather warding off Pacquiao to score a unanimous decision win and stay unbeaten.

Mayweather has fought professionally only twice since, beating Andre Berto in 2015 and Conor McGregor in 2017 to raise his record to 50-0 before retiring for the third time in his career.

For Mathur, having Pacquiao and Mayweather back in the ring together is still a sight to behold despite their age.

“Everybody wants to see Floyd and Manny one more time. That’s what’s going to break all records. That’s what’s going to be the most viewed event again in today’s era, in the streaming era,” he said.

“I think people are always going to be interested in watching that fight. These guys, they’re an anomaly, each one of them, whether Floyd or Manny. Age doesn’t really matter in that spectrum between these two. Everybody’s going to watch the fight. The people that say they’re not going to watch the fight are going to be the first ones to watch the fight.”

“Floyd’s not backing down from this, and neither is Manny.”

Do more

Pacquiao had drawn the curtains on his legendary career in 2021 following his unanimous decision loss to Cuban Yordenis Ugas in their title fight for the World Boxing Association welterweight belt.

But after back-to-back election setbacks that saw him lose in both the presidential and senatorial races in 2022 and 2025, respectively, Pacquiao came out of retirement last year to challenge Mexican-American Mario Barrios for the World Boxing Council welterweight title.

Then 46 years old, Pacquiao fell short in resetting his record as the oldest welterweight world champion as Barrios — who is 16 years younger — narrowly retained the belt by way of a majority draw.

Pacquiao, boxing’s only eight-division world champion, believes he has plenty of gas left in the tank, especially with a longer preparation period for a fight.

The campaign period for the 2025 elections ended in May, with Pacquiao taking on Barrios just a little over two months after in July.

“I can do more. I can do more than that. I can still feel like I can still fight and I’m strong because I’m [a] disciplined person, [with] the way I eat, everything like that,” Pacquiao told the Ring Magazine program Inside The Ring in April.

“To prepare is not two months or two and a half months. You need long preparation because you need your body to have rest during the heavy training days.”

Even now that he is a grandfather, Pacquiao makes sure to keep himself in form.

“At the age of 30-plus, 40-plus, your metabolism is becoming slower. Your recovery is not that easy compared before when you were young. What I discovered is you’re getting slower if you don’t handle it. But there’s a way that you can stay fit, stay in shape, [retain] speed. You can get that as long as you’re taking care of your body,” Pacquiao said.

Other prospects

When it comes to other professional fights for Pacquiao, Mathur said anything is possible.

Talks were in place for Pacquiao to face reigning WBA welterweight champion Rolly Romero early in 2026, but negotiations fell through.

Romero is now set to tangle with Teofimo Lopez in August for his first title defense.

“I actually wanted to put the Rolly fight together. That was my plan from the beginning. I was even talking about it last year because I’m with Manny already and Rolly’s also with me, in my company, Limitless. Rolly is also a dear friend. That’s a very direct situation. But Rolly’s fighting, he has another fight against Teo,” said Mathur.

Mathur also confirmed the possibility of Pacquiao locking horns with reigning WBC welterweight champion Ryan Garcia, who won the belt following a unanimous decision victory over Barrios in February.

Garcia, though, already has a fight lined up as he is set to defend his title against Conor Benn in September.

“Everyone’s on the table. It’s all on the table,” said Mathur.

But for Mathur, the goal is to bring the Pacquiao-Mayweather rematch into fruition.

“We have to focus on what’s in front of us right now,” he said. “We want to break records right now. That’s what we want to do.” – Rappler.com

World.title: E. Samar gov urges closer coordination to boost healthcare delivery
World.content:
Eastern Samar Gov. Ralph Vincent Evardone calls for stronger coordination among mayors, health officials and other stakeholders to overcome geographic and financial barriers to healthcare delivery during the 2026 Universal Health Care Summit.(Eastern Samar Provincial Information Office)

TACLOBAN CITY — Eastern Samar Governor Ralph Vincent Evardone has called for closer cooperation among mayors, health officials and other stakeholders to overcome the province’s geographic and financial challenges in delivering quality healthcare to its residents.

Speaking during the 2026 Universal Health Care Summit held on Friday, July 24, Evardone said the full implementation of the Universal Health Care Act remains a challenge in Eastern Samar, where many communities are located in remote mountainous areas and islands and where several local government units have limited financial resources.

He said the province’s geography continues to complicate the delivery of medical services, while smaller municipalities and barangays often lack the fiscal capacity to independently meet the healthcare requirements under the law.

Article continues after this 

“Part of UHC is having a unified system and strengthening our local government units’ efforts for preventive measures so that we can address common illnesses that Filipinos encounter,” Evardone said.

The governor stressed that a coordinated healthcare system, particularly in preventive medicine, primary care and patient referrals, is necessary to ensure that residents receive timely medical attention regardless of where they live.

“It is very important for us now, and I’m very happy that the municipal mayors are here so that we can have a direction for the province. We have a better referral system, we have better coordination with our local health units so that we can ensure that every Estehanon will have access to quality healthcare,” he said.

To strengthen the province’s healthcare system, the provincial government is undertaking a major rehabilitation of the Eastern Samar Provincial Hospital with a budget of P500 million.

It has also secured an additional P176 million for essential medical supplies, drugs and medicines for district hospitals.

Article continues after this 

Evardone said the provincial government is likewise increasing baseline funding for local medical facilities while seeking additional financial support from the Department of Health.

He urged mayors, doctors and other health stakeholders to share best practices and adopt strategies discussed during the summit to improve primary healthcare delivery and strengthen referral networks throughout the province.

Article continues after this 

The push for a more integrated healthcare system comes as Eastern Samar continues to face the challenge of providing essential services to geographically isolated and disadvantaged communities, making coordination among local governments and health facilities critical to the effective implementation of universal healthcare.

World.title: Rape suspect nabbed in Cavite yields shabu, unlicensed gun
World.content:
LUCENA CITY, Quezon – Police arrested a 42-year-old man facing a rape complaint and recovered suspected shabu (crystal methamphetamine) and an unlicensed firearm during an operation in Bacoor City, Cavite, on Friday.

The suspect, identified only by the alias “Randy,” was arrested by police operatives in Barangay Queensrow East on Friday afternoon, the Calabarzon police said in a report Saturday.

According to the police, the arrest stemmed from a complaint filed by a 16-year-old girl, accompanied by her mother, who alleged that the suspect raped her inside his house on June 24.

Article continues after this 

Authorities said the suspect allegedly resisted arrest but was eventually subdued by the arresting officers.

He sustained minor injuries during the incident.

The suspect allegedly yielded four heat-sealed plastic sachets containing suspected shabu with an estimated value of P13,600, as well as an unlicensed 12-gauge shotgun.

The suspect is now under police custody and is facing charges in connection with the rape complaint, as well as separate complaints for alleged violation of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 and the law on illegal possession of firearms.

World.title: Over P1.7 million shabu seized in Bicol operations; 15 arrested
World.content:
LEGAZPI CITY, Albay — Authorities arrested 15 drug suspects and recovered more than P1.7 million worth of “shabu” (crystal meth) in separate anti-illegal drug operations on Friday in the Bicol region.

In a belated report on Saturday, the Camarines Norte police said authorities arrested a 51-year-old woman identified as “Mylene” in a search operation at her residence in Barangay Tugos in Paracale town.

Recovered from the high-value target were 200 grams of shabu worth an estimated P1,360,000 and other drug-related paraphernalia.

Article continues after this 

In Barangay Palanas in the same town, a 33-year-old woman identified as “Rolan,” was arrested for selling shabu to an undercover agent at around 2:44 p.m.

Police recovered an estimated P61,000 worth of shabu from the suspect identified as a gold panner.

In Daet town, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency arrested three suspects in a dismantled drug den in Barangay Magang at around 1:23 p.m.

The authorities recovered some P81,600 worth of shabu, improvised tooters, lighters, improvised burners, water pipes, and rolled aluminum foil from the residence of the suspect identified as “Erol,” the drug den maintainer.

An initial report from the Daet police said the other two suspects identified as “Fedil” and “Dino” were visitors in the drug den.

Article continues after this 

In Iriga City, Camarines Sur, eight persons were also arrested in separate drug dens in Barangay San Francisco at around 1:46 p.m.

Authorities confiscated an estimated P224,800 worth of shabu and tools from the suspects.

Article continues after this 

In Albay, two suspects identified as “Mark”and “Ron” were arrested with P31,756 worth of shabu in a buy-bust operation in Guinobatan town at around 8:16 p.m..

The suspects are facing a formal complaint for violating the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. /gsg

World.title: Farmers’ group calls for genuine agrarian reform ahead of Marcos’ Sona
World.content:
File photo of farmers harvesting palay in Quezon province (Delfin T. Mallari Jr.)

LUCENA CITY, Quezon – A national peasant organization urged President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to go beyond calls for unity and translate his commitments into concrete measures to address the continuing struggles of Filipino farmers as he delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27.

“The true measure of this administration will not be the promises it makes from the podium, but whether it finally delivers justice, security, and dignity to agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs) and all those who feed the nation,” The Kilusan Para sa Tunay na Repormang Agraryo at Katarungang Panlipunan (Katarungan) said in a recent statement.

The group stressed that without genuine agrarian reform and social justice, government commitments would remain beyond the reach of the very farmers whose labor sustains the country.

Article continues after this 

Katarungan recalled that during Marcos’ fourth SONA following the 2025 midterm elections, he appealed to government officials to set aside political differences and focus on their common responsibility of serving the Filipino people.

The organization noted that Marcos had acknowledged public dissatisfaction over the government’s delivery of basic services despite reported economic gains.

The President also vowed that the remaining years of his administration would focus on improving the lives of Filipinos and fulfilling his government’s commitments.

“One year later, these commitments must be judged not by rhetoric, but by results,” Katarungan said.

The group said the administration’s commitment to farmers should be measured by how effectively it protects, completes, and implements agrarian reform while improving the conditions of rural communities.

Article continues after this 

(Photo of protest rally from Katarungan)

“For millions of ARBs and farmers, dignity cannot be measured by speeches or symbolism,” the organization said.

Instead, Katarungan said dignity means having secure and undisputed rights to the land they cultivate, protection against land grabbing and displacement, full use of awarded lands, fair prices for farm products, sufficient production and marketing assistance, climate resilience, and the ability to provide for their families through farming.

Article continues after this 

“These, not speeches or symbolism, are what give dignity to those who feed the nation,” the group emphasized.

Katarungan said that 38 years after the implementation of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program (CARP) in June 1988, the promise of comprehensive land reform remains largely unfulfilled for millions of Filipino farmers.

The group pointed out that many ARBs continue to experience delays in securing land ownership due to legal disputes, cancellation of land titles, landowner retention claims, land conversion efforts, and lengthy government processes that may take years or even decades to resolve.

It added that several farmers continue to face harassment, intimidation, violence, and legal battles that prevent them from fully exercising the land rights promised under agrarian reform.

The organization also criticized what it described as the failure of Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) Secretary Conrado Estrella III to engage directly and meaningfully with ARBs and farmers to address long-standing agrarian concerns.

“This stands in stark contrast to the considerable time devoted to producing and appearing in vlog-style content, which many have perceived as resembling early senatorial campaigning rather than the urgent discharge of official responsibilities,” Katarungan observed.

The group warned that unresolved land disputes, insecure land tenure, delayed justice, and weak government response continue to erode public confidence in the administration’s commitment to genuine agrarian reform and social justice.

Beyond land ownership, Katarungan stressed that many ARBs still struggle to make their farms productive due to inadequate government support services, high production costs, limited access to credit and infrastructure, low farmgate prices, and growing threats from climate change.

“Land ownership alone cannot uplift rural communities if the state fails to ensure that ARBs can make their lands productive and their livelihoods sustainable,” the group said.

The group concluded that for the country’s tillers of the soil who feed the nation, “a truly meaningful SONA is one that speaks honestly about these realities and commits to concrete action.

“The nation deserves more than carefully crafted words,” the organization said.

Photo of protest rally from Katarungan.

World.title: 2 dead, 1 wounded in Pangasinan gun attack
World.content:
CALASIAO, Pangasinan — Two male residents of Malasiqui died while a woman was wounded after unidentified gunmen opened fire on them late Saturday afternoon.

Local police identified the fatalities, aged 24 and 22, were both single and unemployed.

They and the female survivor are residents of Barangay Barang.

Article continues after this 

Initial investigation showed that the victims were hanging out along the roadside with other community members around 5:30 p.m. when a motorcycle with two riders pulled up in front of them.

The back rider alighted, pulled out a handgun, and repeatedly shot the victims.

Personnel from the Malasiqui Police Station are conducting follow-up operations to identify and arrest the perpetrators.

World.title: Former Vice Mayor Rex Mangubat: Dasmariñas City is for every Dasmarineño
World.content:
DASMARIÑAS CITY, Cavite – Former Dasmariñas City Vice Mayor Rex Mangubat has responded to criticisms questioning his decision to seek a congressional seat in the upcoming special election, saying that his gratitude to the late Congressman Elpidio “Pidi” Barzaga Jr. remains sincere and will never be forgotten.

He, however, stressed that gratitude should not be used to silence a person’s desire to offer the people an alternative or to suggest that Dasmariñas belongs to only one individual, name, or family.

“Nagpapasalamat ako sa pagkakataong makapaglingkod kasama si Cong. Pidi. Siya ang nagbukas ng pinto para mabigyan ako ng pagkakataong matuto, maglingkod, at makatulong sa Dasmariñas,” Mangubat said.

Article continues after this 

Mangubat said the years he spent serving alongside the late congressman helped shape him as a public servant.

“Marami kaming pinagdaanan at pinagsamahan sa serbisyo. Hindi iyon mabubura ng anumang eleksyon o pagkakaiba ng landas.”

But he clarified that the opportunity given to him was ultimately an opportunity to serve the people, not a lifelong obligation to remain politically loyal to one name or family.

“Ngunit ang paglilingkod-bayan ay hindi habambuhay na utang na loob. Ang pagkakataong ibinigay sa akin ay hindi para manatili akong tapat sa isang pangalan o pamilya. Iyon ay para paglingkuran ang bawat Dasmarineño.”

Mangubat emphasized that his candidacy should not be interpreted as a rejection of Pidi Barzaga’s legacy.

Article continues after this 

Instead, he described it as an effort to continue one of the most important lessons he learned in public service: that the people must always come first.

“Ang Dasmariñas ay pag-aari ng bawat Dasmarineño, hindi ng sinuman.”

Article continues after this 

“Hindi pagtataksil ang tumindig at mag-alok ng pagbabago. Karapatan ng bawat Dasmarineño ang malayang pumili.”

The Commission on Elections has estimated that approximately ₱200 million may be required to conduct the special election in Cavite’s Fourth Legislative District.

Mangubat said the considerable cost and significance of the electoral exercise should encourage a more meaningful public discussion centered on the qualifications, experience, independence, and concrete plans of every candidate.

He added that the election should not be reduced to questions of personal loyalty or political inheritance.

Ang tunay na serbisyo ay hindi nasusukat sa kung kanino ka nakasunod, kundi sa kung sino ang handa mong ipaglaban, lalo na kapag may kailangang baguhin.”

Mangubat said he remains grateful to Barzaga for opening the door that allowed him to enter public service. But he believes the next door must be opened by the people themselves.

“Binuksan ni Pidi ang pinto para sa akin. Ngayon, nais kong buksan ang mas malaking pinto para sa ating lahat: ang pagkakataong pumili ng alternatibo at magkaroon ng pagbabagong tunay na mararamdaman.”
